The root sic is in the sense of pouring or trickling. He pours. Pouring. They say 'ubhatobhāsa' (both voices/meanings).

## These are the forms of roots ending in 'ca'.

## Roots ending in 'cha'.

From here on, I will not explain the Parassapada nature etc. of all roots. Because that Parassapada nature etc. is not mentioned in the Teaching.
39:
The root chu is in the sense of cutting. Choti—cuts. 'Having cut the topknot perfumed with excellent scent' (Jātaka). 'O sirs, they have indeed cut down the tree' (Vessantara).

The root mileccha is in the sense of speaking words where syllables and consonants are not clear. Milecchati—speaks indistinctly. Milakkhu—a barbarian or mountaineer. 'He is reborn in the border regions among the Milakkhus (barbarians) who do not understand the Dhamma.'

The root vachi is in the sense of desiring. Vañchati—desires. Vañchitaṃ dhanaṃ—desired wealth.

The root achi is in the sense of pulling or stretching. Añcati—pulls, stretches. 'A turner pulling the string long knows "I pull long."' (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta).

The root huccha is in the sense of crookedness. Hucchati—is crooked.

The root muccha is in the sense of delusion or fainting. Mucchati—is deluded, faints. 'Being fainted due to the power of poison, he reached a state of unconsciousness.' Mucchā—fainting/delusion. Mucchitvā—having fainted.

The root phucha is in the sense of rubbing/shining. Phocchati—rubs/shines.

The root yucha is in the sense of negligence. Yucchati—is negligent.

The root uchi is in the sense of seeking. Uñcho means seeking. Uñchati—seeks. 'Strive without diminishing effort, [subsisting] by the practice of seeking roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits.'

The root ucha is in the sense of thirst. Uchati—is thirsty.

The root puccha is in the sense of asking. Pucchati—asks. Pucchitā, pucchako—one who asks. Puṭṭho, pucchito—one who is asked. Pucchā—a question. 'A monk asks a question to a Vinaya-holder.' Pucchi—asked. Pucchituṃ—to ask. Pucchitvā—having asked. Here, there are five kinds of questions: adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā (asking to illuminate what is not seen), diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā (asking to compare what is seen), vimaticchedanāpucchā (asking to cut off doubt), anumatipucchā (asking for consent/opinion), and kathetukamyatāpucchā (asking with the desire to explain). The distinction between these five questions should be taken from the Atthasālinī etc.

The root viccha is in the sense of going. Vicchati—goes. Vicchikā—a scorpion or a prawn.
40:
The root vuccha (vacchu) is in the sense of cutting. Vucchati means 'cuts'. There are words like vuttā, vuttavā, vuttasiro (one with a shaven head). The 'a' in the letter 'va' is changed to 'u'.

The word vutta is also found in the sense of shaving the hair in the Cakka Sutta etc., such as 'The young Brahmin named Kāpaṭika has a shaven head.' Here, by the word sira (head), the hair growing on the head is meant. For example, just as by the word mañca (bed), those on the bed are meant; or by the word cakkhu (eye), the consciousness dependent on the eye is meant. It is also found in the sense of planting, as in 'Just as a seed sown in the autumn season grows when sown in the field.' It is also found in the sense of speaking, as in the Itivuttaka Pali: 'This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant.' The summary of this meaning is stated thus:
'The word vutta occurs in the senses of shaving hair, planting, and speaking, by the power of the roots vacchu, vapa, and vaca respectively.'

Another way: The word vutta is found in the sense of leveling what has been planted in the Vinaya Vinitavatthu etc., such as 'not yet leveled what was sown.' It is found in the sense of livelihood in places like 'one who has laid down the hair (pride) and lives by what is given by others.' It is found in the sense of being freed/detached in the Vinaya Pali like 'as a yellow leaf is freed from its stalk.' It is found in the sense of the Vedas produced by the power of the Pali in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta etc., like 'sung, produced by the power of Pali, collected.' In the world, it is found in the sense of recitation in places like 'the Pārāyana text is recited.' The summary of this meaning is stated thus:
'The word vutta is seen in these meanings: leveling what is sown, livelihood, being freed, the Vedas produced by the power of Pali, and recitation.'

Another way: The word vutta, whether with or without a prefix, is used in planting, leveling what is sown, shaving hair, livelihood...
41:
The word 'vutta' is found in contexts such as being liberated, in what is produced by the power of the scriptures, in studying, and in speaking, etc. It is truly said:
“Cattle multiply for him who does not betray friends,
What is sown in the field grows.
He enjoys the fruit of what is sown.”
In such passages, it occurs in the sense of sowing (vapana). In “No ca kho paṭivuttaṃ,” it occurs in the sense of leveling what has been sown with an eight-toothed plow, etc. In “Kāpaṭiko māṇavo daharo vuttasiro,” it occurs in the sense of shaving the head (kesaharaṇa). In “Pannalomo paradattavutto migabhūtena cetasā viharati,” it occurs in the sense of livelihood (jīvitavutti). In “Seyyathāpi nāma paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto abhabbo haritatthāya,” it occurs in the sense of liberation from bonds (pamuttabhāva). In “Yesamidaṃ etarahi porāṇaṃ mantapadaṃ gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samīhitaṃ,” it occurs in the sense of what is produced by the power of the scriptures (pāvacanabhāva). In common usage, in “Vutto gaṇo, vutto pārāyano,” it occurs in the sense of studying (ajjhayana). In “Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā, dhammadāyādā me bhikkhave bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā,” it occurs in the sense of speaking (kathana). Regarding this, it is said:
The word 'vutta' should be understood as originating from the roots vapa, vatu, vacchu, and vaca.
It may be with or without a prefix, as appropriate.
It should be noted in the senses of sowing, leveling what is sown, baldness,
livelihood, liberation, the power of scriptures,
studying, and speaking.

The root taccha is used in the sense of thinning or planing (tanukaraṇa). Tacchati—he planes. Tacchako dāruṃ—the carpenter planes the wood.

## Forms of Roots Ending in 'Cha'.
42:
## Roots Ending in 'Ja'
The root ji is used in the sense of conquering. Jeti, jayati—he conquers. Parājayati—he is defeated. A monk investigating a case causes the owner to lose. A monk investigating a case is defeated. They offered an auspicious consecration for the king to conquer enemies and prayed for victory. Having caused to conquer. Here, jayāpesuṃ means they spoke words of aspiration: “May your majesty conquer all such dangers and enemies.” Jayanaṃ (conquering), jitaṃ (conquered), jayo (victory), vijitaṃ (conquered), jino (the Conqueror Buddha), jetā (victor), jetto (victor), the Mara is conquered, he conquered the Mara, he has conquered, he has conquered, the Conqueror of Mara, the Conqueror of the world, the Conqueror of defilements through the path (magga) in a limited sense, one who has not yet conquered defilements in a limited sense through the path, conquered, conquered, to conquer, to conquer, having conquered, having conquered. When this root belongs to the kiyādi group, forms such as jināti and jinitvā occur.

The root ji is used in the sense of subduing or overcoming (abhibhavana). Jeti (he subdues), jino (subduer). The forms are as before. Here, the Pali “Ānanda, by noble ones like you, [hunger etc.] is overcome; future generations will despise rice and meat” establishes the sense of subduing. Here, vijitaṃ means subdued.

The root ju is used in the sense of going (gati). Here, swift movement is intended. Javati (he moves swiftly). Javanaṃ (impulsion), javo (speed), javā (swift), javanto (swift), javanacittaṃ (impulsion consciousness), javanapañño (one of swift wisdom), javanahaṃso (swift swan). He goes where he desires as swiftly as the mind.

The root je is used in the sense of wasting or decaying (khaya). Jīyati (it wastes away, is destroyed). The 'e' is changed to 'īya'. In accordance with the Dispensation, the Pali “Why should I be destroyed by wealth?” is found. Scholars of grammar, however, state the form jāyati.

The root sajja is used in the sense of going. Sajjati (he goes).

The roots kuju and khuju are used in the sense of stealing (theyyakaraṇa). Kojati, khojati (he steals).

The roots vaja, dhaja, and dhaji are used in the sense of going. Vajati (he goes), abbajati (he goes forth). One should also go forth to the human state. Vajo (enclosure/pen), vajanaṃ (going), pavajanaṃ (arriving first), pabbajjā (going forth/ordination), pabbajito (one who has gone forth), pabbājito (one who is banished).
43:
“One who is banished from his own country and has gone to another land should make a great granary in his heart to store the goods of ill-spoken words.”

Dhajati—he goes. Dhajo—a banner. Dhañjati—he goes. Dhañjanaṃ—going. Here, dhaja means a banner-top, and dhañjana means going.

The root aja is also used in the sense of casting away (khepana). (The word 'ca' implies the sense of going.) Ajati—he casts away, he goes. Ajo—a goat. Here, aja means a goat. Its synonyms are 'ajo, eḷako, urabbho, avi, meṇḍo'. Among those terms, urabbha is a goat, also called aja. Avi is a red-haired goat. Meṇḍa is a curly-horned sheep. Accordingly, in the Janaka Jātaka, goat-carriages and sheep-carriages are mentioned separately. In fact, because “aja-eḷaka” mentions sheep separately from goats, the word eḷaka should also be taken to mean sheep. In the Mahosadha Jātaka Commentary, it is stated that there is no difference between sheep (meṇḍa) and goats (eḷaka).

The roots ajja and sajja are used in the sense of dwelling (ajjana). Ajjana is the act of dwelling. Ajjati—he dwells. Sajjati—he dwells.

The root kajja is used in the sense of oppressing (byathana). Byathana means harming (hiṃsā). Kajjati—he oppresses.

The root khajja is also used in the sense of purification (majjana). Majjana means purification (suddhi). (The word 'ca' implies the sense of oppressing.) Khajjati—it is purified, he oppresses. Khajjūro—the date palm or Phoenix dactylifera.

The root khaja is used in the sense of stirring (mantha). Mantha means stirring (viloḷana). Khajati—he stirs.

The root khaji is used in the sense of deficiency in going (gativekalla). “Venerable sir, why is the noble one limping?” Both people are limping. Khañjanaṃ—limping, khañjituṃ—to limp, khañjitvā—having limped.

The root khaja is used in the sense of trembling (kampana). Khajati—he trembles. Ejā—craving. Here too, it is called ejā because it trembles based on gain, etc. This name ejā is a name for powerful craving (taṇhā).

The root buja is used in the sense of penetrating like a diamond (vajiranibbesa). Some scholars say it is used in the sense of a terrifying sound like a thunderbolt (vajiranigghosa). Bojati—he penetrates like a diamond.
44:
The roots khija, kuji, and guji occur in the sense of indistinct or unclear sound. They exist as khijati, kuñjati, and guñjati.

The roots laza, lāza, and tazza occur in the sense of speaking. They exist as lazati, lāzati, and tazzati (he threatens).

The root lazi also occurs in the sense of beauty. By the particle 'ca', it also implies the sense of speaking. It exists as lañjati. The third method, Naya-lañjaka (the method of explaining the meaning of Suttas), is called Sīhavikkīḷita. It is called lañjaka because it clearly manifests the meaning of the Suttas.

The roots zaza and zazi occur in the sense of fighting, which is striking and cutting. They exist as zazati and zañzati.

The root tuza occurs in the sense of oppression. It exists as tozati.

The root tuzi also occurs in the sense of exertion. By the particle 'ca', it also implies the sense of oppression. It exists as tuñzati.

The roots gaza, kuji, muzi, and gazza have the sense of making a sound. They exist as gazati, kuñzati, and muñzati. The elephant roars (gazzati); the cloud thunders (gazzati). In whatever place the slave Nanda, born of a household slave-woman, stands and shouts (gazzati) harsh words. The gem makes a sound (gazzati). He roars (gazzati) with the roar of wisdom. He is able to roar (gazzituṃ). One who roars (gazzitā). Having roared (gazzitvā). Among those terms, 'gaza' means an elephant. Indeed, there are many names for an elephant—

Hatthī, nāga, gaza, dantī, kuñzara, vāraṇa, karī, mātaṅga, dvirada, saṭṭhihāyana, anekapa, ibha, thambha, ramma, and dvipa are names for an elephant. A female elephant is called kareṇukā. A young elephant is called hatthipota, hatthicchāpa, bhiṅka, or kalabha.

The root caza occurs in the sense of relinquishing. It exists as cazati, pariccazati. Cāga, pariccāga, cazana (relinquishing). Cazaṃ, cazanto, cazamāno (one who relinquishes).

The root sañza occurs in the sense of sticking or clinging. It exists as sañcati. Satta (a being who clings). Sazana, satti, āsatti (clinging). Sazituṃ, sazitvā.

The root īza occurs in the sense of going. It exists as īzati.

The root bhazi occurs in the sense of roasting, which is making hot. He roasts sesame seeds. Sesame seeds that are roasted by a man.
45:
The roots eza, bheza, and bhāza occur in the sense of beauty (ditti). 'Ditti' means beauty (sobhā). They take the forms ezati, bhezati, and bhāzati.

The root tiza occurs in the sense of sharpness (nisāna) and also in the sense of patience (khamā). 'Nisāna' means making sharp (sharpening). 'Khamā' means patience (khanti). They exist as tezati (he sharpens), titikkhati (he endures), tezano (arrow), and tezo (sun). Among those terms, 'tezano' means kaṇḍa, sara, or usu (arrow). 'Tezo' means suriya (sun). Alternatively, 'tezo' means heat (tezana), vapor (usmā), the state of being hot (uṇhatta), or heat (tāpo). Or 'tezo' means majesty (ānubhāva) or power (pabhāva).

The root sañza occurs in the sense of embracing (parissagga). 'Āliṅgana' means embracing (parissagga). It exists as sañzati (he embraces).

The root khazi occurs in the sense of giving (dāna) and also in the sense of going (gati). It exists as khañzati (he gives, he goes) and khañzanaṃ (giving, going).

The roots rāza and bhāza occur in the sense of beauty (ditti). They exist as rāzati, bhāzati (it shines beautifully), rāzā (king), rāzinī (queen), vanarāzi (a row of forest), rāzitvā, and virāzitvā (having shone beautifully). In this regard, I shall compose a verse to generate skill in explaining the meaning for the wise—

O Great King, my snake is beautiful.
O Great King, only my snake is beautiful.
Saying, 'This man's snake is not beautiful,'
Two men engaged in a quarrel.

In this verse, in the second word of the first pāda, 'mahi' should be resolved as 'me ahi'. This is like resolving 'puttā me atthi' as 'puttāmātthī'. It should also be resolved as 'mahi arāza mahārāzā'. This is like resolving 'yo pi ayaṃ' as 'yopāyaṃ'. Here, the word 'arāza' should be understood as having the Aorist (parokkhā) tense, like the word 'akara' which expresses the meaning 'akari' in the phrase 'atikaramakarācariya'. 'Arāza' means 'viroci' (it shone). The summary meaning of this verse is: 'O Great King, my snake is beautiful; only my snake is beautiful. Saying that this man's snake is not beautiful, two snake charmers engaged in a quarrel.'

The root rañza occurs in the sense of dyeing or lust/attachment (rāga). A monk dyes (razati) a robe. A being is attached (rañzati) to forms and so on. Razanaṃ, razako, rāgo, virāgo, haliddirāgo, rāzā, rāzinī. When this same root belongs to the Divādi group, it becomes 'razzati' and 'virazzati'.
46:
Forms (rūpa) exist. Among those terms, 'razana' refers to the dyeing material. 'Razaka' refers to a dyer or a washerman. 'Rāga' is so called because beings are attached by that greed, or because it is attached by itself, or because this is merely the extent of attachment; it means craving (taṇhā). These are the names for that craving—

Rāga, lobha, tasiṇā, taṇhā, ezā, visattikā,
Satti, āsatti, mucchā, lubbhitatta, and lubbhanā,
Kāma, nikāmanā, icchā, nikanti, and niyanti,
Vana, vanatha, apekkhā, and bhavanetti,
Anurodha, sārāga, saṅga, paṅka, and sibbinī,
Nandīrāga, anunaya, gedha, and likewise sañzananī,
Janikā, paṇidhi, and ajjhosāna—thus there are many varieties.

'Virāga' refers to the Path (magga) and Nibbāna. 'Rāzā' refers to the lord of the earth (king). In this word 'rāzā', the derivations are presented by the power of two roots (the root rāza and the root rañza). He is called 'rāzā' because he shines (rāzati), plays (dibbati), or glows (virozati) with various successes. He is also called 'rāzā' because he causes the great multitude to be attached (rañzeti) to himself by means of these four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu): dāna (liberality), piyavacana (kindly speech), atthacariyā (beneficial conduct), and samānattatā (impartiality). 'Rāzinī' refers to the king's wife (queen). I shall state the names of the king and queen along with other special names—

Rāzā, bhūpati, deva, manuzinda, disampati,
Patthiva, zagatipāla, bhūbhuza, pathavissara,
Raṭṭhādhipa, bhūmipāla, manussinda, zanādhipa,
Narinda, khattiya, and khettassāmi, pabhāvaka.
A king who has had the consecration (abhiseka) poured upon his head is called 'rāzā'. Other kings, however—
Are called 'rāzañña' or 'khattiya'; they are those born of the warrior caste.
A sub-king (heir apparent) whose head has been consecrated is called 'anurāzā' or 'uparāzā'.
A king of kings who rules over all four great continents is called 'cakkavattī' (Universal Monarch).
47:
## Synonyms for Queen

Rājinī, Upari devī, Mahesī, Bhūbhujanganā, Khattiyā, Rājapadumī, Khattiyānī, and Khattiyī are names meaning 'queen'. The place of women or the concubines are called itthāgāra and orodha; they are also called upari.

The root bhaja occurs in the sense of resorting to or serving. Bhajati (resorts to/serves), bhajanā (resorting to), sambhajanā (resorting to well), bhatti (devotion/service), sambhatti (perfect devotion), bhattā (lord or husband).

The root yaja occurs in the sense of worshipping deities, making associations, giving/sacrificing, and in the Dhamma such as jhāna and virtue (sīla). By the phrase 'worshipping deities', the worship of the Buddha and others is also included. 'Making associations' means the act of combining. Therefore, in the verse from the story of Elder Adhimutta: 'Whatever slight association there is, or where existence is obtained in the collection of beings,' the word saṅgata implies association. Dāna is giving/relinquishing, and Dhamma refers to jhāna, virtue, etc. The root yaja occurs in these senses. One worships (yajati) the Buddha with flowers. One worships a deity. The Blessed One is worshipped (yajiyati) by gods and men. It is worshipped (ijjati). Sacrificed (yiṭṭha). Sacrifice (yañña). Offering (yāga). Offering of Dhamma (dhamma-yāga). One who performs a sacrifice in his own city (yajamāno sake pure). To worship (yiṭṭhuṃ, yajituṃ). Having performed a great sacrifice (puthuyaññaṃ yajitvāna). He wishes to perform a great sacrifice with sixteen requisites.

The root majja occurs in the sense of purification. Majjati (purifies). He polishes and cleanses the exterior. He sweeps (sammajjati) the ground. Majjana (purification). Sammajjanī (broom).

The root niñji occurs in the sense of purification. Niñjati (washes), paniñjati (washes thoroughly). To wash. Having washed. This is the Pāḷi: 'Then, Moggallāna, you should rise from your seat, wash (paniñjitvā) your eyes with water, and look around the quarters.'

The root niji occurs in the sense of indistinct sound. Niñjati (makes a sound).

The root bhaja occurs in the sense of cooking. He roasts (bhajjati) sesame seeds. Also, roasted sesame seeds.

The root uju occurs in the sense of rectitude. Ajjava means the state of being straight. Ojati (is straight). Uju (straight).
48:
The root saja occurs in the senses of abandoning, embracing, and scattering. Sajati (abandons/embraces). One who scatters water in the world.

The root ruja occurs in the sense of breaking or perishing. Rujati (is pained/afflicts). Rujā (pain). Roga (disease). Here, rujā refers to sickness (vyādhi) because of the sense of being pained. Roga is so called because it afflicts and breaks the limbs and organs; it is indeed sickness (vyādhi), which is also called ātaṅka and ābādha.

The root bhuja occurs in the sense of bending. When preceded by ā- or vi-, it also occurs in other senses. A snake coils. Ābhujati (coils). A monk sits cross-legged (pallaṅkaṃ ābhujati); the meaning is he sits with his thighs bent. The great ocean circles; the meaning is it whirls. Some, however, say the meaning is 'it recedes'. He attends to the 'giving of beauty' (vaṇṇadāna); the meaning is he reflects (manasi karoti). Because it cuts roots, it is called mūlavibhuja (a chariot). Here, vibhujati means to cut. Bhoga (the body or hood of a snake). Bhogī (a snake). Ābhoga (reflection/attention). Ābhujitvā (having reflected). Here, bhoga is so called because it is made curved; it is the body of the snake. Bhogī is the snake itself.

The root raji occurs in the sense of piercing. A noble elephant pierces the ground with its tusks. Ārañjati (pierces). Here, the Netti-pāḷi 'tathāgatarañjitaṃ itipi' is an example. Its meaning is: 'This noble Brahma-faring of the Dispensation, comprised of the three trainings, is pierced and repeatedly pierced by the tusks of the Great Vajira-knowledge and Omniscient-knowledge of the Tathāgata-Gandha-elephant; it is also called the place for piercing the phenomena of the three planes of existence.' Rañjita is so called because it pierces (rañjati) these (phenomena of the three planes); thus it is the place of piercing. The formation of this word should be understood as being possible in the locative sense (adhikaraṇa), as in the passage 'this is the place where they stepped (padakkanta)'.

The root vijī occurs in the senses of fear and trembling. This root ends in the vowel ī; therefore, its forms do not have the nasal augment (niggahīta). Vejati (trembles). Vega (impulse/speed). Dhamma-saṃvega (religious urgency). One who is terrified flees with speed (vegena). The speed of a river.
49:
The impulse of a wave, the impulse of the wind. In this context, dhamma-saṃvega is knowledge accompanied by moral dread (ottappa). The words vega, java, and raya have the same meaning. When the root vijī belongs to the divādi group, it has the forms vijjati, saṃvijjati, and ubbijjati, because it belongs to two groups.

The root lajja occurs in the sense of being ashamed. Lajjati (is ashamed). Lajjā (shame). Lajjā is hirī (moral shame). That lajjā is also called viriḷanā.

The root vaḷaji occurs in the sense of using or consuming. Vaḷañjati (uses/consumes).

The root kujja occurs in the sense of turning the face downwards. Kujjati, nikujjati (turns face down). Ukkujjati (turns face up). Paṭikujjati (covers/places face-to-face). One might turn up (ukkujjeyya) what has been turned down. He covers it with another bowl (paṭikujjati). I lie face down (nipajjahaṃ). In that context, the words kujjati and nikujjati have the same meaning, like the words carati and vicarati, because they have the sense of making the face turn downwards. Ukkujjati means making the face turn upwards (turning over). Paṭikujjati means placing face-to-face (covering).

The root mujja occurs in the sense of sinking or diving. Mujjati, nimujjati (sinks/dives). Nimugga (submerged). Ummugga (emerged).

The root opuja occurs in the sense of smearing. He smears the ground with cow dung.

## Forms of roots ending in the letter Ja.

## Roots ending in the letter Jha

The root jhe occurs in the sense of thinking (contemplation). Jhāyati (thinks/contemplates), nijjhāyati, upanijjhāyati (contemplates closely), ujjhāyati (contemplates with reproach/complains), sajjhāyati (recites/studies). Jhāna (contemplation), nijjhāna, upanijjhāna, ujjhāyana, sajjhāyana (recitation). Nijjhātti (satisfaction/agreement). Upajjhā, upajjhāyo (preceptor). Jhāyī (one who meditates), ajjhāyako (one who does not meditate, or a reciter of the Vedas).

In that context, jhāyana (contemplation) is of two kinds: wholesome and unwholesome. Among them, wholesome contemplation is to be understood in such instances as: 'The meditating (jhāyī) Brahmin (Arahant) shines.'
50:
In sentences such as "jhāyāmi akutobhayo," good contemplation should be understood. However, bad contemplation should be understood in sentences such as "tattha tattha jhāyanto nisīdi, adhomukho pajjhāyanto nisīdi." jhāyī refers to one who is habituated to contemplating or thinking, either through ārammaṇūpanijjhāna (samatha) or lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna (vipassanā). It means one who possesses jhāna. The word "ajjhāyaka" arose in the early aeon as a term of reproach for Brahmins who were devoid of jhāna, as in: "Vāseṭṭha, now these people do not contemplate (kasiṇa, etc.)." Nowadays, however, it is used as a term of praise with the meaning that the person recites or reviews the Vedas. This meaning should be taken by the power of the root 'i' (ajjhayana - learning) preceded by 'adhi'. Thus, by the power of the root 'i' preceded by 'adhi', the meaning of this root (jhe) changes. Referring to this change of meaning, it is said: "ajjhāyako mantadharo" (a reciter who bears the mantras). The root jhe occurs in the sense of shining. The lamp burns (jhāyati), the woods burn (jhāyanti). Here, jhāyati means it shines (jalati). The words jhāyana and jalana have the same meaning. The root zazzha occurs in the sense of scolding or threatening. zazzhati (he scolds). The root uzzha occurs in the sense of relinquishing (ussagga). ussagga is the same as discarding (chaḍḍana). uzzhati (he discards), uzzhitaṃ (that which is discarded).

## Roots ending in the letter 'Jha'.

## Roots ending in the letter 'Ña'.
The root ñā occurs in the sense of knowing (avabodhana). Forms such as "ñāti, ñanti, ñāsi; ñātu, ñantu; ñeyya, ñeyyuṃ" should be taken according to the Pali scriptures. There are derivatives such as ñāti, ñātako, añño, ñattaṃ, ñatti, paññatti, viññatti, saññatti, saññā, saññāṇaṃ, paññā, paññāṇaṃ, ñāṇaṃ, viññāṇaṃ.
51:
Among those (words derived from the root ñā), "ñāti" means he knows (jānāti). Again, "ñāti" means a relative (bandhu). A relative is called "ñāti" because of the sense of being known as "this person is our kin." In this way, "ñātako" is also used. "Añño" is so called because he does not know (na ñāti, na jānāti) the benefits of the present life and so on; it means an ignorant fool. "Ñattaṃ" means the state of knowing (jānana-bhāva). The Pāḷi "Yāvadeva anatthāya, ñattaṃ bālassa jāyati" (The skill of a fool is only for his ruin) is an example. "Saññāṇaṃ" means a sign or mark. In the causative (kārita) sense, there are words such as "ñāpeti, saññāpeti, viññāpayati." Since Pāḷi passages are seen such as "aññāti, paṭivijjhati; he will know his own benefit or another's benefit (ñassati); anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ; some did not know (nabbhaññuṃ), some knew (abbhaññuṃ)," the verbal forms (ākhyāta) such as "ñāti" are clearly established by method. This is because: in the word "aññāti," "ā" is a prefix (upasagga); that prefix "ā" is shown as short (rassa) because of the desire to pronounce it in conjunction with the following letter "ñā." Since the verbal form "ñāti" is found in the Dispensation (Sāsana), there is no fault in forming a paradigm (padamālā) as "ñāti, ñanti, ñāsi," etc. 

The root "ñā" is also used in the senses of killing (māraṇa), pleasing (tosana), and sharpening (nisāna). Killing (māraṇa) means cutting off the life faculty (jīvitindriya). Pleasing (tosana) means satisfaction (tuṭṭhi). Sharpening (nisāna) means the state of being sharp (tikkhatā). The words "ñatti, manujñaṃ, paññatti" are formed. Here, "ñatti" means he kills, or he pleases, or he sharpens. This word "ñatti" should also be understood as a verbal form, like the word "vatti" in "vatti etāyāti vါcā." Furthermore, just as the word "te" which is an inflection (vibhatti) in "ādatte" is in conjunction and the final vowel of the root is shortened, here too, the word "ti" which is an inflection is in conjunction and the final vowel of the root "ñā" is shortened. "Manujñaṃ" is so called because it pleases the mind greatly. This meaning should be understood by the power of this root "ñā" preceded by "ā" with the word "mana" as a preceding word (upapada). "Paññatti" is so called because it is a killing (māraṇa) of unwholesome states by preventing them from arising in various ways. Or, it is the causing of joy in many ways in the minds of those listening to the Dhamma through the Dhamma teaching; or, for those of very sharp wisdom...
52:
Killing is called "paññatti" (designation/description). Alternatively, the causing of joy in many ways in the minds of those listening to the Dhamma through the Dhamma teaching, or the making of the wisdom of those with very sharp intellect even sharper in many ways, is called "paññatti." Likewise, making [others] know by pleasing the mind of the listeners and by sharpening the mind should be understood as "paññatti."

## Thus the forms of the roots ending in the Ca-varga in the Bhūvādi group are completed.

## Roots ending in the letter Ṭa.

Now the forms of the roots ending in the Ṭa-varga will be told:

The root "soṭu" is used in the sense of pride (gabba). "Gabba" means harshness. "Soṭati."

The root "yoṭu" is used in the sense of connection (sambandha). "Yoṭati."

The roots "meṭu" and "mileṭu" are used in the sense of madness (ummāda). "Meṭati, mileṭati."

The root "kaṭa" is used in the senses of pouring and obstructing. "Kaṭati."

The root "saṭa" is used in the sense of scolding (paribhāsana). "Saṭati."

The root "laṭa" is also used in the sense of foolishness (bālya). The word "ca" (also) is used in reference to the previously mentioned scolding. "Laṭati, lāṭo."

The root "saṭa" is used in the senses of pain (rujā), spreading (vissaraṇa), and the end of movement (gatyāvasāna). "Rujā" means oppression (pain). "Vissaraṇaṃ" means spreading. "Gatyāvasānaṃ" means the end of movement, which means sitting. "Saṭati." "Sāṭo" is called "sāṭako" (a garment/cloth).

The root "vaṭa" is used in the sense of piercing or wrapping (vedhana). "Vaṭati, vaṭo, vāṭo."

The root "khiṭa" is used in the sense of terror (uttāsana). "Kheṭati, ākheṭako, kheṭo, ukkheṭito, samukkheṭito."

The root "siṭa" is used in the sense of disrespect (anādara). "Seṭati."
53:
The root *jaṭa* is used in the sense of combining, assembling, and entangling. *Jaṭati*—it entangles. There are terms such as *jaṭā* (matted hair), *jaṭilo* (an ascetic), and *jaṭī* (an ascetic). In the Devatā Saṃyutta, it is stated: "The multitude of beings is tangled within (the six internal bases) and tangled without (the six external bases); they are entwined by the entanglement of craving." In the causative sense, there is an example in the Visuddhimagga: "That monk should disentangle this entanglement of craving; at the moment of the Path of Arahatship, it is said he disentangles the entanglement."

The root *bhaṭa* is used in the sense of serving or attending. *Bhaṭati*—he serves. *Bhaṭo*—a servant or soldier. There is the usage: "Just as a servant waits for the time of his wages."

The root *taṭa* is used in the sense of rising or being above. *Ussaya* refers to rising (*āroha*) and height (*ubbedha*). *Taṭati*—it rises. *Taṭo*—a steep bank, *giritaṭo*—a mountain slope, *nadītaṭo*—a river bank; it exists in all three genders as *taṭī* and *taṭaṃ*.

The root *khaṭa* is used in the sense of breaking or digging. *Khaṭati*—he digs. *Khaṭo*—the act of breaking or digging.

The root *naṭa* is used in the sense of bending. *Naṭati*—it bends. *Naṭo*—a dancer or actor, *nāṭakaṃ*—a dramatic performance.

The root *piṭa* is used in the sense of the collection of sounds and meanings. *Peṭati*—he speaks or collects. *Peṭako*—speaking or collecting; *piṭakaṃ*—a Piṭaka (scripture) or a basket, vessel, or container. The word *piṭaka* is seen in the sense of the learned Pali scriptures (*pariyatti*) in texts such as the Kālāma Sutta: "Do not go by the authority of the scriptures (*mā piṭakasampadānena*)." In the Nidānavagga and other texts, it is clearly seen in the sense of any kind of vessel (*bhājana*), such as: "Then a man would come taking a hoe and a basket (*kudālapiṭakaṃ*)."

The root *haṭa* is used in the sense of beauty or brightness. *Haṭati*—it is beautiful. *Hāṭakaṃ*, *haṭakaṃ*—gold. Gold produced by insects or termites is called *haṭaka*.

The root *saṭa* is used in the sense of crumbling or disintegrating. *Saṭati*—it crumbles.

The root *luṭa* is used in the sense of rolling or wallowing. *Loṭati*—he rolls.

The root *ciṭa* is used in the sense of sending or commanding. *Ceṭati*—he commands. *Ceṭako*—a servant.

The root *viṭa* is used in the sense of sound. *Veṭati*—he speaks. *Veṭako*—one who speaks.

The roots *aṭa*, *paṭa*, *iṭa*, *kiṭa*, and *kaṭa* are used in the sense of going. They are *aṭati*, *paṭati*, *eṭati*, *keṭati*, and *kaṭati*. From the root *paṭa*, the noun *paṭo* is found.
54:
It is called *paṭa* because it reaches a state of being worn out. *Paṭa* means cloth (garment). There are many names for cloth—
*Paṭo*, *coḷo*, *sāṭako*, *vāso*, *vasanaṃ*, *aṃsukaṃ*, *dussaṃ*, *acchādanaṃ*, *vatthaṃ*, *celaṃ*, *vasani*, and *ambaraṃ*.

The root *muṭa* is used in the sense of crushing or pressing (*pamaddana*). *Moṭati*.

The root *cuṭa* is used in the sense of being small or few (*appībhāva*). *Coṭati*.

The root *vaṭi* is used in the sense of dividing (*vibhājana*). *Vaṭati*. *Vaṇṭo* (a stalk).

The roots *ruṭi* and *luṭi* are used in the sense of stealing (*theyya*). *Ruṇṭati*, *luṇṭati*. *Ruṇṭako*, *luṇṭako* (a thief).

The root *phuṭa* is used in the sense of spreading (*visaraṇa*). *Foṭati*. *Foṭo*.

The root *ceṭa* is used in the sense of commanding or movement (*ceṭā*). *Ceṭati*. *Ceṭako* (a servant).

The root *ghuṭa* is used in the sense of turning around (*parivattana*). *Ghoṭati*.

The roots *ruṭ* and *luṭ* are used in the sense of striking or obstructing (*paṭighāta*). *Roṭati*, *loṭati*.

The root *ghaṭa* is used in the sense of effort or movement (*cetā*). *Ghaṭati*. *Ghaṭo* (a pot). *Ghaṭo* is also called *kumbho*. These are its names—
*Ghaṭo*, *kumbho*, *ghaṭī*, *kumbhī*, *tuṇḍikiro*, and *ukkhalī*.
A large pot is called *cāṭi*. A very small pot is called *kuṭṭa*.

The roots *caṭa*, *bhaṭa*, and *deṭa* are used in the sense of reviling or scolding (*paribhāsana*). *Caṭati*, *bhaṭati*, *deṭati*.

The root *kuṭa* is used in the sense of crookedness (*koṭillya*). *Kuṭati*, *paṭikuṭati*.

The root *puṭa* is used in the sense of defilement (*saṃkilesana*). *Puṭati*.

The roots *cuṭa*, *shuṭa*, and *kuṭa* are used in the sense of cutting (*chedana*). *Cuṭati*, *shuṭati*, *kuṭati*.

The root *phuṭa* is used in the sense of blossoming (*vikasana*). *Phuṭati*.

The root *muṭa* is used in the senses of making the sound of fire and crushing (*aggisaddapakkhepamaddana*). *Muṭati*.

The root *tuṭa* is used in the sense of quarreling or disputing (*kalahakamma*). *Tuṭati*.

The root *ghuṭa* is used in the sense of striking or obstructing (*paṭighāta*). *Ghuṭati*. *Ghoṭako*.

## Forms of roots ending in 'ṭa'.
55:
## Roots ending in 'ṭha'

The root *ṭhā* is used in the sense of stopping from movement (*gatinivatti*). *Gatinivatti* means the cessation of movement that has arisen. *Ṭhāti*, *ṭhanti*. *Tiṭṭhati*. *Patiṭṭhāti* (it stands/is established). *Adhiṭṭhāti*, *adhiṭṭheti* (he determines/resolves). *Saṇṭhāti*, *saṇṭhahati* (it is well-established). *Adhiṭṭhahati*. *Upaṭṭhahati* (he serves/attends). *Ṭhātu*, *tiṭṭhatu* (let it stand). *Tiṭṭheyya* (it should stand). *Aṭṭha*, *aṭṭhu*. *Aṭṭhā*, *aṭṭhū*, *aṭṭhāsi*, *aṭṭhaṃsu* (it stood). "As long as his body remains" (*yāvassa kāyo ṭhassati*). *Tiṭṭhissati*. "He will stand close to listen" (*upassuti tiṭṭhissatha*). *Aṭṭhissā*, *aṭṭhissaṃsu*. *Atiṭṭhissā*, *atiṭṭhissaṃsu*. *Ṭhātuṃ*, *upaṭṭhātuṃ* (to serve). *Upaṭṭhahituṃ*. *Adhiṭṭhātuṃ*. *Adhiṭṭhahituṃ*. *Ṭhatvā*, *adhiṭṭhitvā*. *Upaṭṭhahitvā*, *adhiṭṭhahitvā*. *Ṭhānaṃ*, *ṭhiti*, *saṇṭhiti*, *avaṭṭhiti* (standing/stability). *Saṇṭhānaṃ*, *paṭṭhānaṃ*. *Upaṭṭhāko* (an attendant), *ṭhito* (stood/standing). *Pabbataṭṭho* (standing on a mountain), *bhūmaṭṭho* (standing on the ground). *Upaṭṭhahaṃ* (serving), and so forth.

Among those terms, the word *ṭhāna* is found in the senses of sovereignty (*issariya*), stability (*ṭhiti*), moment (*khaṇa*), and cause (*kāraṇa*). In passages such as "By performing what deed did the venerable Sakka, King of Devas, reach this *ṭhāna* (sovereignty)?", it is found in the sense of sovereignty (*issariya*). In passages such as "He is skilled in standing (*ṭhāna*), an archer who can hit a hair-breadth," it is found in the sense of stability (*ṭhiti*). In passages such as "That problem appears to the Tathāgata in a moment (*ṭhānaso*)," it is found in the sense of a moment (*khaṇa*). In passages such as "Knowing the cause (*ṭhāna*) as cause, and the non-cause as non-cause," it is found in the sense of cause (*kāraṇa*). A cause is called *ṭhāna* because the effect exists (*tiṭṭhati*) in that cause by way of depending on it.

The word *ṭhāna* occurs in these four senses: sovereignty, stability, moment, and cause.

The root *ṭhe* is used in the senses of making a sound and collecting (*saddasaṅkhāta*). *Ṭhīyati*.

The root *ṭhe* is used in the sense of wrapping or enveloping (*veṭhana*). *Ṭhāyati*.
56:
The root paṭha occurs in the sense of speaking clearly. He recites the Dhamma. Pāṭha (text), an astrologer (one who reads the stars), that person asked the horapāṭhaka (one who reads the hours/horoscope). He will become a sabbapāṭhī (one who has recited all the scriptures). To recite, having recited, and so forth.

Although I wish to explain such analyses of words ending in the suffix -tuṃ and others for all roots as appropriate, I shall not do so for fear of making the text too lengthy. Even if not explicitly stated, such analysis should be applied everywhere according to the method wherever possible. However, where a specific distinction such as the presentation of a Pali example is required, I will demonstrate it in that very place.

The root vaṭha occurs in the sense of being stout. He is stout. Vaṭhara means a stout person. The word vaṭhara is spoken of one who has a dense and stout body. Therefore, it is stated in the Vinaya Commentary: "Vaṭhara means stout; it means this monk is both stout and has a dense body."

The root maṭha occurs in the sense of dwelling. He dwells. Dwelling.

The root kaṭha occurs in the sense of living with difficulty. He lives with difficulty. Firewood.

The root raṭha occurs in the sense of reviling. He mutters and reviles.

The root sāṭha occurs in the sense of using force. Using force (balakkāra) means overpowering a weak person according to one's own will by means of one's own strength. He oppresses by force. Oppression.

The roots uṭha, ruṭha, and luṭha occur in the sense of afflicting. He afflicts, he harms.

The root piṭha occurs in the sense of afflicting and distress/defilement. He afflicts, he is distressed. A rice pot.

The root saṭha occurs in the sense of deceit, as well as in the previously mentioned senses of afflicting and distress. He is deceitful, he afflicts, he is distressed. A deceitful person is called saṭha.

The root suṭha occurs in the sense of obstructing movement. Obstructing movement is called gatipaṭighāta. He obstructs movement.

The roots kuṭhi and luṭhi occur in the sense of laziness, as well as in the previously mentioned sense of obstructing movement. He is lazy, he obstructs movement. Laziness.
57:
The root suṭhi occurs in the sense of drying. It dries. The roots ruṭhi, luṭhi, and aṭhi occur in the sense of going. It goes. The root veṭha occurs in the sense of wrapping. It wraps; it unwraps. A turban; unwrapping. The root vaṭhi occurs in the sense of practicing alone. He practices alone. The roots maṭha and kuṭhi occur in the sense of worrying. He worries. The roots eṭha and heṭha occur in the sense of oppressing or harassing. He oppresses; he harasses. Harassment. The root luṭha occurs in the sense of oppressing. He oppresses. The root paṭha occurs in the sense of becoming manifest. It is manifest. The root luṭha occurs in the sense of being distressed or defiled. He is distressed and defiled.

## Roots ending in the letter 'Ṭha'.

## Roots ending in the letter 'Ḍa'
The root ḍi occurs in the sense of flying in the sky and also in the sense of mere going. He flies; he goes. Flying. "O crow flying in the high sky." "Those children who used to come out to greet me in the past." The root ḍi occurs in the sense of throwing or setting (a snare). He throws; he sets; he snares. Sectarians (pāsaṇḍa) who are outside this Dispensation have faith in wrong views. I do not delight in their teaching; they are not skilled in the Dhamma. In this verse, they are called pāsaṇḍa because they throw (ḍenti) a snare (pāsaṃ); it means they throw the snare of wrong view into the minds of beings. Alternatively, they are called pāsaṇḍa because they set or snare with the snare of craving and the snare of wrong view.
58:
The root muḍi is in the sense of cutting. Muṇḍati—he cuts. Kumāraṃ muṇḍiṃsu—they cut the boy's hair. Muṇḍo—shaven-headed.

The root cuḍḍa is in the sense of making an ornament. Cuḍḍati—he beautifies.

The root aḍḍa is in the sense of litigation (legal action). Aḍḍati—he brings a lawsuit.

The root gaḍi is in the sense of a part of the mouth. Gaṇḍati—it becomes a part of the mouth. Gaṇḍo—the cheek.

The roots huḍi and piḍi are in the sense of accumulation. Huṇḍati—he accumulates. Piṇḍati—he accumulates. Piṇḍo—alms-food, a collection, a lump, or a physical object.

The root hiḍi is in the sense of going. Hiṇḍati, āhiṇḍati—he goes, he wanders.

The root kuḍi is in the sense of burning. Kuṇḍati—it burns. Kuṇḍo—a rice pot.

The roots vaḍi and maḍi are in the sense of wrapping or piercing. Vaṇḍati—he wraps, he pierces. Maṇḍati—he wraps. Maṇḍalaṃ—a circle.

The root baḍi is in the sense of scolding (reproaching). Baṇḍati—he quarrels. Baṇḍanaṃ—quarreling. Baṇḍo—wealth.

The root maḍi is in the sense of rubbing and cleaning. Maṇḍati—he rubs, cleans, and decorates. Maṇḍanaṃ—rubbing and cleaning, or an ornament.

The root tuḍi is in the sense of pecking. Tuṇḍati—he pecks. Tuṇḍo—a beak. "Tuṇḍenādāya gaccheyya" means "he should go taking it with his beak."

The root buḍi is in the sense of bearing or nurturing. Buṇḍati—he bears, he nurtures.

The root caḍi is in the sense of anger. Caṇḍati—he is fierce. Caṇḍo—a fierce person. Caṇḍālo—an outcast. Caṇḍikkaṃ—fierceness.

The root saḍi is in the sense of pain. Saṇḍati—he feels pain. Saṇḍo—pain.

The root taḍi is in the sense of striking (beating). Taṇḍati—he strikes. Vitaṇḍā—sophistry (a person who practices vitaṇḍavāda).

The root paḍi is in the sense of going (knowing). Paṇḍati—he goes, he knows. Paṇḍā, paṇḍito. Here, paṇḍā means wisdom. That wisdom "goes" (knows) even into subtle meanings, and it knows the characteristics of suffering, such as its oppressive nature; therefore, it is called "paṇḍā". A paṇḍita (wise person) is one who has proceeded or acted by means of that wisdom (paṇḍā). Alternatively, one who possesses well-arisen wisdom is a paṇḍita. One who "goes" by the movement of knowledge is also a paṇḍita. Thus—
59:
In the Commentary, it is said: "They are called paṇḍita because they know. It means they go (know) by the way of knowledge regarding benefits in this life and the next."

The root gaḍi is in the sense of intoxication. Gaṇḍati—is intoxicated.

The root khaḍi is in the sense of agitation or disturbance. Khaṇḍati—is agitated. Khaṇḍito—one who is agitated. Khaṇḍo—molasses or a lump of sugar.

The root laḍi is in the sense of destroying taste with the tongue. Laṇḍati—destroys taste. Laṇḍo—excrement.

## Ḍakārantadhāturūpāni.

## Ḍakārantadhātu

The root vaḍḍha is in the sense of growth. Vaḍḍhati—grows. Sirivaḍḍhako—one who increases glory. Dhanavaḍḍhako—one who increases wealth. Vaḍḍhito—one who has grown. Buḍḍho—one who is grown (an elder). In this word 'buḍḍha', the letter 'va' is changed to 'ba', and the letter 'a' is changed to 'u'.

The root kaḍḍha is in the sense of pulling or dragging. Kaḍḍhati, ākaḍḍhati—pulls. Nikaḍḍhati—drives out. "Akāmā parikaḍḍhanti, ulūkaññeva vāyasā" means: just as crows pull an owl from all sides, they pull from all sides (unwillingly).

## Imāni Ḏhakārantadhāturūpāni.

## Ṇakārantadhātu

The roots aṇa, raṇa, vaṇa, bhaṇa, maṇa, and kaṇa are in the sense of making sound. Aṇati—speaks. Aṇako—one who speaks. Brāhmaṇo—a Brahmin. Raṇati—speaks. Raṇam—speaking. Vaṇati—speaks. Vāṇako—a speaker. Bhaṇati—speaks. Bhāṇako—a speaker or a jar. Maṇati—speaks. Maṇiko—a jar. Kaṇati—speaks. Kāṇo—speaking or a one-eyed person. Among these words, 'brāhmaṇa' means one who recites (aṇati) the Brahma (Vedas); it means one who recites the mantras. Grammarians, however, say: "He is called a brāhmaṇa because he is an offspring of Brahma." The Noble Ones (Ariyas) say: he is a brāhmaṇa because he has washed away evil (bāhitapāpatta).
60:
Brāhmaṇa, sottiya, vippa, bhovādī, brahmabandhu, brahmasūnu, dvija, brahmā, and kamalāsanasūnu (are synonyms for a Brahmin).

The word 'raṇa' refers to defilements (kilesa) in phrases such as "saraṇā dhammā araṇā dhammā". Because beings cry and lament due to defilements, those defilements are called "raṇa".

"The peerless prince of great strength, holding a bow, having made war (raṇam) against all enemies, attained self-restraint." In this verse, (the word raṇa) refers to making war. 'Raṇam katvā' means having made war. "Making grass and wood into powder (raṇam), those elephants ran in all eight directions." In this context, (the word raṇa) refers to making something into powder. 'Raṇam karontā' means making into powder. It should be understood that such explanations are made by keeping the meaning of 'sound' internal and applying it through the power of intent, rather than through the various meanings of the root itself. Alternatively, it should be understood that such explanations are made because of the excellence of the roots' meanings.

The root bhaṇa is in the sense of reciting. Parittaṃ bhaṇati—recites protection; vacanaṃ bhaṇati—speaks words. Dīghabhāṇaka, piyabhāṇī, bhāṇavāra. Here, 'bhāṇavāra' is defined as:
"Eight syllables make one pada; one gāthā has four padas.
One gāthā is considered one gantha; one gantha has thirty-two syllables.
Two hundred and fifty of such thirty-two-syllable ganthas
Are known as one bhāṇavāra, which consists of eight thousand syllables."
Thus, a text measuring eight thousand syllables is called a bhāṇavāra.

The root oṇa is in the sense of removing. Oṇati—removes.

The root soṇa is in the senses of color and going. Soṇati—goes. Soṇa—red color (or blood, or a dog).
61:
The roots soṇa and siloṇa are in the sense of assembling. The forms are soṇati and siloṇati, meaning 'assembles'.

The roots ghiṇi, ghuṇi, and ghaṇi are in the sense of taking. The forms are ghiṇṇati, ghuṇṇati, and ghaṇṇati, meaning 'takes'.

The roots ghuṇa and ghuṇṇa are in the sense of going. The forms are ghoṇati and ghuṇṇati, meaning 'goes'.

The root paṇa is in the senses of trading and praising. In the phrase "vāṇijo paṇati", it means the merchant trades, or conducts business (taking another's property and giving one's own). In the phrase "saddhā buddhaṃ paṇati", it means the faithful person praises or honors the Buddha. There are also words like āpaṇam (market) and sāpaṇo gāmo (a village with a market).

The roots gaṇa and raṇa are in the sense of going. The forms are gaṇati and raṇati.

The roots caṇa and saṇa are in the sense of giving. The forms are caṇati and saṇati.

The root phaṇa is in the sense of going. The form is phaṇati. There is also the word phaṇam (the hood of a snake).

The root veṇu is in the senses of knowing, thinking, and investigating. The form is veṇati.

The root pīṇa is in the sense of fullness or plumpness. Pīṇanam means complete fulfillment (satiety). The form is pīṇati. There are usages such as "pīṇo divā na bhuñjati" (he is plump without eating by day) and "pīṇorakkaṃsabāhu" (having a plump chest, collarbone, shoulder, and arm).

The root miṇa is in the sense of oppressing. The form is miṇati.

The root duṇa is also in the sense of going. The word 'ca' (in the Pali text) also includes the sense of oppressing. The form is duṇati.

The root saṇa is in the sense of an indistinct sound. The form is saṇati. In the phrase "saṇateva brahmāraṇyaṃ", it means the great forest is as if sounding. 'Saṇateva' means 'as if sounding' or 'as if roaring'.

The root tuṇa is in the sense of crookedness. The form is toṇati.

The root puṇa is in the sense of subtlety. The forms are puṇati and nipuṇati. There is the term nipuṇadhammo (subtle Dhamma). Here, it should be understood that the words nipuṇa, saṇha, and sukhuma are synonyms, just like the words kusala, cheka, and dakkha.

The root muṇa is in the sense of acknowledging (confessing). The form is muṇati.

The root kuṇa is in the sense of making sound (the instrument of sound). The form is koṇati.
62:
The root cuṇa is used in the sense of cutting. It takes the form coṇati.

The root maṇa is used in the sense of relinquishing. Because it relinquishes enmity (veraṃ), it is called veramaṇī.

The root phuṇa is used in the sense of scattering and shaking off. It takes the form phuṇati. In the phrase "Aṅgārakāsuṃ apare phuṇanti", it means other hell-wardens scatter heaps of glowing coals (over the denizens of hell).

## These are the root forms ending in the letter ṇa.

## Thus, the root forms ending in the ṭa-group within the bhūvādi class are completed.

## Roots ending in the letter ta

Now, the root forms ending in the ta-group will be described:

The root tā is used in the sense of protecting (pālana). Protecting (pālana) is the same as guarding (rakkhana). It takes the form tāyati. There are terms such as tāṇaṃ (protection), gottaṃ (lineage/clan), and nakkhattaṃ (constellation). There are usages such as "aghassa tātā" (protector from suffering) and "kicchenādhigatā bhogā, te tāto vidhami dhammaṃ" (those riches acquired with difficulty, my father destroyed them).

Among those terms, gottaṃ is so called because it protects speech and knowledge (gaṃ). It is called gottaṃ because it protects speech (vacana) and knowledge (buddhi), such as "Gotama" or "Kassapa," by being the singular object of reference. Just as knowledge does not exist without an object of meaning, so a name (abhidhāna) does not exist without the thing named (abhidheyya). Therefore, that meaning known as gotta is said to protect that speech and knowledge. If one asks what that meaning is: it is the common nature (sāmaññarūpa) that arises in the first person of a clan, not shared with other lineages, and pertains to everyone included in that clan.

Nakkhattaṃ is so called because it protects movement (nakkhana) by moving only in its own path without moving in an irregular manner. These constellations are of twenty-seven types, starting with Assayuza (Aśvinī). This is because:
63:
Assayuza, Bharaṇī, Kattikā, Rohiṇī, Migasī, Adda, Punabbasu, Phussa, Assalissa, Māgha, Pubbaphagguṇī, Uttaraphagguṇī, Hattha, Citra, Svāti, Visākhā, Anurādha, Jeṭṭha, Mūla, Pubbāsaḷha, Uttarāsaḷha, Savaṇa, Dhanasiṭṭha, Satabhisajja, Pubbabhadrapada, Uttarabhadrapada, and Revatī—thus there are twenty-seven constellations.

These constellations do not deviate even slightly from their own paths. Some move quickly, some move slowly. Sometimes they are fast, sometimes they are slow. Thus, without moving in an irregular manner from here to there, they move only along their own paths with a uniform measure of movement, as if fixed in order in a mechanical wheel, revolving around Mount Sineru in a circular shape. In this way, because these constellations protect their own movement, they are called 'nakkhatta'. Ancient teachers, however, said based on the root khara: "nakkharanti na nassantīti nakkhattāni" (they are called nakkhatta because they do not decay or perish). The names "nakkhatta", "joti", and "rikkha" are names for the asterisms. The names "uḷu", "tāra", and "tārakā" are common names for all stars. "Osadhī" is the name of a specific star (the morning star).

The root citi is used in the sense of marking (saññāṇa). Saññāṇa means branding or making a mark. Cetati means "he marks." Because this root ends in the vowel i, it does not take the niggahīta augment like the roots saki and saṅkāyaṃ. This same method should be followed in other similar cases.

The root pata is used in the sense of going. Patati (he goes). Papatati (he falls/drops). Papātaṃ (a precipice). "I wish to descend" (papatayyaham). "I have fallen heavily into hell" (pāpattaṃ nirayaṃ bhusaṃ). Here, as it is used with the word 'ahaṃ' (I), 'pāpattaṃ' means 'papatitosmi' (I have fallen). In the phrase "That prince has fallen heavily into hell" (pāpattha nirayaṃ bhusaṃ), as it is used with 'so kumāro' (that prince), 'pāpattha' means 'papatito' (he has fallen). Both of these are forms ending in the parokkhā tense. As in 'pāvadaṃ', 'pāvadā', etc., the prefix (pa-) is lengthened, and then the suffix 'aṃ' is substituted with 'ttaṃ', and the suffix 'a' is substituted with 'ttha'. The methods of the Pali language are indeed difficult to conceive.
64:
The root ata is used in the sense of continuous and repeated occurrence (sātaccagamana). Continuous occurrence without interruption is called sātaccagamana. Atati means it occurs without ceasing. Since the root ata expresses the sense of continuous occurrence, the definition of "attā" (self/soul) is also desired in the sense that one constantly reaches, obtains, or undergoes the various sufferings of saṃsāra—such as birth, aging, sickness, and death—while wandering through various existences. Furthermore, by virtue of specific meanings, it should be understood that: "It is called attā (attabhāva, personhood) because the conceit 'I am' is placed in this self"; "It is called attā because it continuously experiences pleasure and pain"; and "Attamana means one whose mind is seized by joy and happiness." This is because the meaning should be taken in each case according to how the sense is obtained in that particular term.

The root cuta is used in the senses of pouring out and vanishing or being exhausted. Cotati means he pours out, or it is exhausted and destroyed.

The root ati is used in the sense of binding. Antati means he binds. It is called anta (intestine) because it is bound by the small intestine. Here, I shall present the various meanings of the word anta. In the phrase "antaṃ antaguṇaṃ udariyaṃ", the loathsome large and small intestines included in the thirty-two parts of the body are called anta. In the phrase "kāyabandhanassa anto jīrati" or "haritantaṃ vā", the final limit or boundary is called anta. In the phrase "Monks, this living by alms is the lowest (antamidam) among livelihoods," anta means low or inferior. In the phrase "The self-identity (sakkāya) is one part (anto)," anta means a portion or group. In the phrase "Because of the destruction of conditioned things along with their causes, this is the end (anto) of suffering," anta means the extreme end or conclusion. Thus—
65:
The word 'anta' is used to express the meanings of the large intestine, the small intestine, a group, that which occurs at the end, a limit, a bad state, a collection, and an edge.

The root 'kita' occurs in the sense of dwelling and in the sense of removing disease. (For example:) 'Ketati' (he dwells). The city of Sāketa, 'niketo' (house), 'niketaṃ pāvisi' (he entered the house). 'Āmodamāno gacchati sanniketaṃ' (joyfully he goes to his own place). 'Tikicchati', 'cikicchati' (he treats medically), 'cikicchā' (medical treatment), 'cikicchako' (a physician). Among these terms, 'Sāketa' is so called because it is a place of residence taken up in the evening; the word 'yaṃ' is elided.

The root 'yata' occurs in the sense of making an effort or exertion. 'Patiyatana' means making an effort. (For example:) 'Yatati' (he exerts). 'Yati' (a monk), 'yatavā' (one who exerts), 'payatanaṃ' (effort or articulation), 'āyatanaṃ' (sense-sphere), 'lokāyataṃ' (the Lokāyata treatise). Among these terms, 'āyatana' is so called because it is a place of exertion; it refers to the eye, forms, and so on. Indeed, in those [bases] such as the eye and forms, the mental states of consciousness and mental factors that arise depending on the respective doors and objects exert themselves, arise, are incited, or make an effort through their respective functions such as experiencing; therefore, they are called 'āyatanas'. In this context, the meaning of the word 'āyatana' should also be explained by virtue of the roots 'nī' and 'tanu'; this matter will be made clear further above.

The word 'āyatana' is used in the senses of a dwelling place, a source (mine), a meeting place, a place of birth, and a cause. To demonstrate this: in such passages as 'loke issarāyatanaṃ vāsudevāyatanaṃ', the word 'āyatana' occurs in the sense of a dwelling place. In 'suvaṇṇāyatanaṃ rajatāyatanaṃ', it occurs in the sense of a source (mine). In the Dispensation (Sāsana), however, in such passages as 'manorame āyatane, sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā', it occurs in the sense of a meeting place. In 'dakkhiṇāpatho gunnaṃ āyatanaṃ', it occurs in the sense of a place of birth. In 'tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti sati sati-āyatane', it occurs in the sense of a cause.
66:
It should be understood that it has the meaning of 'āyatana'. That meaning should be taken by virtue of the various reasons for the occurrence of the word 'āyatana'.

In dwelling places, in sources,
In places of birth, in causes,
And in meeting places,
The usage of 'āyatana' is found.

That which is called 'Lokāyata' is a sectarian treatise connected with useless reasoning, such as: "Everything is a remnant, everything is not a remnant; the crow is white, the crane is black, because of this and that reason," and so forth. In the world, it is called the "Vitaṇḍa treatise" (sophistry). Referring to that treatise, Vidhura Paṇḍita, who possessed incomparable wisdom and energy, said: "One should not associate with a Lokāyatika; this is not for the increase of wisdom." It is called 'Lokāyata' because, due to that treatise, people do not exert themselves or strive for what is beneficial in the future. It is indeed the Vitaṇḍa treatise. Depending on that text, beings do not even give rise to the thought of performing meritorious deeds. In other texts also, it is said: "The art of Lokāyata is the art of the Vitaṇḍa treatise which denies the next world and Nibbāna, proceeding in such a manner as: 'The crow is white because the bones are white; the crane is red because the blood is red'."

The roots 'yuta' and 'juta' occur in the sense of speaking. Speaking is called 'udīraṇa'. The forms are 'yotati' and 'jotati'.

The root 'juta' occurs in the sense of splendor and radiance. The forms are 'jotati' and 'vijjotati'. 'Juti' is light or glory. 'Joti' is majesty or power. Alternatively, 'joti' refers to the moon and so on. It is also said in the commentary to the Sirimāvimāna-vatthu: "'Joti' is a common name for the moon, sun, constellations, and stars." Alternatively, according to the statement "joti jotiparāyaṇo", one who shines due to being born in a noble family (Khattiya) and so on, and due to the beauty of their physical form, is called 'joti'.
67:
The root 'sita' occurs in the sense of the color white. The root 'sita' occurs in the sense of the color white. Although color in general is mentioned here, in this context of the root 'sita', among colors such as blue and yellow, only the color white should be taken by virtue of seeing its usage. 'Setati' - it is white. 'Setaṃ vatthaṃ' - a white cloth. Because it is an adjective (vāccaliṅga), the word 'seta' should be understood as having three genders.

Seta, sita, suci, sukka,
Paṇḍara, dhavala,
Akaṇha, gora, odāta,
These are indeed the names for white.

The root 'vatu' occurs in the sense of occurring or becoming. The forms are 'vattati', 'pavattati', 'saṃvattati', 'anuvattati', 'parivattati'. 'Pavattaṃ' - occurrence.

The root 'kilota' occurs in the sense of being wet. 'Addabhāva' means the state of being wet. 'Kilotati', 'pakilotati' - it is wet, it is moist (meaning 'temeti'). In the causative form, 'pakiloteti', 'pakilotayati' - he makes wet. 'Uṇhodakasmiṃ pakilotayitvā' - having moistened in hot water (meaning 'temetvā').

The root 'vata' occurs in the sense of begging. 'Vatati' - he begs.

The root 'kita' occurs in the sense of knowledge. 'Ketati' - he knows. 'Ketanaṃ' - knowledge, 'ketako' - one who knows, 'saṅketo' - a sign for knowing (convention).

The root 'kati' occurs in the sense of producing thread. 'Suttaṃ kantati' - he spins thread.

The root 'kati' occurs in the sense of cutting. 'Maṃsaṃ kantati', 'vikantati' - he cuts or slices meat. 'Ayokanto' - that which cuts iron. 'Sallakanto mahāvīro' - the Great Hero (the Buddha) who cuts the arrow-barb. "May the King's cooks in the kitchen not cut us today."

The root 'catī' occurs in the senses of harming and scent. Because this root ends in the vowel 'ī', the augment 'niggahīta' does not occur after this root. 'Catati' - he harms or the scent spreads.

## Forms of roots ending in 'ta'.
68:
## Roots Ending in the Letter Ṭha

The root ṭhā is used in the sense of stopping from going (gatinivattiyaṃ). ṭhāti—he stands or stays. avatthā—staying for a moment (a state); vavatthānaṃ—staying by defining (determination); vavatthitaṃ—that which is defined; vanatho—standing in the forest. In this [Dhammapada verse], "Having cut down the forest (vana) and the undergrowth (vanatha)," large trees are called 'vana', while small trees are called 'vanatha' because they stand (ṭhita) in that forest.

The root thu is used in the sense of praising (thomanā). thavati—he praises; abhitthavati—he praises greatly. thavanā, abhitthavanā, thuti, abhitthuti [all carry the meaning of praise].

If my wisdom had a visible form, my wisdom would not be equal to this earth.

For the Blessed One Anomadassī, this [attainment of great wisdom] is the very fruit of praising his knowledge.

He (the ascetic Sumedha), who is praised by them (devas and brahmas), is one whose virtues are praised; by whom this knowledge is praised, and the Most Excellent Buddha is also lauded. In this context, thavanā means praising (pasaṃsanā). There are many names for praising:

thavanā, pasaṃsā, silāghā, vaṇṇanā, thuti,
panuti, thomanā, vaṇṇo, katthanā, guṇakittanaṃ.

The root the is used in the senses of making a sound and aggregating. thīyati—he speaks or he binds with anger; patiṭṭhīyati—he binds by the power of anger. thī—a woman. In this regard, the Pali passages are: "He clings, gets angry, becomes perverted, binds with anger (patiṭṭhīyati), and manifests anger, hatred, and discontent," and "Women (thiyo) reviled her (Amittā)." In those instances, the words "thīyati" and "patiṭṭhīyati" are formed by substituting 'e' (at the end of the root) with 'īya'. A fetus reaches aggregation (thīyati) in this person; therefore, she is called 'thī'. However, the teachers state this etymology only for the word 'itthī', and not for the word 'thī'.

A fetus reaches aggregation in her, thus she is called 'thī'; this is our preference.
A fetus reaches aggregation in her, thus she is called 'itthī'; so say the teachers.
In their explanation, the formation of the word 'itthī' is very difficult.
This conclusion has been reached; O sirs, listen to my conclusion.
69: The word "itthī" is identical in meaning to the word "thī"; therefore, by attributing the meaning obtained in the word "thī" to the word "itthī", it is appropriate to consider the formation of the longer word "itthī" from the shorter word "thī". Indeed, the instances where "dve" becomes "duve" and "taṇhā" becomes "tasiṇā" serve as evidence. Alternatively, it should be shown that this word "itthī" is also established through linguistic principles (niruttilakkhaṇa) such as letter augmentation (vaṇṇāgama). She is called "itthī" because she desires men, or because she makes men desire her. This etymology should also be known by those seeking the meaning of the derivation. In this context, the names for women are: itthī, thī, vanitā, nārī, abalā, bhīru, sundarī, kantā, sīmaninī, mātugāma, piyā, and kāminī, ramaṇī, pamadā, dayitā, lalanā, mahilā, aṅganā. Even these names of women are further called according to the stages of age as follows: gorī, dārikā, kaññā, kumārī, kumārikā, yuvatī, taruṇī, māṇavikā, therī, mahallikā. In fact, an eight-year-old girl is called both gorī and dārikā. A ten-year-old girl is called kaññā. Alternatively, a young woman who is not yet married is called kaññā. A twelve-year-old girl is called both kumārī and kumārikā. Furthermore, a woman who has not yet reached old age is called yuvatī, taruṇī, and māṇavikā. A woman who has reached old age is called therī and mahallikā. This method should also be understood accordingly for men. Although such a rule is stated here, in some places, usage occurs without such restriction. Therefore, according to these two Pali passages: "The King, taking the prince (kumāra), and the Princess, taking the girl (dārikā)" and "Grant the maiden (kaññā) Kaṇhājinā," the girl who should be called by the word dārikā has also come to be called by the word kaññā.
70:
A woman who should be called by the word kaññā is also called by the word dārikā. Similarly, by the power of these Pali passages: "The King, carrying the prince (kumāra, i.e., Jāli), and the Princess (Queen Maddī), carrying the girl (dārikā, i.e., Kaṇhājinā)" and "Young maidens (kumārikā) who are always adorned with moving bracelets and who sleep near their mother," a woman who should be called by the word dārikā is also called by the word kumārikā. A woman who should be called by the word kumārī is also called by the word dārikā. Moreover, by observing these two Pali passages: "The princess named Rucā" and "Thereafter, the assembled women of the Sivi king also consecrated Queen Maddī," it should be understood that whether she is a virgin or not, as long as she has not reached old age, that woman is simply known as a kaññā.

In this matter, some might say: "You have said that an eight-year-old is called both gorī and dārikā. In that statement, let an eight-year-old be called a dāraka (boy/child) because of the words 'When I was a boy (dāraka), eight years from birth.' However, in the Pali 'He saw that prince (kumāra) enjoying himself in his own palace,' how can it be appropriate to call the Great King Vessantara, who has already flourished with a wife and children and has passed twelve years of age, a 'kumāra'?" It is appropriate by the power of the Blessed One's intention. Because the Blessed One is the Master of Dhamma and is skilled in conventional usage (vohāra), He teaches whatever discourse is suitable for the beings to be tamed (veneyya). Therefore, the Blessed One gave this teaching by referring to the fact that King Vessantara's parents were still living and that he was raised with the retinue and care of a prince. Similarly, the Venerable Kumāra-Kassapa, because he was raised with the retinue of a prince, was called Kumāra-Kassapa even when he was old. In the phrase "This youth (kumāraka) does not know moderation," the Venerable Mahākassapa [addressed] the elder Venerable Ānanda [as such], even though grey hairs had appeared on his head...
71:
Being very familiar, he should be understood as having spoken the word 'boy' (kumāraka) while admonishing in the manner of a youth. However, in the Udāna Commentary (Udāna-aṭṭhakathā), it is stated: "Beings from the day of their birth until fifteen years of age are called boys (kumāraka) or fools (bāla); after that, for twenty years, they are called young adults (yuvāna)."

The roots 'mantha' and 'mattha' occur in the sense of churning or agitation. 'Manthati'—he churns. "Taking the honey-ball (madhupiṇḍika) and the churning stick." "Evil destroys the fool just as a diamond (vajira) destroys the gem (maṇi) from which it was formed." "Making Mount Sineru the churning stick."

The roots 'kuthi', 'puthi', and 'luthi' occur in the senses of oppression (hiṃsā) and defilement (saṃkilesa). 'Kunthati'—he oppresses. 'Kuntha'—oppression; 'kunthakipillika'—ants and insects. "Seeing his son Suvaṇṇasāma fallen, prostrate, and defiled by being covered in dust (paṃsukunthita)." 'Punthati', 'lunthati'.

The root 'nātha' occurs in four meanings: requesting (yācana), tormenting/heating (upatāpa), mastery (issariya), and wishing (āsīsana). The root 'nātha' has its function in these four senses: yācana (requesting), upatāpa (tormenting), issariya (mastery), and āsīsana (wishing). Therefore, the ancient teachers said: "He is called 'Nātha' because he wishes (nāthati); for he wishes for and desires the welfare and happiness of those to be led (veneyya). Or, he torments the destruction of defilements within the continuities of others. Or, he requests the respective practice of welfare, saying, 'Monks, a monk should from time to time reflect upon his own attainment,' and so forth. Or, because he is endowed with supreme mastery of the mind, or because he overcomes and masters all beings through his attributes, the Blessed One, being the Supreme Lord, is called 'Nātha'. Thus, he is 'Nātha' because he wishes/masters (nāthati)." However, scholars of grammar read two roots, 'nātha' and 'nādha', in those four meanings. Because they are in the middle voice (attanopada), the forms 'nāthate' and 'nādhate' occur.

In this context, it might be asked: "If he is called 'Nātha' because of the sense of requesting, then any poor beggar would be..."
72:
"...a 'Nātha'. And one who is not a beggar and is wealthy would be an 'Anātha' because he does not request (na nāthati, na yācati)?"

That should not be said. For although the word 'nātha' occurs in the sense of requesting and so forth, by way of worldly convention (loka-saṅketa), it is established (rūḷha) only for noble persons (uttama-purisa). And the Blessed One is the most excellent among the noble. Therefore, the meaning of the word 'nātha' is stated as 'requesting' (or granting) the respective practice of welfare. 

The word 'anātha', however, is established for lowly people other than the noble. Such a person is called 'anātha' by way of negating the substance (dabba-paṭisedha), meaning "one who is not a protector (na nātho)" or "one for whom there is no protector (natthi nātho)"; it is not called 'anātha' by way of negating the verbal meaning of the root (dhātu-attha-paṭisedha), as in "one who does not request (na nāthati)". In truth, one who is a refuge, a destination, and a support for others is called 'Nātha'. One who is not a refuge, destination, or support for others, and who has no other refuge, destination, or support for himself, is called 'Anātha' by way of convention. Thus it is said: "Conventional speech is truth, having worldly consensus (loka-sammuti) as its cause."

To clarify this meaning, the following Pāḷi passages serve as evidence in this context: "You alone are the Protector of the World (Lokanātha), the refuge of all living beings," and "You are the Protector (Nātha) of the helpless (anāthānaṃ)."

And: "Having thought thus, and having given wealth amounting to many hundreds of millions to those with protectors (nātha) and those without (anātha), I went to the Himālaya."

This is because, in both the Dispensation (Sāsana) and the world, a beggar is not called 'Nātha', nor is one who does not beg called 'Anātha'. Only one who is the refuge of the world is called 'Nātha'. One for whom no refuge exists is called 'Anātha'. Similarly, a wealthy person is called 'Nātha', and one who is not well-off is called 'Anātha'. Therefore, a wise person should not over-rely on the mere literal meaning of the root in all instances, but should grasp the meaning appropriately without overstepping worldly usage. This method should be carefully borne in mind.

The root 'vithu' occurs in the sense of requesting. 'Vethati'—he requests.

The root 'satha' occurs in the sense of laxity (sithila). 'Sathati'—it is lax. This is because a lax (broken) monastic practice greatly scatters the dust of passion (rāga) and so forth. (Therefore, one should strive firmly in that monastic practice.)

There is also the Pāḷi form 'sithilo'. In that case, the cerebral 'ṭha' (muddaja) should be taken.

The root 'kathi' occurs in the sense of crookedness (deceit). 'Kanthati'—he is crooked.
73:
Who is called what? One who is the refuge of the world is called 'Nātha'. One who has no refuge is called 'Anātha'. Similarly, one who is wealthy and prosperous is called 'Nātha'. One who is not prosperous is called 'Anātha'. Therefore, in all instances of the terms 'Nātha' and 'Anātha', the wise should not go beyond the worldly conventional designation by merely taking the sense of 'begging' for the root *nātha*, but should adopt the meaning as appropriate. This method should also be well-reflected upon.

The root *vithu* is used in the sense of begging. *Vethati* — he begs.

The root *satha* is used in the sense of looseness (slackness). *Sathati* — he is loose. For a loose (broken or patchy) monastic practice scatters the dust of defilements excessively. There is also the Pali form '*sithilo*'. In that case, the cerebral letter '*ṭha*' should be taken.

The root *kathi* is used in the sense of crookedness. *Kanthati* — he is crooked.

The root *kattha* is used in the sense of praising. *Katthati*, *vikatthati* — he praises. *Katthanā*, *vikatthanā* — praising. Among these terms, *katthati* means to praise. *Vikatthati* means to boast or brag groundlessly because it demonstrates an unreal matter. Here also, there are usages such as: "He might boast much of himself when he has gone to another country," and "In this world, a certain person is given to praising and especially to boasting; he boasts, 'I am endowed with virtue' or 'I am endowed with practice'," and so on.

The root *vyatha* is used in the senses of suffering, fear, and trembling. *Vyathati* — he suffers, he fears, he trembles. There is the usage: "With trembling and suffering minds." At that time, the young boys, having heard the words of the cruel Brahmin Jūjaka, were terrified and trembled (and ran to hide). Thus, both of these occur: trembling, and suffering or fear.

The roots *sutha*, *kutha*, and *katha* are used in the sense of harming. *Sothati*, *kothati*, *kathati* — he harms.

The root *patha* is used in the sense of going. *Pathati* — he goes. *Patho* — a path. *Patho* means a way (marga). That way is twofold: the ordinary path to be traveled on foot by the general public, and the Noble Path known as the practice (*paṭipadā*) to be practiced by the wise who desire Nibbāna. Among them, the ordinary path is called '*patha*' because it is traveled (*pathiyati*) by people with various affairs. The path of practice, however, is called '*patha*' because it is practiced (*pathiyati*) by sons of good family who, desiring to go to the great city of the Deathless, take the provisions of faith. Alternatively, it is called '*patha*' because it causes the practitioner to reach Nibbāna.
74:
The word *patha* refers only to the practice (*paṭipadā*). I shall speak of the name '*magga*' in the section discussing the root *magga* in the *Curādigana* group.

The root *katha* is used in the sense of cooking or ripening (*nippāka*). *Kathati* — he cooks.

The root *matha* is used in the sense of churning or oppressing (*vilothana*). *Mathati* — he oppresses, he crushes, he churns.

The root *potha* is used in the sense of wandering around (*pariyāyanabhāva*). *Pothati* — he wanders around. *Pothako* — one who wanders around. This root *potha* also occurs in the *Curādigana* group as *potheti*. Therefore, the usage is seen: "They would wander all around, crushing (beings) from the four directions."

The root *gottha* is used in the sense of lineage (*vaṃsa*). *Gotthati* — he relates to a lineage. *Gotthulo*, *gotthu* — a jackal.

The root *puthu* is used in the sense of expansion (*vitthāra*). *Pothati* — he expands. *Pathavī* — the earth.

## Roots ending in the letter 'Tha'.
75:
## Roots ending in the letter 'Da'.

The root *dā* is used in the sense of giving. When the prefix *ā-* is present, it is used in the sense of taking. A person with faith gives a gift. He undertakes (takes) virtue. These terms are simple agent (*suddha-kattu*) terms because they indicate that simple agent. Faith causes one without faith to give a gift, to take virtue, or to undertake it. The virtuous cause only the Dhamma to be undertaken. These terms are called causative (*kārita*) terms or causal agent (*hetu-kattu*) terms because they indicate that. By one with faith, a gift is given, virtue is taken, or it is undertaken. These terms are passive (*kamma*) terms because they indicate that.

This same root *dā*, through its usage consistent with the Dispensation, reaches the *Divādigana* group; when it expresses the action of sleeping, it produces simple agent terms along with noun terms such as "*dāyati*, *niddāyati* (he sleeps), *niddā* (sleep)." When it expresses the sense of cutting, it produces simple agent terms along with noun terms such as "*diyati* (he cuts), *dānaṃ* (cutting), *dāttaṃ* (a sickle)." When it expresses the sense of purification, it produces simple agent terms along with noun terms such as "*dāyati*, *vedāyati* (he is pure), *vodānaṃ* (purification)." In this *Bhūvādigana* group, however, when it expresses the sense of giving, and by the presence of the prefix *ā-*, the sense of taking, it produces simple agent terms along with noun terms such as "*dadāti*, *deti*, *ādadāti*, *ādeti*, *dānaṃ*, *ādānaṃ*." Similarly, when it expresses the sense of despicable going, it produces simple agent terms along with noun terms such as "*dāti*, *suddāti* (he runs away), *suddo* (a low-caste man), *suddī* (a low-caste woman)." Such distinctions should be noted. Just as in this case, the distinctions should be investigated by those who know the method in other cases as well, wherever possible.

Now, the noun terms of this root such as *dānaṃ*, *deyyaṃ*, *dātabbaṃ*, *brahmadeyyaṃ*, *dinnaṃ*, *dāyako*, *dāyikā*, *dakkhiṇā*, etc., and the *tumanta* and other forms such as *dātuṃ*, *padātuṃ*, *dātave*, *padātave*, *datvā*, *datvāna*, *dadātuna*, *daditvā*, *daditvāna*, *dadiya*, *dajjā*, *dadiyāna*, *ādātuṃ*, *ādāya*, *ādiya*, etc., should be applied.

Among those terms, '*dāna*' refers to the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*), and because of the sense "they give by means of this quality," it also refers to the volition of giving (*dāna-cetanā*). Why is only the word '*dinna*' mentioned among those terms and not the word '*datta*'? There is a reason for not mentioning it. In places such as "*dānaṃ dinnaṃ*," the word '*datta*' is not seen in place of the word '*dinna*'; therefore, it is not mentioned.

The word *datta* as a secondary attribute is not seen in the words of the Conqueror.
Just as the term *dinna* is found in "A gift was given by me with the mind,"
The terms "*Devadatto*, *Yaññadatto*, *Datto*," and so on,
Are seen in conventional designations, whether in compound or in isolation.

Therefore, in terms such as "*Devadatto*," having formed the compound as "given by a deva (*devena dinno*)," because it is a conventional designation, the word '*dinna*' should be changed to '*datta*' in accordance with the Dispensation. Later on, you will see the grammatical rule: "*Datta* is sometimes substituted for *dinna* in conventional designations." This is indeed the method (*nīti*) in the Dispensation that should not be transgressed. The distinction here is:
