Other usages have already been shown in “yata patiyatane,” etc.

The root *nī* is used in the sense of reaching (*pāpana*). *Neti*, *nayati* (he reaches). *Nayana* (eye).

The root *nu* is used in the sense of praising (*thuti*). *Noti*, *navati* (he praises). *Nuta* (praised).

The roots *thana*, *pana*, and *dhana* are used in the sense of making sound (*sadda*). *Thanati* (it thunders), *panati* (he speaks), *dhanati* (it roars).

The root *kana* is used in the senses of splendor and desire (*ditti*, *kanti*). *Kanati* (it is splendid/desirable). *Kaññā* (maiden), *kanaka* (gold).

Here, because she stays in the youthful stage, she is called *kaññā* because she is splendid, radiant, and brilliant with the charm of her form. Alternatively, she is called *kaññā* (a young woman) because she is desired and longed for by men. *Kanaka* is so called because it is splendid or because it is desired. Indeed, there are many names for gold.

*Suvaṇṇa*, *kanaka*, *hema*,
*kañcana*, *hāṭaka*,
*jātarūpa*, *tapanīya*, *vaṇṇa*;
The special types of gold are also called *jambunada*, *siṅgī*, and *cāmīkara*.
113:
The roots *vana* and *sana* occur in the sense of resorting to (associating). *Vanati* means he resorts to. *Vanaṃ* means forest. *Sanati* means he resorts to.

Among those terms, *vanaṃ* is called *vana* (forest) because beings such as peacocks and cuckoos resort to that place. It is called *vana* (craving/taṇhā) because it resorts to a person possessed of defilements.

The root *mana* occurs in the sense of excessive desire (longing). *Manati* means he longs for. *Mano* means the mind.

The root *māna* occurs in the sense of investigation. *Vīmaṃsati* means he investigates. *Vīmaṃsā* means investigation.

The roots *jana* and *suna* occur in the sense of making a sound (uttering). *Janati* means it sounds; *sunati* means it sounds.

In this context, the Pali: "Why does one of your arms sound (*janati*), and one of your arms not sound?" is the evidence. In that Pali, *janati* means it sounds or makes a noise.

The root *khanu* occurs in the sense of digging or breaking. *Khanati* means he digs. There are the terms *sukha* (happiness) and *dukkha* (suffering). *Khato* means a dug pit.

Among those terms, *sukha* is so called because it digs out (*khanati*) suffering well (*su*). *Dukkha* is so called because it digs out physical and mental happiness badly (*du*). Indeed, these two phenomena (*dhamma*) are opposites of each other. Alternatively, it is called *dukkha* because it digs into or splits the mind in two. However, by the power of the *Curādi* class, the definitions should be taken as: "*sukha* because it makes one happy (*sukhayati*), *dukkha* because it makes one suffer (*dukkhayati*)." By the power of compound words (*samāsapada*), various etymologies are also taken, such as: "*sukha* because it is easy (*sukaraṃ*) to endure (*khama*), *dukkha* because it is difficult (*dukkaraṃ*) to endure." Indeed, the etymologies, origins, and signifying causes of words are diverse and manifold.

The root *dāna* occurs in the sense of cutting or dividing. *Dānati* means he cuts. *Apadānaṃ* means cutting or severing.

The root *sāna* occurs in the sense of sharpening (making sharp). *Nisānaṃ* means sharpening. *Sānati* means he sharpens.

The root *hana* occurs in the sense of harming and going. In this context, by the word *hiṃsā* (harming), both oppression by harsh speech and striking with sticks, spears, etc., are included. Therefore, the meaning of the root *hana* should be taken as harming, striking, and going. Thus, the commentators, in explaining the meaning of the passage: "Kings, having caught a thief, might strike (*haneyyuṃ*) or bind him," stated: "*haneyyuṃ* means they might both strike and...
114:
...they might also cut." In this context, 'cutting' (*chedana*) refers to the cutting of hands, feet, etc., or killing by means of decapitation. The root *hana* has the substitutes *vadha* and *ghāta*. It takes forms such as *hanti*, *hanati*, *hananti*, *hanasi*, *hanatha*, and so on. All the rest should be understood accordingly.

Four meanings, such as harming (*hiṃsā*), are obtained. In the phrase "He strikes (*hanti*) with hands and feet," *hanti* here means he strikes (*paharati*). In the phrase "An angry person kills (*hanti*) even his father. Crying out, they kill (*hanti*) the best among those sons with sharp spears," *hanti* here means they kill (*mārenti*). The forms *vadhati*, *vadheti*, and *ghāteti* also occur. Among those, in places such as "He strikes (*vadhati*), does not cry, he commits a *dukkaṭa* offense. He cries after repeatedly striking (*vadhitvā*) himself," *vadha* is in the sense of striking (*paharaṇa*). In "He kills (*vadheti*) a living being," "killing of living beings (*pāṇavadha*)," "This is the killing (*vadho*) of Khaṇḍahāla," and "He kills (*ghāteti*) beings," *vadha* is in the sense of killing (*māraṇa*).

In the words *upāhana* (sandal) and *vadhū* (woman), the meaning of the words *hana* and *vadha* is going (*gamana*). Phrases such as "He kills the man," and "He removes (*paṭihanati*) cold and heat," are active voice (*kattu*) terms. "Devadatta is killed (*haññati*) by Yajñadatta." "Then, when there is fierce wind and sun, it is removed (*paṭihaññati*)." The nominative case ending is changed to *-e*, as in the example "*vanappagumbe*." The word "*vihārena*" should be connected; these are passive voice (*kamma*) terms. *Hantā*, *hato*, *vadhako*, *vadhū*, *āghāto*, *upaghāto*, *ghātako*, *paṭigho*, *saṅgho*, *byaggho*, *sakuṇagghi*, *hantuṃ*, *hanituṃ*, *hantvā*, *hanitွာ*, *vajjhetvā*, *vadhitvā*, and so on, are nouns and terms ending in *tum* and other suffixes.

Among those terms, *upāhana* (sandal) is so called because with this sandal, they go to (*upagacchanti*) various places, and from there they return (*āhanati/āgacchanti*). *Vadhū* is so called because she tends to go (*upagamana-sīlā*) even to a dog by the power of defilements; this name is for all...
115:
...women in common. Alternatively, *vadhū* means a daughter-in-law. Thus, it is said (in the Sudinna story): "Daughter-in-law (*vadhu*), if it be so, when you have your season and the flower (menstrual blood) has arisen, then inform me." Here, *vadhū* refers to a daughter-in-law. She is called *vadhū* because she is to be known (*jānitabbā*) or recognized by the parents-in-law as "This is our son's wife." Since roots meaning 'going' sometimes express the meaning of 'knowing', this meaning is obtained. *Suṇhā*, *suṇisā*, and *vadhū* are synonyms.

*Saṅgha* refers to a group of monks. It is called *saṅgha* because it properly arrives at (*samupagacchati*) a harmonious act (*samaggaṃ kammaṃ*). Alternatively, it is called *saṅgha* because it properly kills (*hanti*) defilements, slaying them with the sword of this or that Path. These definitions are stated in terms of worldlings (*puthujjana*) and noble ones (*ariya*).

It is called *byaggha* (tiger) because it kills (*āhanati*) or slays (*ghāteti*) various beings excessively. That same tiger is also called *viyaggha* and *vaggha*. Another name for it is *puṇḍarīka*. It is called *sakuṇagghi* (hawk/falcon) because it kills weak birds. This root *hana*, in the *Divādi* class, produces the intransitive active form *paṭihaññati*. Thus, in the Pali: "The speech (*vohāro*) of the Blessed Buddha strikes (*paṭihaññati*) the worldly ear," and other such passages are seen.

The root *ana* occurs in the sense of breathing (*pāṇana*). *Pāṇana* means breathing in and out. *Anati* (he breathes). *Āna* and *pāna*. Among them, *āna* is *assāsa* (exhalation). *Pāna* is *passāsa* (inhalation). "Among those two, *assāsa* is the wind going out. *Passāsa* is the wind entering inside," so it is stated in the Vinaya Commentary. In the Suttanta Commentaries, however, it appears in the reverse order. In that regard, because for all womb-born beings, at the time of exiting the mother's womb, the internal air first exits to the outside, and later the external air, carrying subtle dust, enters inside and subsides upon hitting the palate, it is stated in the Vinaya Commentary: "*assāsa* is the wind going out, *passāsa* is the wind entering inside."
116: Between these two methods, according to the Vinaya method, the breath that arises internally and goes out is assāsa, and the breath that arises externally and enters is passāsa. However, according to the Suttanta method, even though it is breath that arises externally and enters internally, it is called assāsa because it is inhaled. Even though it is breath that arises internally and goes out externally, it is called passāsa because it is exhaled. It should be understood that this Suttanta method alone is consistent with this Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali text: “For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of assāsa, due to the mind being distracted internally, both the body and the mind become distressed, agitated, and trembling,” and “For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of passāsa, due to the mind being distracted externally, both the body and the mind become distressed, agitated, and trembling.” The root dhana occurs in the sense of dhanya (abundance). Dhananaṃ means dhanyaṃ (abundance), meaning the attainment of glory, merit, and wisdom. Indeed, the meaning of a root is mostly stated in terms of the abstract state (bhāva), excluding specific instances like the bark or skin of a tree. Just as in the sense of the abstract state, the letter na is changed to yya along with the suffix ya to say theyyaṃ for thenanaṃ, so here too, the letter na is changed to ñña along with the suffix ya to say dhanyaṃ for dhananaṃ. Or, the state of one who possesses glory, merit, and wisdom is dhanya; the root dhana occurs in that sense of dhanya. Dhanti, dhanati (it is abundant). Dhanitaṃ (abundance). Dhanyaṃ (abundance). Since the attainment of glory, merit, and wisdom is taken by the word dhanya, in passages such as “She gave birth to a son endowed with the signs of glory, wisdom, and merit,” only glory and wisdom should be taken by the word dhanya, because merit (puñña) is mentioned separately. Nadato parisāyante, vāditabbapahārino. Roaring like a lion in the midst of the assembly, striking the great drum of Dhamma, Ye te dakkhanti vadanaṃ, dhaññā te narapuṅgava. Those who shall behold Your face, O Bull among men, they shall be the fortunate ones. Dīghāṅgulī tambanakhe, subhe āyatapaṇhike. Having long toes, copper-colored nails, a beautiful appearance, and long heels, Ye pāde paṇamissanti, tepi dhaññā guṇandhara. Those who shall bow at Your feet, O Bearer of Virtues, they too shall be the fortunate ones. Madhurāni pahaṭṭhāni, dosagghāni hitāni ca. Sweet, joyful, dispelling faults, and beneficial, Yete vākyāni sossanti, tepi dhaññā naruttamāti. Those who shall hear Your words, O Supreme among men, they too shall be the fortunate ones.
117:
In such words as these, the term dhanya should be understood as the fulfillment of merit (puññasampadā). Alternatively, along with the fulfillment of merit, it should also include the fulfillment of glory and wisdom (siripaññāsampadā). The derivation (nibbacana) here is: "Those who possess glory, merit, and wisdom, which are called dhanya, are thus called dhanyā."

In the phrase "dhanyaṃ maṅgalasammataṃ" from the Vessantara Jātaka, it is called dhanya because it (the Paccaya elephant) is to be believed in and cherished as a "noble jewel." The meanings of being endowed with glory, merit, and wisdom are also appropriate.

In phrases such as "dhanyaṃ dhanaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ," it is called dhanya because it is cherished, according to the Buddha's word: "There is no wealth equal to grain (dhanya)." What is that dhanya? It is grain (pubbaṇṇa). Alternatively, a specific type of medicine (cumin/fennel) is also called dhanya.

Regarding the word dhana, by the power of compound (samāsa), in terms like "adhana" and "niddhana," it refers to a poor person (dalidda) with the meaning "one who has no wealth." In the phrase "nidhanaṃ yāti" (goes to destruction), however, by the power of the root dhū which expresses the sense of shaking, destruction is called nidhana.

The root mun is in the sense of being silent or knowing. Munati—he remains silent, or he knows.

The root cine is in the sense of thinking. This root is an aluttanta root (where the final consonant is not dropped), like the roots gile and mile. Cināyati—he thinks. Ocināyati—he thinks with disregard (despises). The phrase from the Temiya Jātaka, "May all the people despise (ocināyatu) you," is the scriptural evidence here. Ocināyatu means let them know as inferior (let them despise).

## Thus the forms of roots ending in the Ta-group (tavagga) in the Bhūvādi class are completed.

## Roots ending in the letter Pa

Now the forms of roots ending in the Pa-group (pavagga) will be told:

The root pā is in the sense of drinking. Pāna means drinking (pivana). Pāti, pānti, pātu, pāntu, etc., should be applied as appropriate.

Stretch out your neck quickly, I shall not give you your life.
For this arrow, which I have fixed (on the bow), will drink your blood.
118:
In this context, "pāssati" means "pivissati" (will drink). The rest should all be applied by those who know the method, in the manner of "pāssati, pāssanti; pāssasi, pāssatha; pāssāmi, pāssāma," and "apassā, apassaṃsu," etc. For who is capable of extracting and showing all the various and scattered jewel-like forms from the ocean of the Buddha's words? Therefore, for all roots, only the method of grasping them in brief is shown. Pivati, pivanti. Pivaṃ, pivanto, pivamāno—drinking the water of the Ganges called Bhāgirathī. In the causative (kārita) sense: "kumāraṃ khīraṃ pāyeti" (causes the boy to drink milk). "I have caused you to drink milk just enough to quench your thirst for a moment." In the passive (kamma) sense: "pīyati," "pītaṃ." With suffixes like tu, etc.: "pātuṃ, pivituṃ, pitvā, pivitvā, pāyetvā," etc., should be applied. In other places also, the word forms should be applied in this very way according to the Pali method.

The root pā is in the sense of protecting. Pāti. Nipāti. Pitā (father), gopo (cowherd).

The root pā is in the sense of filling. Pāti, vippāti. Vippo.

Vippa means a Brāhmaṇa (Brahmin). That Brahmin is called "vippa" because he fills the desire of the world with his Brahminical duties such as the excellent chanting of the Vedas, and fills the Vedas in his own heart. In the Apadāna passage, "I was born in a vippa family," the Brāhmaṇa is called "vippa." His family is called "vippakula."

The root pū is in the sense of purifying. Pavati. Putto (son), puññaṃ (merit). Here, "putto" is so called because he cleanses or purifies his own lineage. When it reaches the Kiyādi class, however, it should be said as "punāti."

Putto, atrajo, suto, sūnu,
Tanujo, tanayo, oraso.
Furthermore, sons, grandsons, etc.,
Are called "apacca" (offspring).
119:
When spoken in the feminine gender, the terms "puttī" and "atrajā" are used. In other instances (such as with the root 'suta'), the appropriate suffixes (such as -ā, -ī, -inī) should be applied as suitable. In the Pāḷi Canon, a daughter is referred to as "atrajā" and "puttī."

In this context:

“From that day (when King Aṅgati became attached to sensual pleasures), on the fourteenth day (the new moon day of Kattika), the beloved Princess named Rucā, born of the body of that King who ruled the Videha country, spoke [these words] to her foster mother.”

This Pāḷi verse serves as an example. The words "puttī, dhītā, duhitā, atrajā" are synonyms meaning 'daughter'. Since the word "atrajā" is found as a feminine noun in the feminine gender, one should investigate whether the feminine gender form can or cannot be obtained in words like "suta" and others. Similarly, in the world, feminine gender forms are seen as pairs to masculine words: "vessī" (female merchant) for "vesso" (merchant), "suddī" (female laborer) for "suddo" (laborer), "nārī" (woman) for "naro" (man), and "kiṃpurisī" (female kinnara) for "kiṃpuriso" (kinnara). However, feminine gender forms are not seen as pairs for words like "puriso" and "pumā."

Regarding the word "puññaṃ" (merit), it is called "puññaṃ" because it cleanses and purifies the one who performs it. When it belongs to the Kiyādi group of roots, it is said: "punātīti puññaṃ" (it is called merit because it purifies).

Another meaning based on the characteristics of Nirutti (etymology) is also stated. Therefore, here, the derivation through roots such as 'jan' and 'pūj' should be understood. It is called "puññaṃ" because it produces (janeti) an exalted or noble state of existence (pujja-bhava). Alternatively, it is called "puññaṃ" because it produces a state that is always honored. It is called "puññaṃ" because it purifies the person who performs it. It is called "puññaṃ" because it purifies unmerit (apuñña) without remainder.

“Kalyāṇaṃ, kusalaṃ, puññaṃ, subhaṃ”—thus should a wise person skilled in language point out the synonyms for wholesome action (kusala-kamma).

The root 'pe' is used in the sense of going (gati). Peti (he goes), penti (they go). Pesi (he went), petha (they went). "Monks, in this world, a certain bad horse (assakhaḷuṅka), when told by the charioteer to 'Go!' and being urged and prodded, backs away, turns the chariot backward, takes the wrong path, and makes the chariot go onto a crooked road."
120:
The root 'pe' is used in the sense of growth (vuddhi). Payati—he prospers. Pāyo—growth; apāyo—the state of woe (apāya). In this word 'apāya', it is called 'apāya' because "there is no growth (pāyo vuddhi) in this realm." The meaning can also be derived through the root 'aya'; it is called 'apāya' because it is devoid of growth or happiness. These are hell, the animal realm, the peta realm, and the host of asuras.

The root 'pe' is used in the sense of drying up (sosana). Pāyati or payati—it dries up. Nipako—the wise. Here, 'nipako' means one who dries up opposing states, or one who protects himself from those opposing states; he is one possessed of clear comprehension (sampajāno).

The root 'gup' is used in the sense of protecting (rakkhana). Gopati—he protects. Gopako—a protector.

Just as a city on the frontier is guarded within and without,
So should you guard yourself; let not the moment (of the Buddha's appearance) pass you by.

'Gopetha' means one should guard or secure.

The root 'vap' is used in the sense of spreading (santāna). Vapati—it spreads.

The root 'sap' is used in the sense of association or union (samavāya). Sapati—he associates.

The root 'cup' is used in the sense of slow movement (mandagati). Copati—he moves slowly.

The root 'tup' is used in the sense of harming (hiṃsā). Topati or tuppati—he harms.

The root 'gup' is used in the senses of protecting and loathing (gopana, jigucchana). Gopati—he protects; jigucchati—he loathes. Jigucchaṃ, jigucchamāno, jegucchī, jigucchitvā, etc., are formed.

The root 'kapu' is used in the senses of harming, thinking, and smelling. Kappati—he harms. Kappūro—camphor.

The root 'kapu' is used in the sense of capability (sāmatthiya). "This is allowable (kappati) for us," "This is not allowable (na kappati) among us" (the word 'kappati' is used in these contexts).

The root 'kap' is used in the sense of compassion (karuṇā). Kapati—he is pitiable. Kapaṇo—a lonely or miserable person; kāpaññaṃ—the state of being pitiable. In this context, 'kapati' means he is pitiable, and 'kāpaññaṃ' is the state of a pitiable person.
121:
The root 'sap' is used in the sense of reviling or cursing (akkosa). Sapati—he curses. Sapatho, abhisapatho—a curse. Abhisapito—one who is cursed. Sapanako—one who curses.

The root 'vap' is used in the sense of sowing seeds (bījanikkhepa). Bījaṃ vapati—he sows seeds. Vāpako—one who sows. Vāpitaṃ dhaññaṃ—sown grain. Purisena bījaṃ vuttaṃ—the seed was sown by the man. Bījaṃ vappati—the seed is sown. Vappamaṅgalaṃ—the royal plowing festival.

The root 'sup' is used in the sense of sleeping (sayana). Supati—he sleeps. Those sages who are not bound by the net of craving for women sleep happily. Sutto puriso—a sleeping man; supanaṃ, suttaṃ—sleep.

The root 'khip' is used in the sense of grinding or crushing (perana). 'Perana' means 'cuṇṇikaraṇa' (pulverizing) or 'pisana' (grinding). Khepati—he grinds. Khepako—one who grinds.

The root 'khip' is used in the sense of an indistinct sound, such as sneezing (abyattasadda). Khipati—he sneezes. Khipitasaddo—the sound of sneezing. When the Buddha, the supreme leader of the world, was preaching the Dhamma, he sneezed.

The root 'khip' is used in the sense of discarding or throwing (chaḍḍana). Khipati—he throws; ukkhipati—he raises up; vikkhipati—he scatters; avakhipati—he throws down; saṅkhipati—he summarizes. Khittaṃ, ukkhittaṃ, pakkhittaṃ, vikkhittaṃ, etc., are formed.

The root 'opa' is used in the sense of spitting (niṭṭhubhana). 'Niṭṭhubhana' means 'kheḷapātana' (spitting out saliva). Opati—he spits. Having prepared (chewed) the medicine, he spat the saliva from his mouth.

The root 'lipi' is used in the sense of smearing or anointing (upalepa). Lepati—he smears. It is smeared (littaṃ) with a most potent poison.

The root 'khipi' is used in the sense of going (gati). Khimpati—he goes.

The root 'ḍip' is used in the sense of exhausting or throwing (khepa). Depati—it exhausts or he throws.

The root 'nidapi' is used in the sense of plucking or picking (nidampana). 'Nidampana' refers to the act of taking only the grain-heads or leaves from crops or trees by holding them with the hand and pulling them off, without reaping or cutting the stalks and without breaking the small branches. A man plucks the grain-heads (vīhisīsaṃ nidampati); he picks the tree leaves. Nidampako—one who plucks; nidampitaṃ—plucked; nidampituṃ—to pluck; nidampitvā—having plucked.
122:
The root *tapa* occurs in the sense of brilliance (*ditti*). Brilliance means radiance (*virocana*). The sun shines during the day.

The root *tapa* occurs in the sense of anxiety (*ubbege*). Anxiety means terror (*uttrāsa*) or fear (*bhīrutā*). *Tapati*, *uttapati*—he is afraid. *Ottappa*—dread of unwholesome actions; *ottappiya-dhana*—the wealth of moral dread.

The roots *tapa* and *dhūpa* occur in the sense of burning or heat (*santāpa*). *Tapati*—he burns. *Tapodhana*—the wealth of practice that burns away defilements. *Ātāpa*—the effort that burns away defilements. *Ātāpī*—one who possesses great effort to burn away defilements. *Ātapa*—the effort that causes burning. *Dhūpati*—he burns. *Sandhūpana*—burning. In the passive voice (*kamma*): *tāpiyati*, *dhūpiyati*—it is burned. In the abstract sense (*bhāva*): *tāpana*, *tāpa*, *paritāpa*, *santāpa*, *dhūpana*—burning.

## The forms of roots ending in 'pa' are finished.

## Roots ending in 'pha'

The root *puppha* occurs in the sense of blooming (*vikasana*). This root is both intransitive (*akammaka*) and transitive (*sakammaka*). *Pupphati*—it blooms. *Pupphaṃ*—flower; *pupphana*—blooming; *pupphita*—bloomed; *pupphituṃ*—to bloom; *pupphitvā*—having bloomed. Trees with flowers bloom. All flowers, whether land-grown or water-grown, bloom at that time. The tree named Mañjūsaka blooms with as many flowers as there are, whether in water or on land.

The root *tupha* occurs in the sense of oppressing (*hiṃsā*). *Tophati*—he oppresses.

The roots *dapha*, *daphi*, and *vappha* occur in the sense of going (*gati*). *Daphati*, *damphati*, *vapphati*—he goes.

The root *dipha* occurs in the senses of speaking, fighting, blaming, oppressing, giving, and taking (*kathana*, *yuddha*, *nindā*, *hiṃsā*, *dāna*). *Dephati*—he speaks, fights, blames, oppresses, gives, or takes. *Depha*—the act of [these].

The root *tapha* occurs in the sense of contentment (*titti*). Contentment means satisfaction (*tappana*). *Taphati*—he is content.

The root *dupha* occurs in the sense of defilement or exhaustion (*upakkilesa*). *Upakkilissana* means defilement (*upakkilesa*). *Dophati*—he is defiled.

The root *gupha* occurs in the sense of binding or composing (*gantha*). *Gantha* means the act of tying or composing (*ganthikaraṇa*). *Gophati*—he binds.

## The forms of roots ending in 'pha' are finished.
123:
## Roots ending in 'ba'

The root *babba* occurs in the sense of oppressing. *Babbati*—he oppresses. *Babbo*—oppression.

The roots *pabba*, *vabba*, *mabba*, *kabba*, *khabba*, *gabba*, *sabba*, and *cabba* occur in the sense of going. *Pabbati*, *vabbati*, *mabbati*, *kabbati*, *khabbati*, *gabbati*, *sabbati*, and *cabbati* all mean 'he goes'.

The roots *abba* and *sabba* also occur in the sense of oppressing. By the word 'ca' (and), the sense of going is also to be taken. *Abbati*, *sabbati*—he oppresses, he goes.

The root *kubi* occurs in the sense of covering (*acchādana*). *Kubbati*—he covers.

The roots *lubi* and *tubi* occur in the sense of moistening (*addana*). *Lumbati*—it moistens. *Tumbati*—it moistens. *Lumbinīvanaṃ*—the Lumbinī Sal grove. *Udakatumbo*—a water pot. Furthermore, there are also two *tumbas* (gourds/pots).

The root *cubi* occurs in the sense of contact of faces, i.e., kissing (*vadana-saṃyoga*). He kisses the son on the head. He kisses on the face. Here, one might ask: 'If the root *cubi* occurs in the sense of contact of faces, why is the kissing of raindrops on a mountain peak, which has no face and no consciousness, described as "the mountain peak kissed by raindrops" (*ambudhara-bindu-cumbita-kūṭa*)?' It is true; such a statement is made by keeping in mind the occurrence of an action similar to the act of kissing. For example, although seeing is impossible, because an action similar to seeing occurs, it is said, 'Seeing the weeping child, the tall and large trees (shook),' thus attributing 'seeing' to eyeless trees. Similarly here, because an action similar to the act of kissing occurs, 'kissing' is attributed to faceless raindrops. In reality, inanimate things have no seeing or kissing; these actions belong only to animate beings. This method should also be applied to roots like '*kamu pada-vikkhepe*' (stepping).

The roots *ubbi*, *tubbi*, *thubbi*, *dubbi*, and *dhubbi* have the sense of oppressing. *Ubbati*, *tubbati*, *thubbati*, *dubbati*, and *dhubbati*—he oppresses. *Dubbā* refers to *dabba* grass. Here, *dubbā* is *dabba* grass (*dabba-tiṇa*), which is mentioned in the Pāḷi Canon as 'a species of grass named *tiriyā*'. It should be noted that here *dubbā* is feminine gender, while *dabba* is neuter gender.
124:
The root *mubbi* occurs in the sense of binding (*bandhana*). *Mubbati* (he binds).

The root *kubbi* occurs in the sense of rising upwards (*uggama*). *Kubbati* (he rises).

The roots *pubba*, *pabba*, and *sabba* occur in the sense of filling (*pūraṇa*). *Pubbati*, *pabbati*, *sabbati* (it fills). In this regard, a question may arise: 'Venerable Sir, are not the words *pubba* and *sabba* pronouns (*sabbanāma*)? Why are they included in this investigation of roots?' To answer that question: There is no consideration of them as roots in the case of pronouns, indeclinables (*nipāta*), and prefixes (*upasagga*) that are devoid of suffixes like *tumanta*. However, these (*pubba*, *sabba*) are not pronouns here. They merely appear like pronouns due to similarity in sound. Therefore, because they are distinct from that pronominal nature, and because usages like '*pubbati*' and '*sabbati*' are found, ancient teachers included them in the investigation of roots. If that is so, why do these forms not exist in the Buddha's words (the Canon)? They do not exist because they were not used, not because they are non-existent. Although these forms do not exist in the Buddha's words, they should be accepted as ancient language approved by the elders. For example, in the phrase '*nāthatīti nātho*' (one is a protector because he protects), the form '*nāthati*' must be accepted even though it does not exist in the Buddha's words; likewise, these forms should also be accepted. Therefore, for the sake of the proficiency of the wise in terminology, even if they do not directly exist in the Dispensation (*sāsana*), worldly usages that are consistent with the Dispensation should be adopted; thus, the forms '*pubbati*' and '*sabbati*' are taken. This method should be understood in other places as well.

The root *camba* occurs in the sense of eating or sucking (*adana*). *Cambati* (he eats).

The roots *kabba*, *khabba*, and *gabba* occur in the sense of pride or arrogance (*dabba*). *Dabba* is indeed *ahaṅkāra* (the conceit of 'I'). *Kabbati*, *khabbati*, *gabbati* (he is proud).

The roots *abi* and *dabi* occur in the sense of making a sound (*sadda*). *Ambati* (he speaks, he sounds). *Ambā* (mother, woman), *ambu* (water). *Dambati* (he speaks, he sounds).

The root *labi* occurs in the sense of hanging down (*avasaṃsana*). *Avasaṃsana* is indeed *avalambana* (hanging down). *Lambati*, *vilambati*, *byālambati* (it hangs down). The sun hangs low in the sky.
125:
Holds; depends on. Ālambana, tadālambana, tadālambaṇa, or tadālamba (object, registration). Lābu or alābu (gourd); in the word 'alābu', the letter 'a' exists in the sense of that gourd itself.

## Forms of Roots Ending in 'Ba'.

## Roots Ending in 'Bha'.

The root bhā occurs in the sense of shining. The moon shines; the problem appears clearly to me. The night is bright. Bhāṇu (sun or radiance), paṭibhāna (wisdom). The night has become bright.

The root bhī occurs in the sense of fearing. Fears. Bhaya (fear), bhayānaka (fearful), bhīma (dreadful), bhīmasena, woman, bhīru (timid person), bhīruka (fearful person), bhīrukajātika (one of a fearful nature). In the causative (kārita), the forms are "bhāyeti, bhāyayati, bhāyāpeti, bhāyāpayati."

The roots sabhu and sambhu occur in the sense of harming. Harms. Harms.

The root sumbh also occurs in the sense of speaking. The word 'ca' implies harming. Speaks; harms. Sumbha (pit). Kusumbha (small pit).

Here, sumbha means a pit. The Pali phrase "Sumbhaṃ nikkhunāhi" (Dig a pit) is the evidence for this word sumbha meaning a pit. Kusumbha means a small pit; the Pali phrase "Pabbatakandarapadarasākhāparipūrā kusumbhe paripūrenti" (When the mountain clefts, chasms, and gullies are full, they fill the small pits/pools) is the evidence for this word kusumbha meaning a small pit.

The roots abbha, vabbh, and mabbh occur in the sense of going. Goes. Abbha (cloud). Goes. Goes.

Here, abbha means a cloud. That cloud is called "abbha" because it moves having many hundreds of layers. It is said, "Vijjumālī satakkakū" (A cloud with garlands of lightning and a hundred layers). Satakkakū also means having many hundreds of layers. Here, the word abbha should be understood as having three genders.
126:
Indeed, this word abbha is masculine in this context: "Abbhuṭṭhitova sa yāti, sa gacchaṃ na nivattati." It is feminine in this context: "Abbhā, mahikā, dhūmo, rajo, rāhū." It is neuter in this context: "Abbhāni candamaṇḍalaṃ chādenti."

These are the names for a cloud:
Megha, valāhaka, laṅghi, jīmūta, ambuda, ghana, dhārādhara, ambudhara, pajjuñña, and himagabbhaka.

The root yabh occurs in the sense of sexual intercourse. This act of a pair of people oppressed by lust is called methuna; the root yabh occurs in the sense of that sexual intercourse. Yabhati—engages in sexual intercourse. Yābhassaṃ—sexual intercourse.

Here, the word "methuna" is the language of the virtuous because it is the language spoken by persons endowed with shame. Indeed, this language appears in the sphere of elegant speech as "Methuno dhammo na paṭisevitabbo" (Sexual practice should not be indulged in) and "Na me rājā sakhā hoti, na rājā hoti methuno" (The king is not my friend, the king is not my companion). The language such as "yabhati," however, is the language of the unvirtuous, like the language "sikharaṇī." Indeed, even a worldly person endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) does not speak such words. Even so, the Blessed One, though possessing supreme shame and fear of wrongdoing, spoke this in the midst of the assembly out of compassion for the world, his heart urged by great compassion. How wonderful is the great compassion of the Tathāgata!

These are the names for the practice of sexual intercourse:
Saṃvesana, niddhuvana, methuna, surata, rata, byathaya, gāmadhamma, yābhassaṃ, mohana, rati, asaddhamma, vasaladhamma, mīḷhasukha, dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti, dvanda, gamma, and odakantika.

The roots sibh and vibh occur in the sense of praising. Sibhati—praises. Vibhati—praises.
127: The roots debh, abhi, and dabhi occur in the sense of making a sound. The forms are debhati, ambhati, ambho, and dambhati. Here, 'ambho' refers to water. Even though it is inanimate, it is called 'ambho' because it makes a sound while flowing in currents and such. The names for water are: pānīya, udaka, toya, jala, pāta, ambu, daka, ka, salila, vāri, āpo, ambho, papa, nīra, kepuka, pāni, amata, and ela. These names for water come from various scriptures. Here, usage such as "In the tips of horse-hair and in the pool named Kepuka, the water drunk causes them great burning" should be shown. The roots thabhi and khabhi occur in the sense of supporting, being firm (or being free from stiffness). The forms are thambhati, vitthambhati, khambhati, and vikkhambhati. Thambha (pillar), thaddhā (stiffness), upatthambha (support), upatthambhini (chock/support for a cart), vikkhambha (removal), vikkhambhita-kilesa (one whose defilements are removed), etc. The roots jabh and jabhi occur in the sense of bending the body. The forms are jabhati, jambhati, and vijambhati. There are also words such as vijambhanaṃ, vijambhita, vijambhanto, vijambhamāno, and vijambhito. The root sabbh occurs in the sense of speaking. The form is sabbhati. The root vabbh occurs in the sense of eating. The form is vabbhati. The root gabbh occurs in the sense of carrying. The forms are gabbhati and gabbho. Here, the word 'gabbho' refers to the mother's womb as well as the child in the womb. Thus, in the context "In whatever single night a being first dwells in the womb (gabbhe)," the mother's womb is called 'gabbho'. In the contexts "Great King, a child (gabbho) is established in me" and "The fetus (gabbho) fell to the ground," it refers to the child in the womb. Furthermore, 'gabbho' refers to a special dwelling (a chamber).
128: In contexts such as "He enters the chamber," the chamber (royal apartment) is called 'gabbho'. The root rabha occurs in the sense of acting excessively. The root rabha preceded by the prefix ā- occurs in the senses of harming, doing, and exerting effort. Rābhassaṃ refers to the state of one who acts excessively. Those endowed with such excessive action are mentioned in the Pali as: "They are fierce, obstructed, and act excessively." In that context, 'rabhasā' means having the quality of acting excessively. The forms are rabhati, ārabhati, samārabhati, ārambhati, rabhaso, ārambho, samārambho, ārabhanto, and samārabhanto. Examples include: "I have exerted energy (vīriya)," sārambhaṃ (harmful or dangerous), anārambhaṃ (not having such), "Your oppression, characterized by excessive speech, shall not exist," pakaraṇārambho (the beginning of a treatise), vīriyārambho (the exertion of energy), ārabhituṃ, ārabhitvā, and ārabbha. Here, 'vīriyārambho' means the exertion known as energy. The word ārambha appears in many senses: action (kamma), offense (āpatti), activity (kriyā), effort (vīriya), harming (hiṃsā), and destruction (vikopana). For instance, in the passage: "Whatever suffering arises, it is all due to the cause of action (ārambha); with the cessation of actions, there is no arising of suffering," the word 'ārambho' refers to kamma. In "He commits an offense (ārabhati) and becomes remorseful," it refers to an offense (āpatti). In "Great sacrifices have many activities (mahārambhā), yet they are not of great fruit," it refers to activities such as erecting sacrificial posts. In "Exert effort (ārambhatha), go forth, apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching," it refers to energy (vīriya). In "They harm (ārambhanti) living beings for the sake of the ascetic Gotama," it refers to harming (hiṃsā). In "He abstains from destroying (samārambhā) seeds and plants," it refers to destruction (vikopana) such as cutting or breaking. Thus, it is shown that the word ārambha occurs in the senses of action, offense, effort, harming, activity, and destruction. The root labha occurs in the sense of obtaining. The forms are labhati, labbhati, lābho, laddhaṃ, alattha, and alatthuṃ. The root subha occurs in the sense of beauty. The forms are sobhati, sobhā, sobhanaṃ, and sobhito.
129: One should indicate that the word ārambha occurs in the senses of action, offense, effort, harming, activity, and destruction. The root labha occurs in the sense of obtaining: labhati, labbhati, lābho, laddhaṃ, alattha, alatthuṃ. The root subha occurs in the sense of beauty: sobhati, sobhā, sobhanaṃ, sobhito. The root khubha occurs in the sense of agitation: khobhati, saṅkhobhati. "When the white elephant Paccaya was donated, the city of Jetuttara was then agitated (khubbhittha)." Forms include khobhā and saṅkhobho. The roots nabha and tubha occur in the sense of harming: nabhati, tubhati. The root sambha occurs in the sense of intimacy: sambhati, sambhatti, sambhatto. The root lubha occurs in the sense of delusion: lobhati, palobhati. Example: "The seduction of a young woman (thullakumārīpalobhanaṃ)." In the causative, the forms are lobheti, palobheti, and palobhetvā. When belonging to the Divādi class, it occurs in the sense of greed as lubbhati. The root dabhi occurs in the senses of showing, cutting, and binding: dambhati, dambhanaṃ. The root rubhi occurs in the sense of obstructing: rumbhati, sannirumbhati, sannirumbho, sannirumbhitvā. The roots ubha, ubbha, and umbha occur in the sense of filling: ubhati, ubbhati, umbhati, ubhanā, ubbhanā, umbhanā, obho, keṭubhaṃ, ubbhaṃ, kumbho, kumbhī. In the causative, the forms are obheti, ubbheti, and umbheti. Among these, keṭubhaṃ is a treatise that assists poets in the variation of ritual actions. The etymology here is: it makes known (kiṭeti gameti) the division of actions, or it fills and completes (obheti pūreti) that knowledge without remainder; thus it is called keṭubhaṃ by the power of the roots kiṭa and ubha. Ubbhati...
130:
It is called 'ubbha' because it fills; it means filling. Such a usage of the word is also seen in the Cariyāpiṭaka. That usage is: "He gave a great gift, extremely full (accubbhaṃ), like the ocean." In that context, 'accubbha' means extremely fulfilling the desires of the supplicants. There is also a variant reading 'akkumbha'. It is called 'kumbha' because it is filled with water, which is called 'ka'. That same word 'kumbha' becomes 'kumbhī' in the feminine gender. In this context, there is the usage: "Stooping, she washes the pot (kumbhī)."

The word 'kumbha' can occur in the sense of a pot, the frontal globe of an elephant, and a measure of ten ambaṇas; thus should the wise who observe the method understand.

## Forms of roots ending in -bha.

## Roots ending in -ma

The root mā- is used in the senses of honoring and making a sound. It exists as 'māti'. There is the word 'mātā' (mother). Here, 'mātā' refers to the biological mother, or a stepmother, or an aunt.

The root mū- is used in the sense of binding. It exists as 'mavati'. In the Kiyādi group, however, the form of this root is 'munāti'.

The root me- is used in the senses of giving and taking. It exists as 'meti' and 'mayati'. There is the word 'medhā' (wisdom).

Here, 'medhā' means wisdom. That wisdom is called 'medhā' because it quickly takes and bears even subtle meanings and the Dhamma. In this context, 'meti' means taking (understanding). Accordingly, it is stated in the Atthasālinī: "It is called medhā because it destroys (medhati) defilements like a thunderbolt destroys a mountain; or it is called medhā in the sense of quickly grasping and bearing." Furthermore, by the power of the root medh-, which expresses the sense of combining, it should be understood as 'medhā' because it combines with the true Dhamma such as virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi), and with glory (siri). In this regard, it is said:
131:
“The formation of the word 'medhā' in the Teaching of the Sugata should be understood as being accomplished through two roots, through a single root, and with two meanings each.”

The root OMA is used in the sense of capability (sāmatthiya). Sāmatthiya means the state of being capable. This root is one where the final vowel of the root is not dropped; thus, there are forms such as omāti (is capable) and omanti (are capable). In this context, the Pali text states: “Venerable Sir, is the Blessed One able (omāti) to approach the Brahma world with a mind-made body through psychic power?” In that Pali, omāti means is able or is capable.

The root TIMU is used in the sense of wetness (addabhāva). Addabhāva means the state of being moist or wet. There are forms such as temati (is wet), tinto (wet), temiyo (King Temiya), temitukāmā (those wishing to be wet), and temiṃsu (they became wet). Here, Temiya is the name of the son of the King of Kāsi, who was the Bodhisatta. He is called “Temiya” because he was born moistening the hearts of the King and the great multitude, bringing about a state of coolness.

The root NITAMI is used in the sense of fatigue (kilamana). Nitammati (is fatigued). There are expressions such as “The heart burns; I am fatigued (nitammāmi).”

The roots CAMU, CHAMU, JAMU, JHAMU, UMU, and JIMU are used in the sense of eating (adana). Camati (eats). Camū (army); camū means a military force (senā). Chamati, jamati, jhamati, umati, and jemati are likewise.

The root KAMU is used in the sense of stepping (padavikkhepa). Padavikkhepa means walking by foot. This is merely the primary meaning according to common usage. Therefore, in passages such as “Neither fire, nor poison, nor weapons fall upon or penetrate (kamati) his body,” meanings other than stepping should also be taken. Kamati (goes), caṅkamati (walks back and forth), atikkamati (transgresses/surpasses), abhikkamati (advances), paṭikkamati (retreats), pakkamati (departs), parakkamati (strives), vikkamati (exerts), nikkamati (leaves), saṅkamati (transfers/crosses). Saṅkamanaṃ (bridge/crossing), saṅkanti (transition), kamanaṃ (going), caṅkamanaṃ (walking meditation), atikkamo (transgression), abhikkamo (advancing), paṭikkamo (retreating), pakkamo (departure), vikkamo (exertion), nikkamo (leaving). Atikkanto puriso (a man who has passed). Abhikkantā ratti (the night has passed / the beautiful night). Nikkhamati (goes out), abhinikkhamati (goes forth/renounces).
132:
In the causative sense (kārita), there is the form nikkhāmeti (causes to go out). Other words should also be applied in this manner. However, when this root (kamu) belongs to the Curādi class, it occurs in the senses of desire and liking (icchākanti). Therefore, although the extraction of the meaning of the word 'abhikkanta' with the distinction of prefixes (upasagga) should be explained here, I will explain it later only in the section on the Curādi class.

The root YAMU is used in the sense of ceasing or abstaining (uparama). Uparama means viramana (abstaining). Yamabhi (yamati). Yamo (restraint/death). “Others do not realize that we here must die (yamāmase)”—this Pali from the Kosambakkhandhaka is the illustration here. In that Pali, 'yamāmase' means we cease, we perish, or we die.

The root NAMA is used in the sense of a loud or famous sound (bahuttasadda). Bahuttasadda means a tumultuous, famous sound. Namati (a tumultuous sound of fame arises).

The roots AMA, DAMA, HAMMA, MIMA, and CHAMA are used in the sense of going (gati). Amati, damati, hammati, mimati, chamati (goes). Chamā (earth).

Chamā means the earth (pathavī). The word 'chamā' should be understood as feminine. This is seen from its usage in the training rule: “I will not preach the Dhamma to one who is not ill, who is sitting on a seat while I am sitting on the ground (chamāyaṃ),” and in the verse: “I writhe on the ground (chamāyaṃ) like a fish in the heat.” That word 'chamā' should be applied with seven or eight case endings and in both numbers. It is called 'chamā' because they go (chamanti) upon this earth.

The root DHAMA is used in the senses of making a sound and connection with fire (blowing). The root dhama occurs both in making a sound and in connection with fire along with the breath from the mouth. Among those two, in the first sense, there are usages such as: “He blows (dhamati) the conch. A conch-blower. He beats (dhamati) the drum. A drum-beater. One should blow what should be blown; one should not blow excessively.” In the second sense, there are usages such as: “He blows (dhamati) the fire. He rouses himself; just as one blows (sandhamaṃ) a small fire into a flame.”

The root BHAMA is used in the sense of anger (kodha). Bhamati (is angry).
133:
The root NAMU is used in the sense of bending and saluting (namana). Namati (bends/salutes), namo (homage/salutation), nataṃ, namanaṃ (bending), nati (bending), namaṃ (bent), namamāno, namanto (bending/saluting), namito (bent/saluted), nāmaṃ (name/noun), nāmitaṃ (caused to bend), namituṃ (to bend/salute), natvā, natvāna, namitvā, namitvāna, namituna (having bent/having saluted)—these are the forms. In the causative (kārita) sense, the forms are nāmeti, nāmayati (causes to bend), nāmetvā, nāmayitvā (having caused to bend). Among those words, words of the type 'namati' and 'namitvā' should be understood in both the sense of bending and the sense of saluting. However, words of the type 'namo' and 'natvā' should be understood only in the sense of saluting. In this regard, the illustrative usages to be noted are: A tree with fruit breaks, having bent (namitvā) under the weight of the fruit. An elderly person walks bending (namati) and having bent (namitvā) due to the infirmity of old age. A person with faith goes having saluted (namitvā) the Buddha. May there be homage (namo) to the Buddha; having saluted (natvāna) the Buddha who is the Teacher, he departed. Here, the word 'namo' is also found among indeclinables (nipāta). Therefore, the nominative and accusative forms are seen to be identical: “O King of Devas, homage (namo) be to you.” “Having paid homage (namo) to the Great Sage.” This root should also be applied with prefixes (upasagga), such as paṇamati (salutes), paṇāmo (salutation), uṇṇamati (raises up/is proud), uṇṇati (elevation/pride), and so on.

The root KHAMU is used in the sense of patience or endurance (sahana). Khamati (endures), khanti (patience), khamo, khamanaṃ (endurance)—these occur in the sense of the state (bhāva). In the sense of the agent (kattar), there are usages such as khantā, khamitā (one who endures), and “He is one who endures (khamo) both cold and heat.”

The root SAMA is used in the sense of non-seeing (extinguishing). Samati (is extinguished), vūpasamati aggi (the fire is extinguished).

The root YAMU is used in the sense of entering or serving (parivesana). Yamati (enters/serves), yamo, yamarājā (King Yama).

The root SAMA is used in the sense of making a sound. Samati (speaks).

The roots SAMA and THAMA are used in the sense of dangling or hanging (velamba). Samati, thamati (dangles).

The root VĀYAMA is used in the sense of exertion (īhā). Vāyamati (strives), vāyāmo (exertion/effort).
134:
The root *gamu* is used in the sense of going. The words *gacchati*, *gamako*, *gato*, *gati*, and *gamanaṃ* are formed from it. In the causative (*kārita*) sense, words such as *gameti*, *gamayati*, and *gacchāpeti* are formed.

The root *ramu* is used in the sense of delighting or playing. The words *ramati*, *viramati*, *paṭiviramati*, *uparamati*, *ārati*, *virati*, *paṭivirati*, *uparati*, *veramaṇī*, *viramaṇaṃ*, *rati*, *ramaṇaṃ*, *rato*, *ārato*, *virato*, *paṭivirato*, *uparato*, *uparamo*, and *ārāmo* are formed from it.

The root *vamu* is used in the sense of vomiting or emitting. The words *vamati*, *vamathu*, and *vammiko* are formed from it.

"Woe to that poison which has been vomited, which I would swallow again for the sake of life!
Let that vomited poison be loathsome.
Death is better for me than living by swallowing back what has been vomited."

In that context, regarding the word *vammika* (anthill): it is called *vammika* because it 'vomits' (emits), because it is 'vomited' (produced), because it rises up through 'vomiting', and because it is bound together by 'vomited' moisture. Indeed, that anthill is called *vammika* because it 'vomits' out various kinds of creatures such as snakes, mongooses, rats, and house lizards. It is called *vammika* because it is 'vomited' by termites. It is called *vammika* because it is built up to the height of a waist or even the height of a man by the dust powder 'vomited' by termites and carried by their mouths. It is called *vammika* because, being bound by the moisture of saliva 'vomited' by termites, it does not crumble even when it rains for seven weeks; and even in the summer, if one takes a handful of earth from that anthill and squeezes it, moisture comes out. Thus, it is called *vammika* because it is composed of 'vomited' moisture.

In this context, words such as "Bhagavā" and "Himavā" should not be established solely by the power of the *vantu* suffix; rather, they should also be established by the power of the root *vamu*. Therefore, the author of the *Visuddhimagga* stated: "Since this Blessed One has vomited out the 'going' known as craving in the three realms of existence, He should be called 'one who has vomited the going in the realms' (*bhavesu vanta-gamano*). By taking the letter 'bha' from the word *bhava*, the letter 'ga' from the word *gamana*, and the letter 'va' from the word *vanta* (making the 'va' long), He is called 'Bhagavā'. Just as in the world—"
135:
—the teacher Buddhaghosa, who stated ‘mekhalā’ where it should have been said ‘mehanassa khassa mālā’, showed the formation of the word through the method of Nirutti (linguistic analysis).

In this regard, an objection might arise: “This illustration is not balanced. In the case of ‘mehanassa khassa mālā’, the taking of the letters *ma*, *kha*, and *la* in sequence is evident. However, in the case of ‘bhavesu vanta-gamano’, the taking of the letters *bha*, *va*, and *ga* in sequence is not evident.” This is true. However, in this word ‘Bhagavā’, although it should be said ‘bhavesu gamana-vanto’ by placing the attribute at the end as in ‘aggāhito’ or ‘vijjācaraṇasampanno’, it is not said so. Because in the grammatical treatises, the placement of attributes at the beginning is generally desired, and in order to satisfy the minds of grammarians and certain wise men, it is stated as ‘bhavesu vanta-gamano’ by way of placing it at the beginning—similar to ‘āhitaggi’ or ‘sampannavijjācaraṇo’—illustrating only the meaning without regarding the alphabetical order. In such instances, whether the words stand as ‘āhitaggi’ or ‘aggāhito’, or as ‘chinnahattho’ or ‘hatthacchinno’, there is no such thing as unsuitability in meaning, because those words are synonymous with each other.

However, in places such as ‘vedajāto’, it should be noted that the meaning would indeed be unsuitable (if reversed). Thus, in the *Visuddhimagga*, the formation of the word ‘Bhagavā’ is shown by the power of the root *vamu*; and in its commentary (*Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā*), it is also shown as: “Bhage vamīti bhagavā; bhāge vamīti bhagavā.” The definition (*nibbacana*) should be understood thus: He is ‘Bhagavā’ because He vomited out (*vami*), emitted (*uggiri*), and discarded without lingering concern, like a lump of spittle, the glory (*siri*), sovereignty (*issariya*), and fame known as *bhaga*.

Alternatively, stars are called ‘bhā’. Because they move and exist together with those stars, they are called ‘bhagā’—referring to the physical worlds (*okāsaloka*) such as Mount Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, and Himavā, because they are special foundations, beautiful, and endure for an aeon. He is ‘Bhagavā’ because He ‘vomited’ those physical worlds by transcending the abodes of the beings living there, and because He abandoned them by relinquishing the desire and lust (*chandarāga*) connected with them.
136:
Because the Blessed One abandoned the glory of a Universal Monarch (*Cakkavatti*), as well as fame, sovereignty, and happiness, and the diverse stars, Mount Sineru, Yugandhara, and so forth in the world, He is called *Sugata*; therefore, He is also called *Bhagavā*. Likewise, having utterly cut off all mental proliferation (*papañca*), all bonds (*yoga*), all knots (*gantha*), and all fetters (*saṃyojana*) within the groups of phenomena such as the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), and having fully realized the Deathless Element (*amata-dhātu*), He vomited, emitted, and discarded them without lingering concern, never to swallow them again; thus He is called *Bhagavā*. Alternatively, because He vomited, emitted, and abandoned without lingering concern all wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, inferior and superior states, and states with dark and bright counterparts, through the mouth of the Knowledge of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga-ñāṇa*), He is called *Bhagavā*.

Because the Great Sage (*Mahesī*) has vomited out the various phenomena such as the aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as the dark and bright states, He is therefore regarded as *Bhagavā*.

In the Jātaka Commentary, the formation of the word *Himavā* is also shown by the power of the root *vamu*. For instance, in the Sambhava Jātaka Commentary, it is said: “He is *Himavā* because he is possessed of snow (*hima*) during the winter when snow falls. He is *Himavā* because he vomits (melts/emits) snow during the summer.” Thus, the Jātaka Commentary shows the formation of the word *Himavā* through the root *vamu*; this method should also be applied in similar instances. However, it should not be applied to words such as *guṇavā* (virtuous) or *gaṇavā* (one with a group). If it were applied, the words *guṇavā* and *gaṇavā* would come to mean “one devoid of virtue” or “one whose virtue has diminished,” and so forth. Therefore, this method should not be applied in all cases.

In this regard, an objection might arise: “If words such as *Bhagavā* are formed by the power of the root *vamu*, how are forms like *bhagavanto* and *bhagavantaṃ* established?” Just as the word *Bhagavā* is established by the method of Nirutti, those words are also established by that same method. For the method of Nirutti is inconceivably profound; it is bound only by the suitability of meaning (*atthayutti*). When there is suitability of meaning, even forms that cannot be established (by standard grammar) are established by this very method.
137: In this context, if the characteristics of Nirutti (linguistic analysis) should be brought forth and shown, I shall declare those Nirutti characteristics along with examples in the section on the formation of words later on. O good person, desiring supreme proficiency in this Tipitaka, which is the doctrine of the King of Sages and is understood by the noble ones, constantly associate with this Saddanīti treatise, which bears extensive meanings and purifies the intellect. ## Thus, the division of roots called the Five Groups of Vowels, the fifteenth chapter in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the proficiency of the wise in the ways of speech in the ninefold dispensation with its commentaries and the Tipitaka. ## 16. The Chapter on the Bhūvādi Group. From this chapter onwards, following the views of the teachers who are skilled in the varieties of roots and so forth, I shall speak of the roots ending in non-group consonants (avagga) as well as the mixed roots. ## Roots ending in -ya. The root yā- is used in the senses of going and reaching. It exists as yāti, yanti; yātu, yantu; yeyya, yeyyuṃ, anupariyeyyuṃ. The paradigm (padamālā) should be expanded as appropriate. A man who goes (yanto puriso). A woman who goes (yantī itthī). A family that goes (yantaṃ kulaṃ). Vehicle (yānaṃ), gift (upayānaṃ), garden (uyyānaṃ), and so forth. In the Divādi group, however, the forms of this root are yāyati, yāyanti, etc. Among those words, in words like yāna, it is called yāna (vehicle) because one goes by means of this chariot, cart, etc. It is called upayāna (gift) because one approaches the presence of a ruler or a beloved person by means of this gift. In the passage, "O prince, when you have gone, they should give me gifts (upayānāni)," here 'upayāna' refers to gifts.
138:
Gifts (paṇṇākāra) are called "upayānāni." Because it is endowed with beautiful flowers, fruits, and so forth, a place where people go while looking upwards is called a "garden" (uyyāna).

The root VYĀ is used in the sense of opening the eyes. Vyāti, vyanti, etc. The paradigm should be connected as far as possible. In this regard, there is this Pali: "yāva vyāti nimmīsati, tatrāpi rasatibbayo" (even in the time it takes to open and close the eyes, age wanes). Here, "yāva vyāti" means "as long as the eyes are opened." This is an ancient language; for this was the usage of people at the time when the Bodhisatta was the wandering ascetic Cūḷabodhi.

The root YU is used in the sense of mixing and going. Yoti, yavati, etc. Āyu (life), yoni (origin/class). 

In the word "āyu," the sound "ā" is a prefix (upasagga). It is called āyu because beings are, as it were, mixed (āyavanti) by means of this life. Or, it is called āyu because when that life exists, mental phenomena (arūpadhammā) arise and continue. Thus, it is said in the Atthasālinī: "It is called āyu in the sense of arising. For when that life exists, mental phenomena arise and continue; therefore, it is called āyu." "Āyu, jīvita, pāṇa"—these are synonyms according to worldly usage. According to the Abhidhamma, "ṭhiti, yapanā, yāpanā, jīvitindriya" are also synonyms along with them.

"Yoni" refers to that conception by which the egg-born (aṇḍaja) and so forth are mixed with other egg-born beings and so forth. The derivation (nibbacana) here is: "Beings are mixed with one another in this [conception] through the continuity of the same class; therefore, it is called yoni."

And here, the extraction of the meanings of the word "yoni" is presented. Yoni is a name for a group of aggregates (khandhakoṭṭhāsa), for a cause (kāraṇa), and for the urinary passage (passāvamagga). In the passage, "four classes of Nagas (nāgayoniyo), four classes of Garudas (supaṇṇayoniyo)," the group of aggregates is called yoni.
139:
In the passage (from the Bhūmija Sutta), "This is the cause (yoni) for the attainment of the fruit," the word yoni occurs in the sense of cause. In the passage (from the Dhammapada), "I do not call him a Brahmin just because he is born from a womb (yonija)," the word yoni occurs in the sense of the birth canal (passāvamagga).

In this regard, it is said:
In the sense of a group of aggregates,
in the urinary passage (muttamagga), and in the sense of cause—
in these three meanings, the word yoni is used.

The root VYE is used in the sense of covering or protecting. Vyāyati—he protects.

The root VYE is used in the sense of occurring. Vyeti—it occurs. Sahabyo—occurring together.

Here, sahabyo is so called because it tends to occur together (saha vyeti); it means a companion (sahāya) or one who has reached the same state of existence (ekabhavūpaga). Thus, in such passages as "he was reborn into the company (sahabyataṃ) of the Tāvatiṃsa devas," one who has reached the same state of existence is called "sahabyo."

The root HAYA is used in the sense of going. Hayati—he goes. Hayo—a horse. Hayo means a horse. It is called hayo because it goes (hayati) swiftly. Its names are as follows:
Assa, turaṅga, turaga, vājī, vāha, and haya.
Its varieties are sindhava, goja, and assatara.
A noble horse (hayuttama) that knows what is a cause and what is not is called an ājānīya (thoroughbred).
An inferior horse is called ghoṭaka, khaḷuṅkassa, or vaḷava.
A young horse (colt) is called kisora or khaḷuṅka.

The root HARIYA is used in the senses of going and being pained (gelañña). Hariyati—he goes, he is pained.

The roots AYA, VAYA, PAYA, MAYA, TAYA, CAYA, and RAYA are used in the sense of going. Ayati, vayati, payati, mayati, tayati, cayati, rayati—they go. Aya (iron/gain), samaya (time/occasion), vaya (age), paya (milk/water), raya (speed/force). The noun forms of the roots MAYA, TAYA, and CAYA should be investigated (in the scriptures).
140:
Among those words, 'aya' means iron (black iron). It is called 'aya' because it is used (associated) in various blacksmithing tasks. 'Vaya' refers to a portion (stage) of life, such as the first stage of life. It is called 'vaya' because it leads to decline. 'Paya' is a name for both milk and water. It is called 'paya' because it reaches the state of being drinkable by people. 'Raya' means speed (velocity). This speed is also called 'java' (swiftness). Therefore, moving swiftly is called 'raya'.

In this context, the extraction of the meaning of the word 'samaya' will be stated along with its derivative definition. The word 'samaya' is found in the senses of concordance, opportunity, time, assemblage, cause, view, attainment, abandoning, and penetration (paṭivedha).

Indeed, in the Subha Sutta and others, in the passage, "Depending on the proper time and concordance, if we could approach even tomorrow, it would be good," it shows the meaning of 'samavāya' (concordance). In the Aṅguttara Nikāya and others, in the passage, "Monks, there is only one moment and opportunity (samaya) for living the holy life," it shows the meaning of 'khaṇa' (opportunity). In the Vinaya Pāḷi and others, in the passage, "hot time, sweltering time," it shows the meaning of 'kāla' (time). In the Mahāsamaya Sutta and others, in the passage, "There is an assembly of devas and brahmas (mahāsamaya) in the Great Forest," it shows the meaning of 'samūha' (assemblage). In the Bhaddāli Sutta and others, in the passage, "Bhaddāli, you did not even know the cause (of reproach)," it shows the meaning of 'hetu' (cause). In the Pañcakaṅga Sutta and others, in the passage, "At that time, the wanderer Uggāhamāna was staying in Queen Mallikā's park, at the Tinduka tree row, which was a place for discussing various views (samayappavādaka)," it shows the meaning of 'diṭṭhi' (view).

In the Kosala Saṃyutta and others, in the passage, "Because of attaining the benefit in the present life and the benefit in the future life, the wise one is called a pandit," it shows the meaning of 'paṭilābha' (attainment). In the Sabbāsava Sutta and others, in the passage, "By rightly abandoning conceit, he has made an end of suffering," it shows the meaning of 'pahāna' (abandoning). In the contexts of the oppressive nature, conditioned nature, burning nature, and the nature to be penetrated of the truth of suffering, it shows the meaning of 'paṭivedha' (penetration).
141:
(At the beginning) it expresses the meaning of attainment (paṭilābha). In sentences such as "By rightly abandoning conceit, he has made an end of the suffering of the round," it expresses the meaning of abandoning (pahāna). In sentences such as "the oppressive nature, conditioned nature, burning nature, and the nature to be penetrated of the truth of suffering," it expresses the meaning of penetration (paṭivedha). Here too, because prefixes (upasagga) are merely indicators of the meaning, the word 'samaya' alone expresses those various meanings. Therefore, in extracting the meaning of the word 'samaya,' the word 'abhisamaya' with its prefix is also mentioned.

Among those meanings of 'samaya': Because it is a cause that acts together with [the result], it occurs together in unity; therefore it is 'samaya,' meaning concordance (samavāya). In this opportunity, the person who is the locus of that holy life of the path arrives together; therefore it is 'samaya,' meaning opportunity (khaṇa). At this time, or by this [time], states arise together with conascent states or with [stages like] arising etc.; therefore it is 'samaya,' meaning time (kāla). In truth, because there is only the occurrence of states, although time does not exist in an ultimate sense, it is spoken of through a form established merely by conceptualization, as if it were the locus or the instrument for the occurrence of states. The standing of parts equally or together is 'samaya,' meaning assemblage (samūha), just like 'samudāya.' Indeed, only the standing together of parts is called an assemblage. When meeting with other conditions, the result arises from this cause; therefore it is 'samaya,' meaning cause (hetu), just like 'samudaya.' Because it is a fetter, it occurs connectedly; it occurs in its own object. Or, because it is a firm grasping (clinging), beings proceed by this view, being conjoined according to their adherence; therefore it is 'samaya,' meaning view (diṭṭhi). Indeed, by the fetter of view, beings are bound exceedingly. Conjunction is 'samaya,' meaning attainment (paṭilābha). Reaching the peaceful cessation (nirodha), or the complete departure or non-occurrence, is 'samaya,' meaning abandoning (pahāna). It is to be known rightly and directly by wisdom; therefore it is 'samaya,' meaning the undistorted nature of states. It knows rightly by way of being direct; therefore it is 'samaya,' meaning the realization of the true nature (yathābhūtasabhāvāvabodha). Thus, the occurrence of the word 'samaya' in those various meanings should be understood.
142:
One might ask: Do words not adhere to a single meaning? Therefore, can a single word not express multiple meanings? This statement is true if one considers the specific linguistic context. When considering the specific linguistic context, it is not possible for a single word to express multiple meanings. This is because the word samaya in the sense of 'time' does not express meanings such as 'assemblage' and so on. However, here, based on the commonality of being meanings expressed by the word samaya, it is said that the word samaya has multiple meanings. In this way, the intention should be understood in the extraction of all meanings.

The completion of the word samaya, which expresses 'assemblage' (samavāya) and so on,
Is stated by the wise through the roots i, yā, and aya.

Through these roots of identical meaning—i, yā, and aya—
It should be said that identical forms and identical sounds such as 'samaya' arise.

The root nay is used in the sense of 'protecting'. The word ca implies the sense of 'going' (gati). Nayati: he protects, he goes. Nayo: method. It is called nayo because it is 'leading' or 'going' (nayanaṃ gamanaṃ); this is the Pali usage (pāḷi-gati). Alternatively, it is called nayo because one carries or protects the meaning by this means; such as the 'method of suchness' (tathatta-naya) and so on.

The root day is used in the senses of giving, going, harming, taking, and protecting. Dayati: he gives, he goes, he harms, he takes, he protects. Dayā: loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā).

The word dayā is referred to as both mettā and karuṇā. In the phrase 'dayāpanno', dayā refers to mettā; the meaning is 'one who has attained a state of loving-kindness'. In the phrase 'adayāpanno', however, dayā refers to karuṇā; the meaning is 'one who has attained a state of being without compassion'. Thus, the occurrence of the word dayā in the senses of mettā and karuṇā should be understood. Regarding this, it is stated in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā: 'Wherever the word dayā occurs, it should be applied according to the intended meaning. Indeed, the word dayā, while carrying the internal sense of 'protecting', occurs in both mettā and karuṇā.'

The word-definition (vacanattha) here should be understood as follows: Through this mettā, one gives fearlessness (dayati dadāti) to beings; therefore, it is called dayā. Just as water spreads equally with coolness, washing away dust and impurities without discriminating between the low, the noble, the bad, or the good, so too does it occur and proceed equally among beings without discriminating between the low, the noble, the bad, or the good (dayati gacchati vattati); therefore, it is also called dayā. It obtains mettā.

Alternatively, it harms (dayati hiṃsati) the compassionate person for as long as the desired welfare of others has not yet been achieved; therefore, it is called dayā. By this compassion, the virtuous person supports (dayati anuggaṇhāti) even the wicked; therefore, it is also called dayā. By this compassion, the virtuous person abandons his own happiness and takes on (dayati gaṇhāti) weariness; therefore, it is called dayā.
143:
It is stated in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā: 'The word dayā occurs in various Pali passages; in those places, it should be applied according to the intention of the speaker. In truth, the word dayā, carrying the internal sense of 'protecting', occurs in both mettā and karuṇā. Therefore, it should be so applied.'

The word-definition (vacanattha) of this word dayā should be understood as follows: Because one gives fearlessness to beings through this mettā, it is called dayā. Just as water spreads equally with coolness and washes away dust and impurities, it is called dayā (mettā) because it arises equally toward the low and the noble, the bad and the good, without discrimination. Alternatively, it is called dayā because it causes weariness to (distresses) the compassionate person as long as the welfare and desires of others are not fulfilled. Because the virtuous person supports even the wicked through this quality, it is called dayā. Because the virtuous person abandons his own happiness and takes on weariness and suffering through this quality, it is called dayā.

By this quality, when the noble Bodhisattas make the aspiration for Buddhahood, they discard even the Fruit of Arahantship that is within their reach, desiring to rescue beings from the ocean of saṃsāra. Because they take on the great suffering of saṃsāra, which is without relief and extremely terrifying, and in their final birth, they take on Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), which is adorned with many qualities along with the attainment of the Deathless Element (amata-dhātu), it is called dayā (karuṇā). Indeed, all the attributes of the Buddha have compassion as their root.

Another method: It is called dayā because one protects beings through this quality, or because one protects oneself, or because it is merely the act of protecting. This dayā refers to both mettā and karuṇā. I shall state some examples here: 'O householder Potaliya, just as a vulture, a heron, or a hawk might fly away taking a piece of meat'; 'Queen Maddī, you should practice love (dayesi) toward your children, your mother-in-law, and your father-in-law'; 'Great King, (Prince Pañcālacanda) should be loved (dayitabbo)'.

Among those examples, 'dayeyya' means 'should fly up and go'; this word should be understood through the sense of 'going' (gati). 'Dayesi' means 'you should practice a mind of loving-kindness'. 'Dayitabbo' means 'should be loved'. Both of these explanations should be understood as being made by incorporating the sense of 'protecting' within the intended meaning.

The root ūyī is used in the sense of 'stretching threads'. Ūyati: he weaves (spins). Ūto, ūtavā: woven.

The root pūyī is used in the senses of 'spreading' and 'foul smell'. Pūyati: it spreads, it rots. Pūto, pūtavā: rotted. There is the example: 'The man who wraps a rotting fish with the tip of kusa grass'.
144: The root kanuyi is used in the sense of making a sound. It has the form kanuyati. The past forms are kanuto and kanutavā. The root khamāya is used in the sense of shaking. It has the form khamāyati. The past forms are khamāto and khamātavā. The roots phāyi and pāyi are used in the sense of growth (vuddhi). It has the form phāyati. The past forms are phīto and phatavā. In those examples, the elision of the letter 'ya' and the change of the root-ending vowel to 'i' due to the suffixes -ta and -tavantu should be noted. This same method should be noted in words like 'pūto' and 'pūtavā' as appropriate. It has the form pāyati. There are words like pāyo and apāyo. It is called 'apāyo' because there is no growth (pāya) in this realm of misery. Or else, it is defined as 'apāyo' because it is away from a good destination (aya) or happiness. As for 'apāya', there are the four states of misery: hell (niraya), the animal kingdom, the realm of ghosts (peta), and the host of asuras. The root tāyu is used in the senses of spreading and protecting. It has the form tāyati. There is the word tāyanaṃ. In the Divādi group, however, look at the root 'tā' in the sense of protecting; it has the forms tāyati and tāṇam. The verbal forms of both roots are the same. Although there is a difference only by the suffixes -a and -ya, the nominal forms 'tāyanaṃ' and 'tāṇam' are different. The root cāyu is used in the senses of honoring and observing/listening (nisāmana). 'Pūjā' means honoring. 'Nisāmana' refers to looking and listening. In passages such as "Maddī, look (nisāmehi)" and "O virtuous ones, listen (nisāmayatha)," looking and listening are expressed by the word 'nisāmana'. Furthermore, investigating with wisdom should also be understood as 'nisāmana'. It has the forms cāyati and apacāyati. There are usages such as: "One should honor the homeless monks," "Those who honor the elders," "He shows respect (apaciti)," and "Those who constantly honor the elders." ## Forms of roots ending in -ya.
145:
## Rakāranta-dhātu

The root rā is used in the sense of taking. It has the form rāti. The root ri is used in the sense of spreading. It has the form reti. There is the term reṇu. Reṇu refers to dust (rajo). The root ru is used in the sense of going and oppressing. The forms are ravati and viravati. The root ru is used in the sense of making a sound. The forms are roti and ravati. There are terms such as ravo and uparavo. In the usage "The cry is pleasant, and the back is desirable", rutaṃ refers to crying or sound. The root re is used in the sense of making a sound. It has the form rāyati. There are terms such as rā and ratti. Here, rā is sound. Ratti refers to the night, which is the time when the sounds of beings are stilled. It is called ratti because at this time, sound (rā) is cut off (tiyyati).

The root brū is used in the sense of speaking clearly. There is the usage: "Even after striking himself, he says, 'Another has struck me'".

(The present tense forms are:) bravīti, brunti; brūsi, brūtha; brūmi, brūma; brūte, bruvante; brūse, bruvhe; bruve, brumhe.

(The imperative forms are:) brūtu, bruvitu, bruvantu; brūhi, brūtha; brūmi, brūma; brūtaṃ, bruvantaṃ.

In this context, the form "bruvitu" is mentioned because it is found in the Pali of the Ambaṭṭha Sutta: "Let the Venerable Gotama speak again". In this way, the method should be understood by investigating all terms.

(The optative forms are:) bruveyya, bruve, bruveyyuṃ; bruveyyāsi, bruveyyātha; bruveyyāmi, bruveyyāma; bruvetha, bruveraṃ; bruvetho, bruveyyāvho; bruveyyaṃ; bruveyyāmhe.

Forms with prefixes are: pabrūti, anubrūti; pabrūtu, anubrūtu; pabruveyya, anubruveyya. In this way, the paradigm should be combined accordingly with prefixes such as pa and anu in all instances.

(The perfect tense forms are:) āha, āhu; brave, bravittha, bravire; bravittho, bravivho; braviṃ, bravimhe. These are the forms stated by the power of the parokkhā suffix.
146:
The terms abravā, abravū, abravō, abravattha, abravaṃ, abravamhā, abravattha, abravatthuṃ, abravase, abravhaṃ, abraviṃ, abravimhase are stated by the power of the hiyyattanī suffix. The terms abravi, abravuṃ, abravō, abravittha, abraviṃ, abravimhā, abravā, abravū, abravase, abravivhaṃ, abravaṃ, abravimhe are stated by the power of the ajjatanī suffix. (In the future tense, they are:) bruvissati, bruvissanti. (In the conditional, they are:) abravissā, abravissaṃsu. All remaining terms should be derived in this same manner. The passive form (kammapada) is not well-known. However, if it were to exist, the form would be "brūyati" (it is said), similar to the terms "luyati, lūyati".

The root jīra is used in the sense of increasing (brūhana). Brūhana means growth (vaḍḍhana). The forms are jīrati, jīraṃ, jīramāno, jīraṇaṃ. There is the usage: "This man of little learning grows like an ox (his flesh increases, but not his wisdom)".

The root pūra is used in the sense of filling (pūraṇa). Pūrati (it fills). The great ocean is indeed full. May all intentions be fulfilled. The forms are pūrituṃ, pūritvā, pūraṃ, pūritaṃ, puṇṇaṃ, paripuṇṇaṃ, sampuṇṇaṃ, pūraṇaṃ. There is also the name Pūraṇa Kassapa. In the causative sense (kārita), the forms are: "He fulfills the perfections (pūreti, pūrayati, pūrāpeti, pūrāpayati)", "Having fulfilled (pūretvā, pūrayitvā, pūrāpetvā, pūrāpayitvā, paripūretvā)", and so on.

The root ghora is used in the sense of obstructing movement (gatipaṭighāta). Gatipaṭighāta means the blocking of movement (gatipaṭihanana). Ghorati (he obstructs movement).

The root dhora is used in the sense of skill in movement (gaticāturiya). Gaticāturiya means the state of being clever or skilled in movement (gatichekabhāva). Dhoreti (he is skilled in movement).

The root sara is used in the sense of going (gati). The forms are sarati, visarati, ussarati. There are terms such as ussāraṇā, saro, saṃsāro, and so on. Among those terms, saro means a lake (rahado). Saṃsāro means the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa), which is also called "bhava" (existence).

The root cara is used in the sense of practicing or behaving (caraṇa). The forms are carati, vicarati, anucarati, sañcarati.
147:
The root cara occurs in the senses of going and eating (afflicting). There are verbal forms such as carati, vicarati, anucarati, sañcarati, and paṭicarati. There are also terms such as cariyā, caritā, cāro, vicāro, anuvicāro, upavicāro, caraṇaṃ, cārako, ocarako, and brahmacariyaṃ.

Among these, 'carati' means he goes or he eats (afflicts). Likewise, the teachers say that the meaning of the word 'cara' is going and eating. 'Paṭicarati' means he covers or conceals. 'Cārako' refers to a prison or a cage because it 'eats' (afflicts) the happiness of the beings placed within it. 'Ocarako' is one who habitually goes below (or one who enters inside, i.e., a spy). 'Brahmacariya' is said to refer to giving (dāna), performing services (veyyāvacca), precepts (sikkhāpada), the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), preaching the Dhamma (dhammadesanā), abstinence from sexual intercourse (methunavirati), contentment with one's own wife (sadārasantosa), the uposatha observance, the Noble Path (ariyamagga), the entire Dispensation (sāsana), and also disposition (ajjhāsaya).

"O Naga King, what is your practice? What is your holy life (brahmacariya)? By the fruit of what well-practiced conduct has this psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy arisen? And for what conduct is this great mansion of yours the result?"

"When my wife and I were in the human world, we were both faithful donors. At that time, my house was like a well or a pond, and I fully satisfied the recluses and brahmins. That (systematic giving) was my practice; that practice was indeed the holy life (brahmacariya). O wise one, this psychic power, splendor, strength, energy, and this great mansion are the fruits of that well-practiced conduct."

In this Puṇṇaka Jātaka, giving (dāna) is called 'brahmacariya'.
148:
“Why is your hand wish-fulfilling? Why does what is desired flow from your hand? By what kind of holy life (brahmacariya) is this merit accomplished in your hand?”
