In this context, the Pali, 'Monks, of those who are harmonious and rejoicing... would two monks differ in their views regarding the Abhidhamma?' is the evidence.
186:
This Aṅguttara Pali is the evidence (*nidassana*). In that Pali, '*siyaṃsu*' means 'would they be?'. '*Abhidhamme*' means in the noble Dhamma of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*).

Now, the extraction of the meaning and the classification of the word '*siyā*' will be stated. The word '*siyā*' exists in the sense of certainty (*ekaṃsa*) and in the sense of option/uncertainty (*vikappana*). In the passage, 'The earth element is either internal (*ajjhattika*) or external (*bāhira*),' it is in the sense of certainty. In the Vinaya passage, 'There might be an offense of transgression for a certain monk,' it is in the sense of option.

The word '*siyā*' is one verbal form (*ākhyāta*) and one indeclinable form (*avyaya*). As a verb, it has a singular ending. As an indeclinable, it exists according to the Pali scriptures. In the Dhammapada passage, 'I have sons, I have wealth,' just like the indeclinable '*atthi*', it can have both singular and plural endings. Its usage as a verb is well-known. As an indeclinable, the singular and plural usages should be understood as in: 'Happiness is not accompanied by pleasure, sometimes (*siyā*) it is accompanied by joy,' and 'These states sometimes (*siyā*) have limited objects.' In this indeclinable word '*siyā*', there is no function of the root *asa*. In the perfect tense (*parokkhā*), based on the commentary explanation 'thus it has been (*asa*), thus it has been (*asā*)', the word '*asa*' should be taken. The forms of the imperfect tense (*hiyyattanī*) are not well-known. In the aorist tense (*ajjattanī*), these words '*āsi, āsiṃsu, āsuṃ; āsi, āsittha; āsiṃ, āsimhā*' are well-known. In the future tense (*bhavissanti*), '*bhavissati, bhavissanti*', etc., occur. In the conditional tense (*kālātipatti*), '*abhavissā, abhavissaṃsu*', etc., occur.

The root *sāsa* occurs in the sense of instructing (*anusiṭṭhi*). *Sāsati* (he instructs), *anusāsati* (he instructs repeatedly). He directs your work (*sāsati*). The words *sāsana*, *anusāsana*, *anusāsanī*, *anusiṭṭhi*, *satthā* (teacher), *sattha* (treatise), *anusāsako*, *anusāsikā* are formed.

Among those words, '*sāsana*' is the teaching comprised of the three trainings such as higher virtue (*adhisīla*), etc. Or, *sāsana* is that which is known as learning (*pariyatti*), practice (*paṭipatti*), and realization (*paṭivedha*). Because one instructs by means of this learning, etc., or within this learning, etc., it is called '*sāsana*'. Furthermore, '*sāsana*' is a word that is sent (a message), as in the context, 'He sends a message to the king.' Likewise, '*sāsana*' is advice (*ovāda*). That very advice is also called '*anusāsanī*' or '*anusiṭṭhi*'.

'*Satthā*' is so called because he instructs the world including the devas, having the vehicle of the three characteristics at the forefront. It means he is called '*Satthā*' because he properly instructs beings with the benefits of the present life, the benefits of the future life, and the benefit of the noble Nibbāna. '*Sattha*' is so called because by this treatise, words and meanings are shown. The treatise that makes those meanings and words known is the grammar treatise (*byākaraṇa*).

This root *isa* occurs in the sense of lordship (*issariya*). The state of being a lord is called '*issariya*'. *Isati* (he rules). *Vaṅgīsa* (the Elder Vaṅgīsa), *janapadesa* (ruler of a country), *manujesa* (ruler of men), etc., are formed.
187:
The word 'Sāsana' refers to a message that is delivered, as in the phrase 'He sends a message (sāsana) to the king.' Similarly, the word 'Sāsana' also refers to instruction (ovāda), which is also called 'anusāsanī' or 'anusiṭṭhi.' He is called 'Satthā' (Teacher) because he instructs the world, including the devas, through methods such as the three vehicles (tividhayāna). It means he appropriately instructs beings regarding the benefits of the present life, the benefits of the future life, and the ultimate benefit of Nibbāna. It is called 'Satthā' (Treatise) because through this work, grammar and meaning are taught or shown. What is that treatise? It is the science of grammar (byākaraṇa).

The root 'Īsa' is used in the sense of lordship (issariya). 'Issariya' means the state of being a lord (issarabhāva). 'Īsati' means he rules or masters. For example: Vaṅgīsa (the Elder Vaṅgīsa), Janapadesa (ruler of a country), Manujesa (ruler of men).

Among these, 'Vaṅgīsa' is so called because he is a master of speech (vācāya isso). Who is he? He is the Arahant, Venerable Vaṅgīsa. He himself said:
'Because I was born in the Vaṅga country, I am called Vaṅgīsa; and because I am a master of speech, I am also called Vaṅgīsa.
My name "Vaṅgīsa" has become well-known in the world.'

The root 'Āsa' is used in the sense of sitting (upavesana). It is used as in 'The Saṅgha is seated on the seats (āsane upaviṭṭho).' 'Āsati' and 'acchati' mean he stays or sits. 'Āsīno' means one who is seated. 'Āsana' means a seat. 'Upāsati' means he attends or serves. 'Upāsaka' means a lay follower.

In that context, 'Āsana' is so called because one sits here; it refers to any suitable sitting place such as a couch or a bench.

The root 'Kasī' is used in the senses of going (gati) and drying (sosana). This root is an ī-ending (īkāranta) root; therefore, there is no niggahīta augment (niggahītāgama) after this root. 'Kasati' means he goes or he dries.

The root 'Nisī' is used in the sense of kissing (cumbane). 'Nisati' means he kisses.

The root 'Disī' is used in the sense of dislike or aversion (appīti). 'Dhammaṃ desseti' means he hates the Dhamma. 'Diso' and 'Diṭṭho' mean an enemy. 'Dessī' means one who habitually hates. 'Desso' means one who is unloved. 'Dessiyo' means one who is hated.

In that context, the names 'Disa' and 'Diṭṭha' are synonyms for an enemy (paccamitta). Indeed, he hates others and does not love them, or he is hated by others.
188:
Because love is not shown, he is called 'Disa' or 'Diṭṭha.' Alternatively, 'Disa' refers to a thief or an enemy. 'Diṭṭha,' however, refers strictly to an enemy. In this regard, there are these illustrative examples:
'Whatever (harm) an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to a hater; a wrongly directed mind can do one even greater harm than that.'
And: 'May my enemies also hear the Dhamma-talk (concerning the Four Noble Truths which I have heard from the Buddha).'
And: 'Whatever wholesome qualities the virtuous undertake, may my enemies also associate with those virtuous ones.'
And: 'Monkey king, just as you possess these four qualities—truth, wisdom, fortitude, and generosity—whoever possesses these four qualities overcomes the enemy (just as you have overcome me, the crocodile enemy).'

'Dessī' means one who has the nature of hating or the nature of not loving. 'One who loves the Dhamma prospers; one who hates the Dhamma (dhammadessī) declines.' This (from the Parābhava Sutta) is an illustrative example here. 'Dessa' means one who is unloved; likewise 'Dessiyo' means one who is unloved. In this regard also:
'I do not hate both my children, nor is Queen Maddī unloved by me; but omniscience is dearer to me, therefore I gave away my beloved ones.'
And: 'I do not hate that brahmin woman, nor is it that I lack the power to stop her.'
And: 'I do not hate my mother and father, nor do I hate the great royal glory; but omniscience is dearer to me, therefore I undertook this practice (of pretending to be deaf and dumb).'

In all these examples, the words 'me' and 'mayhaṃ' should be understood as the genitive case (sāmivacana) showing possession. These are the names for an enemy:
'Paccamitta, Ripu, Diṭṭha, Disa, Verī, Sattu, Ari, Amitta, and Sapatta—thus say those who assign names.'

The root 'Esu' is used in the sense of going. 'Esati' means he goes.
189:
The root 'Bhassa' is used in the senses of speaking and shining (ditti). 'Bhassanaṃ' means speaking. 'Ditti' means splendor or beauty. 'Bhassati' means he speaks or he shines. 'Bhassaṃ' and 'Pabhassaraṃ' mean radiant or shining brilliantly.

The root 'Dhisa' is used in the sense of sound. 'Dhisati' means he speaks.

The root 'Disa' is used in the sense of informing or pointing out (atisajjana). 'Disati,' 'upadisati,' 'sandisati,' 'niddisati,' 'paccādisati,' 'paṭisandisati,' and 'uddisati' all mean he points out or instructs. Examples include 'Deso' and 'Uddeso.'

The root 'Pisu' is used in the sense of dividing into parts or grinding (avayave). 'Pisati' means he grinds.

The root 'Isi' is used in the sense of going. 'Isati' means he goes.

The root 'Phusa' is used in the sense of contact (samphassa). 'Phusati' means he touches or contacts. 'Phasso,' 'phusanā,' 'samphusanā,' and 'samphusitattaṃ' are related terms. 'Such was the bodily contact (kāyasamphassa).' 'Phoṭṭhabba' and 'phusita' mean the tangible object. 'The rain sprinkles (phusāyati) drop by drop.' 'Phuṭṭhuṃ,' 'phusituṃ,' 'phusitvā,' 'phusitvāna,' 'phusiya,' and 'phusiyāna' are various forms. 'Touching again and again (phussa phussa), he brings about cessation.'

In that context, 'Phassa' is so called because by this state an object is touched, or it touches by itself, or it is merely the act of touching. It is a state characterized by touching the object.

The roots 'Rusa' and 'Risa' are used in the sense of harming (hiṃsā). 'Rosati' and 'risati' mean he harms. 'Puriso' means a man or person.

In this regard, teachers say: 'Hell is called "puṃ"; because he harms or suffers that hell, he is called "purisa".'

The root 'Risa' is used in the sense of going. 'Resati' means he goes.

The root 'Visa' is used in the sense of entering (pavesana). 'Visati' and 'pavisati' mean he enters. 'Paveso,' 'pavesanaṃ,' 'nivesanaṃ,' and 'pavisaṃ' are related terms. Here, 'nivesanaṃ' refers to a house.

The root 'Masa' is used in the sense of touching or handling (āmasana). 'Masati,' 'āmasati,' and 'parāmasati' mean he touches or handles. 'Parāmāso' and 'parāmasanaṃ' are related terms.
190:
In this context, regarding the term 'parāmāsa': it is called 'parāmāsa' because it misapprehends or touches wrongly. It means taking things such as the impermanent as permanent. Many synonymous terms such as 'parāmāsa', 'micchādiṭṭhi' (wrong view), 'kummagga' (wrong path), and 'micchāpatha' (wrong way) should be taken from the Abhidhamma.

The root 'isu' is used in the sense of desiring. 'Icchati', 'sampaticchati' (desires, accepts). 'Sampaticchanaṃ', 'icchā', 'abhicchā', 'icchaṃ', 'icchamāno'.

The root 'vesu' is used in the sense of giving. 'Vecchati', 'pavecchati', 'paveccheti' (gives). 'Pavecchaṃ', 'pavecchanto'.

The root 'nisa' is used in the sense of rigidity or binding. 'Baddhā' means firm binding (vinibaddhā). This is a designation for 'ahaṅkāra' (egoism or conceit). 'Nisati' (acts with egoism).

The root 'jusi' is used in the senses of delight and service. 'Josati' (delights in, serves).

The root 'isa' is used in the sense of seeking. 'Esati' (seeks). 'Isi' (sage), 'iṭṭhaṃ' (desirable object), 'aniṭṭhaṃ' (undesirable object), 'esaṃ', 'esamāno'.

The root 'saṃkase' is used in the sense of dwelling. 'Acchanaṃ' means sitting (nisīdanaṃ). 'Saṅkasāyati' (dwells).

## Forms of Roots Ending in 'Sa'.

## Roots Ending in 'Ha'.

The root 'hā' is used in the sense of abandoning. 'Jahati', 'vijahati' (abandons). 'Vijahanaṃ', 'jahituṃ', 'jahātave', 'jahitvā', 'jahāya'.

The root 'mhi' is used in the sense of slight smiling. 'Mhayate', 'umhayate', 'vimhayate'.

Among these, 'mhayate' means one smiles. 'Umhayate' means one shows a cheerful manner. 'Vimhayate' means one shows wonder (or laughter). In this regard, there is this Pali: 'Seeing him, she does not show a cheerful manner (na umhayate). They entice with looks and smiles.'
191: She speaks only after first smiling. 'When Princess Prabhāvatī looks at me, showing a cheerful manner, Prabhāvatī might make me smile gently; Prabhāvatī might make me laugh heartily.' In that verse, 'umhayamānā' means laughing while showing a cheerful manner. 'Umhāpeyya' means gladdening by merely smiling. 'Pamhāpeyya' means gladdening by laughing heartily. The root 'hu' is used in the sense of giving or offering. 'Havati' (offers, sacrifices), 'huti' (offering). The root 'hu' is used in the sense of preparing in various ways. The act of preparing in various ways is called 'pasajjakaraṇa'. 'Havati' (prepares), 'huto', 'hutavā', 'hutāvī', 'āhuti' (an object of offering). The root 'hū' is used in the sense of existence (being). 'Hoti', 'honti', 'hosi', 'hotha', 'homi', 'homa'. 'Pahoti', 'pahonti' (is able, is sufficient). 'Pahūtaṃ', 'pahūtā' (abundant, arisen). It is as in the sentence: 'From where do quarrels and disputes arise?' 'Honto', 'hontā', 'hontaṃ', 'pahonto' (being, being able). 'One should be a junior monk' (pacchāsamaṇena hotabbaṃ). For the sake of being (hotuṃ, hotuye), for the sake of being able (pahotuṃ), having been (hutvāna). These are the forms of the present tense (vattamānā) etc. Here, only the well-known forms are taken. 'Hotu', 'hontu', 'hosi', 'hotha', 'homi', 'homa' are the forms of the imperative mood (pañcamī). Here too, only the well-known forms are taken. 'Huveyya', 'huveyyuṃ', 'huveyyāsi', 'huveyyātha', 'huveyyāmi', 'huveyyāma', 'huvetha', 'huveraṃ', 'huvetho', 'huveyyāvho', 'huveyyaṃ', 'huveyyāmhe' are the forms of the optative mood (sattamī). Here, however, because the word 'huveyya' is found in the Pali: 'Upaka the Ājīvaka, having said, "It may be so, friend (huveyya pāvuso)," shook his head, took a wrong path, and departed,' the forms 'huveyya', 'huveyyuṃ', etc., are stated according to that method. The reading 'hupeyya' is also seen, just as 'paccavekkhaṇā' is used as 'paccapekkhaṇā'. By the power of that reading (hupeyya), 'hupeyya'...
192: ...'hupeyyuṃ', 'hupeyyāsī', etc., the forms which are substitutions of 'pa' for 'va' should also be taken. Another method: 'heyya', 'heyyuṃ', 'heyyāsi', 'heyyātha', 'heyyāmi', 'heyyāma', 'hetha', 'heraṃ', 'hetho', 'heyyāvho', 'heyyaṃ', 'heyyāmhe'. These are the forms taken according to the method of the Commentaries. In this regard, this example should also be noted: 'Arising does not occur. If it were to occur (heyya), it would reach the arising of arising.' 'Huva', 'huvu', 'huve', 'huvittha', 'huvaṃ', 'huvimha'. 'Huvittha' and 'hotha' also mean 'ahosi' (was/became) due to the elision of the conjunct 'ta'. For instance, when the teachers explain the meaning of the word 'Livelihood was difficult (hotha)', the meaning is stated as 'Our livelihood became painful (ahosi)'. 'Huvire', 'huvittho', 'huvivhaṃ', 'huviṃ', 'huvimhe' are the forms of the perfect tense (parokkhā). 'Ahuvā', 'ahuvū', 'ahuvō', 'ahuvattha', 'ahuvaṃ', 'ahuvamha', 'ahuvattha', 'ahuvatthuṃ', 'ahuvase', 'ahuvavhaṃ', 'ahuviṃ', 'ahuvamhase' are the forms of the imperfect tense (hiyattanī). Here, 'ahuvamhase' means 'we have become' (bhavamhase). However, in the Pali: 'We did your task; whatever strength we had (ahuvamhase),' the word-analysis should be made as 'ahuva amhase' or 'ahu amhase'. In the latter method, with the augment 'va', both 'ahuvā' and 'ahū' mean 'was/became' (ahosi). 'Amhaṃ' means 'our'. 'Se' is merely a particle. This is what is meant: Whatever strength was ours, we did your task with that strength. 'Ahosi', 'ahuṃ', 'ahesuṃ', 'ahuvo', 'ahuvittha'. There is also 'ahosittha'. There are also 'ahosiṃ', 'ahuvāsiṃ', 'ahosimha'...
193: Ahumhā. Ahuvā, ahuvū, ahuvase, ahuvivhaṃ. There are also the forms ahuvaṃ and ahuṃ. Ahuvimhe. These are the forms of the Aorist (ajjatanī) tense. In this context, because the usage "I was (ahuṃ) a fisherman's boy in the village of Kevaṭṭagāma" is found, it is stated as "ahu," meaning "I was (ahosiṃ)." Because the usage "Venerable Sir, in the past I was (ahuvāsiṃ) a disciple of the Conqueror named Sumedha" is found, it is stated as "ahuvāsiṃ," and this very meaning should be understood. This is because the teachers who explained the meaning of this Pali in the Anekavaṇṇavimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā showed the meaning of "ahuvāsiṃ" as "I was (ahosiṃ)." These four—"hessati, hehissati, hehiti, hohiti"—should be known as the matrix terms (mātikāpada) of the Future (bhavissantī) tense. Now I shall analyze those terms: Hessati, hessanti. Hessasi, hessatha. Hessāmi, hessāma. Hessate, hessante. Hessase, hessavhe. Hessaṃ, hessāmhe. These terms are stated because the usage "In the future time, we shall be (hessāma) in the presence of this [Buddha]" is found. Hehissati, hehissanti. Hehissasi. The rest should be understood in detail. Hohissati, hohissanti. Hohissasi. The rest should be understood in detail. Hehiti, hehinti. Hehisi. The rest should be understood in detail. Hohiti, hohinti. Hohisi. The rest should be understood in detail. These are the forms of the Future (bhavissantī) tense. Ahuvissā, ahuvissaṃsu. Ahuvissase, ahuvissatha. Ahuvissaṃ, ahuvissamhā. Ahuvissatha, ahuvissisu.
194: Ahuvissase, ahuvissavhe, ahuvissiṃ, ahuvissāmhase. These are the forms of the Conditional (kālātipatti). The root vhe is used in the senses of calling (avhāyana), pride (baddhā), and sound (sadda). Calling is termed avhāyana. Baddhā refers to either the conceit of 'I' (ahaṅkāra), or striking (ghaṭṭana), or harassment and oppression (sārambhakaraṇa). Sound is termed sadda (rava). The forms vheti, vhāyati, avheti, avhāyati, and avhāsi also occur. "O King, I am the youth Kaccāyana; they call (mavhayanti) me by the name Anūna (Puṇṇaka)." (In the word avhayanti) the sound 'ā' is merely a prefix (upasagga); that prefix 'ā' becomes short (a) because it is followed by the conjunct 'vh'. Avhito (called). 'Anavhito' (uncalled) he came from there. Avhā, avhāyanā (calling). Trees called Vāraṇa. In the sense-object called Kāma. The prince named Canda. "I taught the art of the lute, which has seven strings, is very sweet, and is delightful. That disciple now harasses and challenges (avheti) me in the public arena; O Kosiya (Sakka), be my refuge." In this verse, 'avheti' means he strikes and oppresses in order to show his own power through harassment. In the passage, "When the one hundred and one kings had assembled together in unity, the Yakkha Puṇṇaka challenged (avhettha) them without trembling," the term avhāyana also refers to striking through harassment. "There they dance and sing, and they challenge (avhāyanti) one another excellently. Like celestial nymphs among the gods, the women are well-adorned (and they dance and sing)." Here, 'avhāyanti varāvaraṃ' should be understood to mean that while performing dancing and singing most excellently, they engage in harassment (sārambha). The root pañha is used in the sense of questioning (pucchā). The monk asks (pañhati) a difficult question to the teacher. Pañho (a question). This is the Pali: "He inquires (paripucchati), he questions (paripañhati), 'Venerable Sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?'" The word pañha should be taken as masculine. "Pañho..."
195: "...maṃ paṭibhāti, taṃ suṇā" (It is clear to me, listen to that [question]), because the masculine usage is mostly seen, it should be designated as masculine (pullinga). However, in some places, it also occurs as feminine (itthilinga) and neuter (napuṃsakalinga). This is shown in the Pali passages such as "Pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā" (This question has been thought out by the wise) and "Koṇḍañña pañhāni viyākarohi" (Koṇḍañña, answer the questions). Alternatively, it should be regarded as a change of gender (lingavipallāsa) in those instances. The root pañha is also used in the sense of desire (icchā). Pañhati, pañho. In this context, "pañho" means the meaning that is desired to be known. The derivation (nibbacana) of this word is: "Pañhiyati ñātuṃ icchiyati soti pañho" (It is called pañha because it is desired to be known). Therefore, in explaining the meaning of the Netti-pāḷi passage "vissajjitamhi pañhe," it is stated: "Pañheti ñātuṃ icchite atthe" (In the word pañhe, it means in the sense that is desired to be known). The root miha is used in the sense of sprinkling (secana). Mihati, ummihati. Megho, mehanaṃ. Among them, "ummihati" means to urinate (passāvaṃ karoti). "Megho" is called megha (cloud) because it sprinkles (mihati siñcati) the world with streams of rain; it is also called pajjunna. "Mehanaṃ" refers to the female pudenda (guyhaṭṭhāna). The root daha is used in the senses of reducing to ashes (bhasmīkaraṇa) and holding or considering (dhāraṇa). Fire burns (dahati) the houses. This man considers (dahati) this woman as a grandmother; it means he holds (dhāreti) her as "my grandmother." The intention is that this woman is the grandmother to this man. In this regard, there is the Pali: "Sakyā kho ambaṭṭha rājānaṃ okkākaṃ pitāmahaṃ dahanti" (Ambaṭṭha, the Sakyans consider King Okkāka as their grandfather). A house burnt by fire is called "daḍḍhaṃ gehaṃ." Dayhati, dayhamānaṃ. By changing the letter 'da' to 'ḍa', there is the form "ḍahati." Usages such as "Ḍahantaṃ bālamanveti, bhasmāchannova pāvako" (Like a fire covered by ashes burns the one who steps on it, evil follows and burns the fool) are examples here. The root caha is used in the sense of striving (parisakkana). Cahati. The root raha is used in the sense of abandoning (cāga). Rahati. Raho (a secret/secluded place), rahito (devoid of/abandoned). The root rahi is used in the sense of going (gati). Rahati. Raho, rahaṃ.
196: The roots dahi and bahi are used in the sense of growth. There are forms such as dahati and bahati. The root bahi is also used in the sense of faith (belief). The word 'ca' implies the sense of growth. There is the form bahati. The roots tuhi and duhi are used in the sense of wetting (or oppressing). There are forms such as tuhati and duhati. The roots araha and maha are used in the sense of worship. There are forms such as arahati, arahaṃ, and arahā. There is the form mahati. Mahanaṃ and maho mean worship. Vihāramaho (monastery festival). Cetiyamaho (pagoda festival). In the word 'arahā', because of being free from defilements and being truly worthy of offerings, one makes the offerings and honors given to oneself bear great fruit; thus, in the sense of being worthy of worship and honor, one is called 'arahā' (an Arahant). It refers to one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava). The root īha is used in the sense of urging (exertion). There is the form īhati. Īhā (exertion). Īhā is said to be energy (vīriya). The roots vaha and maha are used in the sense of growth. There are forms such as vahati and mahati. The roots ahi and pilahi are used in the sense of going. There are forms such as ahati, pilahati, and ahi. Here, although the derivation of 'ahi' is the same, it is called 'ahi' (snake) because it is capable of going without feet. The roots garaha and kalaha are used in the sense of contempt. There are forms such as garahati, garahā, kalahati, and kalaho. The roots varaha and valaha are used in the senses of being a leader, abusing, oppressing, and taking. There are forms such as varahati and valahati. Varāho. Here, the word 'varāho' refers to both a pig and an elephant. This is so because in places such as 'Eneyyā ca varāhā ca' and 'Mahāvarāhova nivāpapuṭṭho', the pig is called by the name 'varāha'. However, in places such as 'Mahāvarāhassa nadīsu jaggato, bhisaṃ ghasamānassa', the elephant is called by the name 'varāha'. 'Mahāvarāhassa' means 'of the great elephant'. The roots vehu, jehu, and vāhu are used in the sense of effort. There are forms such as vehati, jehati, and vāhati. Vāhano.
197: A horse is called vāhana. This is because when matters such as war arise, people exert effort and use energy (vīriya) with this horse; thus it is called vāhana. The root dāhu is used in the sense of waking from sleep. There is the form dāhati. The root ūha is used in the sense of thinking. There are forms such as ūhati, āyūhati, viyūhati, byūhati, and apohati. There are forms such as ūhanaṃ, āyūhanaṃ, byūho, and apoho. Among them, ūhati means thinks; āyūhati means strives; viyūhati means removes (scratches) dust. The word byūhati is also understood in this same way. Apohati means discards or separates. The root gāhu is used in the sense of agitation (movement). There is the form gāhati. Gāho, candaggāho (lunar eclipse), suriyaggāho (solar eclipse), nakkhattaggāho (stellar eclipse). The root gaha is used in the sense of taking. There are forms such as gahati and paggahati. 'Āhutiṃ paggahissāmi' (I shall take the offering). There are forms such as paggaho and paggāho. Paggaho is an alms-bowl. Paggāho is energy (vīriya). The root saha is used in the sense of endurance. Endurance is called parisahana (khanti). There is the form sahati. There are forms such as saho, asaho, and asayho. The root ruha is used in the sense of the manifestation of bark (the growth of new flesh). There is the form ruhati. Rukkho (tree). The root mātu is used in the sense of reverence. There is the form māhati. The root guhū is used in the sense of concealing (hiding). There are forms such as guhati and nigguhati. Guho and guyhako (a Guyhaka deity). The root vaha is used in the sense of reaching. There is the form vahati. vārivaho (a river or ocean that carries water). The root duha is used in the sense of filling (milking). There are forms such as duhati and dohati. Duyhamānā gāvī (a cow being milked). The root diha is used in the sense of increasing (accumulation). There is the form dehati. Deho. Deha means the body.
198: The root liha is used in the sense of enjoying (licking). There are forms such as lehati and palehati (licks). Lehanīyaṃ (that which is to be licked). Here, the Pali text is: "Dogs licked the feet of this boy." The meaning of this statement is: Dogs licked the soles of the feet of this boy with their tongues. The root oha is used in the sense of abandoning. Ohati (abandons). One discards all that is harmful (apohati). Apoho (abandoning). The root brahma is used in the sense of rising upwards. Brahati (rises). Brahā (one who rises). The roots daha and thaha have the sense of oppressing. Dahati and thahati (oppresses). The root brūha is used in the sense of increasing. Because of increasing step by step, one is called Brahmā. In the causative form, there is the usage: "It is fit to develop (anubrūhetuṃ) seclusion." Because of being developed with various special qualities, one is called Brahmā. By the name Brahmā, Mahābrahmā is meant, as well as the Buddha, a Brahmin, parents, and the most excellent. In phrases such as "Brahmā with a thousand followers, Brahmā with two thousand followers," Mahābrahmā is called 'Brahmā'. In the statement, "Bhikkhus, 'Brahmā' is a designation for the Tathāgata," the Buddha is meant. "The Buddha, the dispeller of darkness, the All-seeing One, Who has reached the end of the world, Who has transcended all existence, Free from taints, with all suffering abandoned, Whose name is Truth—that Brahmā I have attended upon." In this verse, a Brahmin (brāhmaṇa) is meant. In the statement, "Parents are called Brahmās and first teachers," parents are meant. In the statement, "He sets in motion the Brahmā-wheel," the most excellent is meant. In this regard, it is said:
199: "The word 'Brahmā' is used for Mahābrahmā, for a Brahmin, and also for parents, for the Tathāgata, and for the most excellent." Another way: There are three types of Brahmās: Sammuti-brahmā (conventional Brahmā), Upapatti-brahmā (Brahmā by rebirth), and Visuddhi-brahmā (Brahmā by purity). "Kosiya, the parrots are eating your rich field of Sāli rice; O Brahmā, I inform you, I am not able to stop them," and "O Mahābrahmā, run away; other beings are also cooking"—in such instances, Sammuti-brahmās are referred to by the word 'Brahmā'. "The doors to the Deathless are open for them; let those who have ears release their faith. O Brahmā, thinking it would be wearying, I did not speak the refined Dhamma among men." "Then Sahampati Brahmā..."—in such instances, Upapatti-brahmā is referred to by the word 'Brahmā'. Because of statements such as "He sets in motion the Brahmā-wheel," the Noble Dhamma (Ariya-dhamma) is called 'Brahmā'. All Noble Ones (Ariyas) who arise from that Noble Dhamma are also called Visuddhi-brahmās without distinction, because they are Brahmās in the ultimate sense. Specifically, according to the statement, "Bhikkhus, 'Brahmā' is a designation for the Tathāgata," the Fully Enlightened Buddhas are called Uttama-brahmās (Supreme Brahmās) because they have reached the pinnacle of perfections through qualities that are Brahma-like in the world with its devas. In this regard, it is said: "Brahmās are of three types by way of Sammuti, Upapatti, and Visuddhi; they are of four types including the Uttama (Supreme)."
200:
The root dhimha is used in the sense of spitting or vomiting. Dhimheti—he spits. The Pali passage: "Look at the arrow that entered from the right side and exited through the left; I spit blood (or look at me spitting blood)" is the evidence. In that Pali, dhimhāmi means I spit or vomit.

## Forms of roots ending in the letter Ha.

## Roots ending in the letter Ḷa.

The root biḷa is used in the sense of scolding. Beḷati—he scolds. Biḷāro—a cat.

The root kīḷa is used in the sense of playing or dwelling. Kīḷati—he plays or sports. Kīḷā—playing.

The root aḷa is used in the sense of arising or ascending. Aḷati—it arises. Vāḷo—a wild beast.

The root laḷa is used in the sense of sporting or gracefulness. Laḷati—he sports. Laḷito asso—a graceful or elegant horse.

The root kaḷa is used in the senses of intoxication and harshness. Kakkassaṃ means a harsh or rough nature. Kaḷati—he is harsh.

The root tuḷa is used in the sense of piercing or prodding. Toḷati—he pierces.

The roots huḷa and hoḷa are used in the sense of going. Huḷati, hoḷati—he goes.

The root roḷa is used in the sense of disrespect. Roḷati—he treats with disrespect.

The root loḷa is used in the sense of madness or fickleness. Loyati—he is mad or fickle.

The roots heḷa and hoḷa are used in the sense of disrespect. Heḷati, hoḷati—he treats with disrespect.

The root vāḷa is used in the sense of calling. Vāḷati—he calls.

The roots dāḷa and dhāḷa are used in the sense of spreading. Dāḷati, dhāḷati—it spreads.

The root haḷa is used in the sense of praising. Haḷati—he praises.

The root hīḷa is used in the sense of disrespect (contempt). Hīḷati—he treats with contempt. Hīḷā—contempt, hīḷiko—one who treats with contempt, hīḷito—that which is treated with contempt.
201:
The root kaḷa is used in the sense of pouring. Kaḷati—he pours. Kaḷanaṃ—pouring.

The root heḷa is used in the sense of wrapping or enveloping. Heḷati—he wraps.

The root īḷa is used in the sense of praising. Īḷati—he praises.

The root juḷa is used in the sense of going. Juḷati, joḷati—he goes.

The roots puḷa and muḷa are used in the sense of happiness. Puḷati, muḷati—he is happy.

The root guḷa is used in the sense of protecting. Guḷati—he protects. Guḷo—molasses (or jaggery).

The root juḷa is used in the sense of binding. Juḷati—he binds.

The root kuḷa is used in the sense of eating. Kuḷati—he eats.

The root khuḷa is used in the senses of foolishness and eating. The word 'ca' implies the sense of eating. Khuḷati—he is foolish; he eats.

The roots suḷa and buḷa are used in the sense of restraint or closing. Suḷati, buḷati—he restrains.

The root puḷa is used in the sense of gathering. Puḷati—he gathers. Puḷinaṃ—sand.

The root saḷa is used in the sense of making an indistinct sound. Saḷati—it chirps or sounds. Sāḷiko, sāḷikā—a myna bird.

"The earth bellows like a bull,
The earth roars like a king of beasts (lion),
The earth sounds indistinctly like a crocodile;
What will be the consequence?"
This Pali verse is the evidence.

## These are the forms of roots ending in the letter Ḷa.

Thus, the forms of roots ending in non-vagganta consonants in the Bhūvādi group are completed. By this much, all the roots in the Bhūvādi group have been shown.

Now, among the roots belonging to the Bhūvādi group, some have different sounds, and some have different final consonants. Among those roots, some have been stated by ancient teachers by combining them based on having the same meaning. We shall explain those very roots in part, along with the demonstration of their forms and so on. How is that shown?
202:
The roots hū and bhū are used in the sense of existence (being). Hoti, bhavati (it is/becomes). Pahoti (it is sufficient/he is able), pabhavati (it flows). "Friend, it should indeed be." "If arising should occur." "The Yakkha conquered the noble hero among men; in that contest, a great roar occurred." "This mango tree was here before." "There was a king of the Videhans." "Sakka, I have much wealth." "The noble one performs much merit." "A man of much wealth." "The Blessed One has a large and long tongue." "Quarrels and disputes arising from the beloved." "The junior monk should be." "It should be." To be (hotuṃ, hetuye, bhavituṃ). Having been (hutvā, hutvāna, bhavitvā, bhavitvāna).

In this context, the Pali: "There is that path, it will be; it is not possible for it not to be" is the evidence. In that Pali, "nahetuye" means not to be (abhavituṃ). It should be understood that from the root hū, the suffix -tuṃ or -tave is replaced by -tuye, and the vowel ū is replaced by e. Alternatively, it also means "it is not impossible to be a cause." However, this meaning is not intended here; only the former meaning is intended, because it is the meaning of the word cited as an example of the root hū.

Among those words, "pahoti" means this cloth is sufficient to make a robe because of its breadth; it is not insufficient. Or "pahoti" means a man is able to conquer enemies. Or else, "pahoti" means it is (hoti). "Pabhavati" means it flows. "Pahūtaṃ" means abundant or great. "Pahūtavitto" means one who has abundant wealth, a very wealthy person. "Pahūtajivho" means one who has a very large, very long, and very soft tongue. "Piyappabhūtā" means those (things) born from love.

The roots gamu and sappa are used in the sense of going (gati). Gacchati, gamati, ghammati, āgacchati, uggacchati, atigacchati, paṭigacchati, avagacchati, adhigacchati, anugacchati, upagacchati, apagacchati, vigacchati, nigacchati, niggacchati. Other words should also be combined. As in "samuggacchati" and so on...
203:
They may also be combined by the power of two prefixes (upasagga) as appropriate. They are: sappati, saṃsappati, parisappati. Other words should also be combined.

Among those roots, gamati means gacchati (he goes). In the causative (kārita), the forms "devadattaṃ gameti, gamayati" (he causes Devadatta to go) occur. The illustration "He causes to go to the states of deprivation, thus it is called apāyagamanīya" is the example here. For this root gam, which belongs to the Curādi group and has the prefix ā-, the active voice (suddhakattu) forms are "āgameti, āgamayati, āgamento, āgamayamāno".

Among those forms, āgameti means he endures (waits) for a moment. Ghammati means he goes. Āgacchati means he comes. Uggacchati means he ascends or goes upwards. Atigacchati means he goes beyond (surpasses). Paṭigacchati means he goes again (returns). Avagacchati means he knows. Adhigacchati means he attains or knows. Anugacchati means he follows behind. Upagacchati means he approaches. Apagacchati means he departs. Vigacchati means he disappears. Nigacchati means he attains. The sentence "A man attains fame" is the illustration here. Niggacchati means he exits. Sappati means he goes. Saṃsappati means he goes while crawling. Parisappati means he goes all around.

Now, for the sake of producing great skill in the Tipiṭaka, the Word of the Buddha, along with the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) for the wise, I shall describe the conjugation table (padamālā) along with examples. For instance: So gacchati, te gacchanti, gacchare. Tvaṃ gacchasi, tumhe gacchatha. Ahaṃ gacchāmi, mayaṃ gacchāma. So gacchate, te gacchante. Tvaṃ gacchase, tumhe gacchavhe. Ahaṃ gacche, mayaṃ gacchāmhe. These are the forms of the Present tense (Vattamanā).

So gacchatu, te gacchantu. Tvaṃ gacchāhi, gaccha, gacchassu, tumhe gacchatha. Ahaṃ gacchāmi, mayaṃ gacchāma. So gacchataṃ, te gacchantantāṃ. Tvaṃ gacchassu, tumhe gacchavho. Ahaṃ gacche, mayaṃ gacchāmase. These are the forms of the Imperative tense (Pañcamī).
204:
He should go, he should go. They should go. You should go. You (plural) should go. I should go. We should go, we should go. He should go. They should go. You should go. You (plural) should go. I should go. We should go. These are the forms of the Potential tense (Sattamī).

He went. They went. You went. You (plural) went, you went. I went. We went, we went. He went, he went. They went. You went. You (plural) went. I went, I went. We went. These are the forms of the Perfect tense (Parokkhā).

He went. They went. You went. You (plural) went. I went. We went. He went. They went. You went. You (plural) went. I went. We went. These are the forms of the Aorist tense (Ajjatanī).

He will go. They will go. You will go. You (plural) will go. I will go. We will go. He will go. They will go. You will go. You (plural) will go. I will go. We will go. These are the forms of the Future tense (Bhavissantī).

He would have gone. They would have gone. You would have gone. You (plural) would have gone. I would have gone. We would have gone. He would have gone. They would have gone. You would have gone. You (plural) would have gone. I would have gone. We would have gone. These are the forms of the Conditional tense (Kālātipatti).

Among those tenses, it should be understood that although the arrival of the letter 'a' (augment) in the Ajjatanī and Kālātipatti tenses can be found in all persons and all numbers, it occurs inconsistently in the Dispensation (Sāsana). Therefore, two forms each are seen, such as 'agacchi, gacchi, gacchissā, gacchissā', etc. Gamati, gamanti. Gamatu, gacchantu. Gameyya, gameyyuṃ. All the rest should be understood in detail.
205:
Now, the distinctions in the Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, and Ajjatanī tenses (of the root gamu) will be stated—That man went to the path (ga); that woman came to the house (āga). They went to the path (gu); those women came to the house (āgu). By substituting the letter 'a' for the Parokkhā second person singular 'e' inflection: 'You went to the path (ga)'; 'You came to the house (āga)'. You all went to the path (guttha); you all came to the house (āguttha). I went to the path (gaṃ); I came to the house (āgaṃ). I followed after that man (anvagaṃ). We went to the path (gumha); we came to the house (āgumha); we followed after that man (anvaguṃha). These are the distinct forms of the Parokkhā tense.

'He went to the path (agamā), they went to the path (agamū),' etc., are forms of the Hiyattanī tense. 'He went (agami), they went (agamuṃ), they went (guṃ),' etc., are forms of the Ajjatanī tense.

Now, to clarify the word-forms (padarūpa) of these three tenses, some verses (illustrative sutta) will be cited—'He (the king of the Kumbhīra spirits) also came to the Mahāvana forest where the assembly of devas and brahmas gathered (āgā). Then, the fifth brahmin came to that forest (āgā). The glorious devas came (āguṃ). Just as an unintelligent crow follows the will of sensual desires, may I not follow the will of sensual desires (anvagaṃ). The Buddha went to the city of Rājagaha (agamā). (They) went to Mount Vaṅka (agamu). The brahmins approached me (upagacchu).' Such are the examples.

ga, gu, ga, guttha, gaṃ, gumha (Parokkhā forms); agu, agamu, agamuṃ (Ajjatanī forms); agamā, agami, gacchanti—these various forms should be borne in mind.

Now, the nominal forms (nāmika) will be stated—one who has gone (gato), one who goes (gantā), one who is going (gacchaṃ), a woman who is going (gacchantī), a family that is going (gacchantaṃ kulaṃ), associated with (sahagataṃ), destination/course (gati), the act of going (gamanaṃ), going (gamo), coming/tradition (āgamo), understanding/comprehension (avagamo), that which should be gone to (gantabbaṃ), that which is fit to be gone to (gamaniyaṃ), that which is reachable (gammaṃ), that which is being gone to (gammamānaṃ), that which is being reached (gamiyamānaṃ), an ox/cow (go), a woman (mātugāmo), asafoetida (hiṅgu), a living being (jagu), a living being (indagū), a quarrel (medhago), and so forth. In the causative (kārita) sense—causes to go (gacchāpeti, gacchāpayati, gaccheti, gacchayati, gammeti). In the passive (kamma) sense—is gone to (gammati, gamiyati), is attained/understood (adhigammati, adhigamiyati). In the infinitive and absolutive forms—to go (gantuṃ, gamituṃ), having gone (gantvā, gantvāna, gamitvā, gamitvāna, gamiya, gamiyāna, gamma, āgamma, āgantvā, adhigamma, adhigantvā), and so forth.
206:
And so forth. The forms of the root sappa, however, are 'sappo (snake), sappinī (female snake), pīṭhasappī (a cripple), sappi (clarified butter),' and so on.

Among those, the word 'sahagata' is seen in these five meanings: tabbhāva (nature/state of being), vokiṇṇa (interspersed/mixed), nissaya (dependence), ārammaṇa (object), and saṃsaṭṭha (conjoined).

Among these meanings, in the passage 'This craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust (nandirāgasahagatā),' it should be understood in the sense of tabbhāva, meaning it is the very nature of delight and lust. In the passage 'O bhikkhus, this investigation which is interspersed with sloth, conjoined with sloth (kosajjasahagatā),' it should be understood in the sense of vokiṇṇa, meaning it is interspersed with sloth that arises from time to time. In the passage 'He develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by the perception of a skeleton (aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ),' it should be understood in the sense of nissaya, meaning it is obtained by depending on and developing the perception of a skeleton. In the passage 'He is an obtainer of attainments having form as an object (rūpasahagatānaṃ) or those having the formless as an object (arūpasahagatānaṃ),' it should be understood in the sense of ārammaṇa, meaning attainments that have form or the formless as their objects. In the passage 'This happiness is accompanied by this joy (pītiyā sahagataṃ), co-nascent, and conjoined,' it should be understood in the sense of saṃsaṭṭha, meaning it is mixed with this joy. On this matter, it is said:

The word 'sahagata' is seen in five senses:
In nature (tabbhāva), in being interspersed (vokiṇṇa),
In dependence (nissaya), in object (ārammaṇa),
And in being conjoined (saṃsaṭṭha).

As for 'gati,' there are many varieties such as gatigati, nibbattigati, ajjhāsayagati, vibhavagati, nipphattigati, and ñāṇagati.

Among these, in the phrases 'Having passed away, I go to that destination (gatiṃ)' and 'Whose destination (gatiṃ) the devas, gandhabbas, and humans do not know,' this is called gatigati (destination of rebirth).
207:
In the statement, "I do not know the destination (gati) or the non-destination (agati) of these virtuous monks," the word gati is called 'nibbattigati' (the course of arising/birth). In the statement, "O Brahma, thus I know your destination of intent (gati) and I know your splendor," the word gati is called 'ajjhāsayagati' (the course of inclination). In the statement, "Destruction (vibhava) is the destination (gati) of conditioned phenomena; Nibbāna is the destination (gati) of the Arahant," the word gati is called 'vibhavagati' (the course of disappearance/ending). In the statement, "There are only two destinations of completion (gati), no others," the word gati is called 'nipphattigati' (the course of result/completion). In the statement, "In that assembly, that person who possesses wisdom (gatimā) and energy..." and "He has gone to the beautiful Nibbāna by knowing it," the word gati is called 'ñāṇagati' (the course of knowledge).

This meaning is stated as follows:
The word 'gati' is employed in the sense of destination (gatigati), in arising (nibbatti),
In destruction (vibhava) and inclination (ajjhāsaya),
In completion (nipphatti), and in knowledge (ñāṇa).

It is called 'go' because it goes (moves). It is called 'mātugāma' (woman) because she arrives at a state similar to a mother or at a state of mixing. It is called 'hiṅgu' (asafoetida) because it goes against (cures) disease while afflicting it.

These are its names:
Hiṅgu, hiṅgujatu, and also hiṅgusipāṭikā;
These varieties of hiṅgu are mentioned in the Vinaya Commentary.

It is called 'jagu' because it goes from death (cuti) to birth (jāti). It is called 'indagū' because it goes by means of the senses (indriya). Or, it is called 'indagū' because it goes by means of powerful (inda-bhūta) kamma. There is also the Pali form 'hindagū.' There, 'hinda' means death (maraṇa). Because it goes to that death, it is called 'hindagū.' All of these are designations for living beings (satta), and grammatically they are masculine (pullinga). It is called 'medhago' because it proceeds (goes) by harming (medhamāna) its own support (body) and others; it refers to a quarrel (kalaha). Indeed, in the verse, "Because of knowing that (we must die), quarrels (medhagā) are stilled," the Blessed One used the word 'medhaga' to mean quarrel. Regarding the word 'gamitvā':

"Having gone (gamitvāna) to the forest named Isipatana,
And having disciplined the group of five (pañcavaggiya),
Thereafter, the Blessed One disciplined (others),
Going and going (gantvā gantvā) here and there."
208:
This Pali passage is an illustration. 'Sappa' is so called because it moves; the meaning is that it moves by wriggling. Therefore, the Venerable Sāriputta, in the Niddesa of this Kāma Sutta Pali, which states, "He who avoids sensual pleasures as one avoids the head of a snake with one's foot," taught as follows: "A snake is called 'sappa'. For what reason is it called 'sappa'? It is called 'sappa' because it moves by wriggling. It is called 'bhujaga' because it moves in a winding manner. It is called 'uraga' because it moves with its breast. It is called 'pannaga' because it moves with its head lowered. It is called 'sarīsapa' because it moves with its body. It is called 'bilāsaya' because it sleeps (dwells) in a hole. It is called 'dāṭhāvudha' because its fangs are its weapons. It is called 'ghoravisa' because its venom is terrible. It is called 'dujivha' because its tongue is forked. It is called 'dvirasaññū' because it tastes (perceives) flavor with two tongues."

'Sappinī' refers to a female snake (uragī). 'Pīṭhasappī' is so called because one moves by means of a stool; it refers to a person with disabled legs (a cripple). 'Sappi' is so called because it occurs (moves/proceeds) to increase the strength and longevity of the consumer; it refers to clarified butter (ghata).

The roots 'sakka', 'ṭeka', and 'langha' occur in the sense of movement. 'Sakkati', 'nisakkati' (moves or will sit), 'parisakkati' (exerts effort). 'Nisakka' (movement), 'parisakkana' (exertion). 'Ṭekati' (moves). 'Ṭīkā' (a sub-commentary). 'Langhati' (moves by jumping or overstepping), 'ullanghati', 'olanghati', 'langhaka' (one who jumps), 'ullanghikā pīti' (uplifting joy that causes one to leap).

The roots 'ke', 're', and 'ge' occur in the sense of making a sound. 'Kāyati' (sounds/speaks), 'rāyati', 'gāyati'. 'Jātaka' (birth story), 'rā' (sound), 'gīta' (song). 'Kāyituṃ', 'rāyituṃ', 'gāyituṃ'. 'Kāyitvā', 'rāyitvā', 'gāyitvā'.

In that context (regarding the word Jātaka), 'Jātaka' is so called because the Buddha tells (kāyati) his past conduct (jāta) that has occurred in previous lives through this (Pali). Here, the Jātaka Pali is referred to as 'Jātaka'. In other contexts, however, 'jātaka' should be understood as simply 'jāta' (that which has arisen). Indeed, the word 'jātaka' is used in the sense of Pariyatti (scriptural texts) in such passages as "Itivuttakaṃ, Jātakaṃ, Abbhutadhammaṃ," and in the sense of Jāti (birth/existence) in such passages as "Jātakaṃ samodhānesi." 'Rā' is said to mean sound. 'Gīta' means singing.

The roots 'khe', 'je', and 'se' occur in the sense of exhaustion or destruction (khaya). 'Khāyati' (is exhausted), 'jāyati', 'sāyati'. The meaning is that it reaches destruction.

An objection (codanā) might be raised here: "Venerable Sir, should not the meaning of the word 'khāyati' be 'eats' (khādati) or 'is apparent' (paññāyati)? Similarly, should not the meaning of 'jāyati' be 'arises' (nibbattati), and the meaning of 'sāyati' be 'tastes' (assādeti)? This being so, why is the meaning 'reaches destruction' stated here?" (The answer is:) True, but because roots have multiple meanings (anekattha), it is permissible to state the meaning in this way.

For example, in the passage, "This man of little learning grows old (jīrati) like an ox," the word 'jīrati' here does not express the meaning of reaching old age, but rather expresses the meaning of increasing (in flesh). This case should be understood in the same manner.

The roots 'gu', 'ghu', 'ku', and 'u' occur in the sense of making a sound. 'Gavati' (sounds/speaks), 'ghavati', 'kavati', 'avati'.

The roots 'khu', 'ru', and 'ku' occur in the sense of making a sound. 'Khoti' (sounds/speaks), 'roti', 'koti'.

The roots 'cu', 'ju', 'pu', 'plu', 'gā', and 'se' occur in the sense of movement (gati). 'Cavati' (shifts/passes away), 'javati' (is swift), 'pavati' (runs), 'plavati' (floats), 'gāti' (moves), 'seti' (moves). 'Cavana' (shifting), 'cuti' (death/shifting).
209:
The roots 'khe', 'je', and 'se' occur in the sense of exhaustion. 'Khāyati', 'jāyati', and 'sāyati' mean reaching exhaustion.

In this context, one might ask: "Venerable Sir, does not the word 'khāyati' mean 'to eat' or 'to be apparent'? Similarly, does not 'jāyati' mean 'to arise', and 'sāyati' mean 'to taste'? This being so, why is the meaning stated in this way here?" It is true, but because roots have multiple meanings, such a meaning can be stated. For example, in the passage, "This man of little learning grows (jīrati) like an ox," the word 'jīrati' does not mean reaching old age, but only means growing; in the same way, it should be understood here.

The roots 'gu', 'ghu', 'ku', and 'u' occur in the sense of making a sound. There are 'gavati', 'ghavati', 'kavati', and 'avati'.

The roots 'khu', 'ru', and 'ku' occur in the sense of making a sound. There are 'khoti', 'roti', and 'koti'.

The roots 'cu', 'ju', 'pu', 'plu', 'gā', and 'se' occur in the sense of movement. There are 'cavati', 'javati', 'pavati', 'plavati', 'gāti', and 'seti'. 'Cavanaṃ', 'cuti' (shifting/passing away). 'Javanaṃ', 'javo' (swiftness). 'Pavanaṃ', 'plavanaṃ' (floating). 'Gānaṃ' (movement). 'Setu' (bridge). 'Poto' (boat). 'Plavo' (boat).

In this context, 'gānaṃ' means movement. 'Poto' is so called because one runs (moves) on water by means of this boat. Similarly, 'plavo' is so called because it floats and does not sink. Indeed, in the Jātaka Pali, it is seen: "Like one whose boat is broken (bhinnaplavo) in the midst of the ocean." 'Nāvā', 'poto', 'plavo', 'jalayānaṃ', and 'taraṇaṃ' are names for a boat.

The roots 'dhe' and 'the' occur in the senses of making a sound and collection. 'Dhāyati', 'thāyati'. In the bhāva-sādhana, there are 'dhiyati' and 'thiyati'. 'Itthī', 'thī' (woman).

The roots 'de' and 'te' occur in the sense of protection. 'Dāyati', 'dayā' (protection/compassion), 'tāṇaṃ' (refuge).

The roots 'rā' and 'lā' occur in the sense of taking. 'Rāti', 'lāti'.

The roots 'ati' and 'adi' occur in the sense of binding. 'Antati', 'andati'. 'Antaṃ' (intestine), 'andu' (shackle or binding).
210:
The roots juta, subha, and ruca occur in the sense of shining. Examples: jotati, sobhati, rocati, virocati.

The roots aka and aga occur in the sense of crooked movement. Examples: akati, agati.

The roots nātha and nādha occur in the senses of requesting, oppressing, mastery, and wishing. Examples: nāthati, nādhati.

The roots sala, hula, and cala occur in the sense of trembling. Examples: salati, hulati, calati. Kusalaṃ (wholesome).

In this context, it is called kusalaṃ because it causes contemptible, evil states to tremble; this derivation should be understood in the sense of the causal agent (hetukattu). Therefore, in the Atthasālinī commentary, the meaning is stated in the sense of the causal agent: "They are called kusalā because they cause contemptible, evil states to tremble, to shake, to quiver, and they destroy them." This is the derivation of the word kusala by way of the root sala. The derivation of the word kusala can also occur by way of other roots. Thus, other derivations are also shown in the Atthasālinī.

How? "They are called kusā (unwholesome) because they lie (exist) in a contemptible manner; they are called kusalā because they cut (lunanti) those kusa known as unwholesome states. Or, wisdom is called kusa because it makes contemptible unwholesome states thin (attenuates them); they are called kusalā because they should be taken (lātabbā) or developed by that kusa (wisdom). Or, just as kusa grass cuts the part of the hand that holds it on both sides, so too these [wholesome states], by their nature of having arisen or not yet arisen, cut the side of defilements on both parts (past and future); therefore, they are called kusalā because they cut like kusa grass." Thus, other derivations are also shown.

In that [commentary] context, the designation was made as "kusalā" in the masculine plural, corresponding to the gender and number of the word "dhammā." However, here, we have designated it as "kusalaṃ" in the neuter singular by way of a general designation. Indeed, the word kusala expressing merit (puñña) and the word kusala expressing health (ārogya) are invariably of the neuter gender. When expressing other meanings (faultlessness or skillfulness), however, it can be of all three genders, for example: kusalo phasso, kusalā vedanā, kusalaṃ cittaṃ.
211:
The word kusala should be understood as having reached completion in this Bhūvādi group by way of the roots lā and sala. Thus, the roots occurring collectively in the Bhūvādi group are finished.

In this way—
The group of roots beginning with bhū, together with the concise summary (uddesa) and the detailed explanation (niddesa), has been appropriately analyzed by me both in detail and in brief.

The words in this Bhūvādi group have been shown individually, associated with prefixes (upasagga) and particles (nipāta) which are endowed with various meanings.

Along with the Pali examples and so forth, the forms ending in tyādi suffixes and the forms ending in syādi suffixes have been shown in every manner.

The similarity of words and their dissimilarity, as well as the determination of meaning along with objections (codanā) and resolutions (parihāra), have been shown.

The extraction of meaning, the stating of names, the mixing of the three genders, and the specific words in the genders of the things signified (abhidheyyaka-liṅga) have been shown.

The collection of various words and the collection of many words have also been shown. The well-analyzed and clear conventional terms (rūḷhī-sadda) and so forth have also been shown.

Pronouns (sabbanāma) and words similar to pronouns have been appropriately shown for the purpose of connecting them with other words.

For the sake of the proficiency of the wise in the Pitakas, all these forms ending in tumaṃ suffixes and forms ending in tvā and other suffixes have been explained.

Those who well understand this division in the Saddanīti treatise will, in the teaching of the Sage, be free from doubt in all meanings and remain undaunted like lion-kings.
212:
I, who speak for the sake of the proper growth of wisdom in men in the teaching of the Self-become One (the Buddha), the supreme among manifest beings—attend to that Bhūvādi-kaṇḍa which has been spoken by me in the Saddanīti treatise, O you who desire your own welfare.

## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the sake of the proficiency of the wise in the linguistic paths of the three Pitakas along with the ninefold commentaries, the Sixteenth Chapter named the Bhūvādi Group, adorned with fifteen sections, is completed.

## 17. The Six [Groups] starting with Rudhādi

## The Rudhādi Group

Henceforth, I shall speak of the groups starting with Rudhādi in order, for the benefit of the Dispensation, among the sixfold groups.

The root rudhi occurs in the sense of obstructing. The root rudhi has its function in the sense of obstruction (āvaraṇa). Here, "obstruction" means closing, forbidding, blocking, or not giving for the purpose of taking; all this is applicable. The forms are rundhati, rundhiti, rundhīti, rundheti, avarundheti. In the passive voice: "Maggo purisena rundhiyati" (The path is obstructed by the man). There are also nouns: rodho, orodho, virodho, paṭivirodho, viruddhā, paṭiviruddhā, pariruddhā. There are also forms like rundhituṃ, parirundhituṃ, rundhitvā, parirundhitvā.

Among those words, "rodho" means a prison (or a jailer). He is called "rodho" because he forbids the movement of beings with cruel deeds who have been put into prison. "Orodho" means the king's harem (the palace women). Those harem women are called "rodho" because they are obstructed and prevented from moving about as they wish, not being given [freedom].
